indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B3.1.1.1: Demonstrate understanding of a variety of songs
indicator.objective: Talk about the benefits of songs

skills.description: Recognise familiar song types and their moral lessons.
Explain in simple words the benefits of singing songs.
Sing a familiar song rhythmically with claps, gestures or dance.
Link the benefits of a song to a real-life situation.

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 questions at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4.
misconceptions: Songs are only for entertainment, not for learning.
Only patriotic songs have benefits.
Any song is suitable for school.
Singing well is the same as understanding the song's message.

questions.stem: Which of these is a song often sung at school assembly in Ghana?
hints: Think of a song that shows respect for the country.
It is sung when pupils stand at assembly.
questions.explanation: The National Anthem is a patriotic song sung at school assembly and national events.
questions.misconception: Songs are only for entertainment, not for learning.

questions.stem: Which song can help pupils learn to love their country?
hints: Patriotic means showing love for your country.
Think of songs about Ghana.
questions.explanation: A patriotic song teaches love and respect for the country.
questions.misconception: Only patriotic songs have benefits.

questions.stem: A song that teaches good behaviour is mainly a song with...
hints: A moral lesson teaches right and wrong.
Good behaviour is a lesson.
questions.explanation: A song with a moral lesson teaches pupils good behaviour and values.
questions.misconception: Any song is suitable for school.

questions.stem: Which is the best reason a teacher may use a song in class?
options: to help pupils remember a lesson
hints: Songs can help memory.
Think about learning, not play only.
questions.explanation: Songs can help pupils remember words and lessons more easily.
questions.misconception: Songs are only for entertainment, not for learning.

questions.stem: Two songs are sung at a school event. One is a noisy play song, and one is the National Anthem. Which is more suitable for showing respect at assembly?
hints: Assembly is a formal school event.
Respect is shown with a serious song.
questions.explanation: The National Anthem is suitable for assembly because it is formal and shows respect.
questions.misconception: Any song is suitable for school.

questions.stem: Why do people often sing together at a festival?
hints: Festivals are happy events.
Singing together can bring people together.
questions.explanation: Singing together at a festival helps people share joy and feel united.
questions.misconception: Songs are only for entertainment, not for learning.

questions.stem: What can pupils learn from a song with a moral lesson?
hints: Moral means right behaviour.
The song teaches something good.
questions.explanation: A song with a moral lesson teaches good behaviour and values.
questions.misconception: Songs are only for entertainment, not for learning.

questions.stem: Which benefit of singing is shown when pupils remember words more easily?
hints: Remembering is about memory.
Songs can make words stick in the mind.
questions.explanation: Singing can help memory because the tune and rhythm make words easier to remember.
questions.misconception: Songs are only for entertainment, not for learning.

questions.stem: A class sings a song about washing hands. What is one benefit of this song?
options: It teaches pupils to avoid water
It helps pupils remember healthy habits
hints: The song is about health.
Songs can help remember steps.
questions.explanation: The song helps pupils remember healthy habits such as washing hands.
questions.misconception: Songs are only for entertainment, not for learning.

questions.stem: Why can a song help a shy pupil join a class activity?
options: Singing together can make the pupil feel part of the group
hints: Shy pupils may feel safer in a group.
Singing together is a shared activity.
questions.explanation: Singing together can help a shy pupil feel included and part of the group.
questions.misconception: Songs are only for entertainment, not for learning.

questions.stem: A school wants pupils to remember a safety rule. Which is the best reason to choose a short song for this?
options: Songs can make words easier to remember
Songs are only for break time
hints: The aim is to remember a rule.
A short song is easy to repeat.
questions.explanation: A short song can make the safety rule easier to remember because pupils can repeat it.
questions.misconception: Songs are only for entertainment, not for learning.

questions.stem: Your class is welcoming a new pupil. Which song is best to help everyone feel happy together?
hints: The new pupil should feel welcome.
Choose a happy and friendly song.
questions.explanation: A friendly welcome song helps the new pupil feel happy and included.
questions.misconception: Any song is suitable for school.

questions.stem: At a school festival, pupils will sing about keeping the compound clean. What benefit should the teacher mention?
hints: The song is about cleanliness.
The benefit should match the song's message.
questions.explanation: The song helps pupils remember to keep the compound clean.
questions.misconception: Songs are only for entertainment, not for learning.

questions.stem: Two classes sing at assembly. Class A sings a song about honesty with clear words. Class B sings a noisy song with words that do not match the value. Which song better supports the value of honesty?
hints: The words of the song should match the value.
Clear words help pupils understand the lesson.
questions.explanation: Class A's song better supports honesty because its clear words match the value being taught.
questions.misconception: Any song is suitable for school.

questions.stem: You want your group to remember the steps for washing hands. Which activity best uses a song?
hints: Choose an activity that uses singing.
The song should match handwashing.
questions.explanation: A short handwashing song helps the group remember the steps.
questions.misconception: Songs are only for entertainment, not for learning.

questions.stem: Which of these is a folk song?
options: A traditional song from the community
hints: Folk songs come from the community.
They are traditional songs.
questions.explanation: A folk song is a traditional song from the community.
questions.misconception: Only patriotic songs have benefits.

questions.stem: Why is it good to discuss the moral lesson of a song after singing it?
options: So pupils can forget the words
So pupils can understand the good behaviour it teaches
So pupils can make the song longer
hints: A moral lesson is about good behaviour.
Discussion helps understanding.
questions.explanation: Discussing the moral lesson helps pupils understand the good behaviour the song teaches.
questions.misconception: Singing well is the same as understanding the song's message.

questions.stem: A teacher wants pupils to feel happy while learning a new topic. Which is the best first step?
hints: The teacher wants pupils to feel happy.
A song can make learning enjoyable.
questions.explanation: Choosing a suitable learning song can make pupils feel happy and ready to learn.
questions.misconception: Songs are only for entertainment, not for learning.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B3.1.10.1: Plan and present information and ideas for a variety of purposes
indicator.objective: Present ideas logically

skills.description: Identify important people in the community and what makes them important.
Arrange ideas in a logical order for a presentation.
Deliver a short presentation keeping ideas in a sensible order.
Give clear reasons for their choices or ideas during a presentation.
Identify if a presentation's ideas are presented in a logical order and suggest a simple improvement.

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 questions at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4.
misconceptions: Any order of speaking is fine; the listener will understand.
You don't need to explain why someone or something is important.
A presentation is just saying random facts about a topic.
The end of a presentation does not need to connect to the beginning.

questions.stem: Who is an important person in the community who helps sick people?
hints: This person works in a hospital or clinic.
They take care of patients.
questions.explanation: A nurse is an important person in the community because they help sick people get better.
questions.misconception: You don't need to explain why someone or something is important.

questions.stem: Why is a teacher important in the community?
hints: Teachers work in schools.
They help pupils gain knowledge.
questions.explanation: A teacher is important because they help children learn and prepare for the future.
questions.misconception: A presentation is just saying random facts about a topic.

questions.stem: A pupil says: 'My father is important because he is a police officer and he keeps our community safe.' Why is this a good reason?
options: Because it explains what the father does to help the community.
hints: A good reason tells what the person does.
Keeping the community safe is a service.
questions.explanation: It is a good reason because it explains the father's job and how it helps the community stay safe.
questions.misconception: You don't need to explain why someone or something is important.

questions.stem: Which sentence is the best beginning for a presentation about 'My Father'?
hints: The beginning should introduce the person and what they do.
It should tell the audience who the person is.
questions.explanation: 'My father is a farmer' is a good beginning because it introduces the person and his job.
questions.misconception: The end of a presentation does not need to connect to the beginning.

questions.stem: Put these presentation points in a logical order: (1) Why my father is important, (2) Who my father is, (3) What my father does.
hints: First, say who the person is.
Then say what they do, and finally why they are important.
questions.explanation: The logical order is: who my father is (2), what he does (3), and why he is important (1).
questions.misconception: Any order of speaking is fine; the listener will understand.

questions.stem: Which is the best order for a presentation about 'My Friend'?
options: First, say the friend's name. Next, say what the friend likes. Last, say why the friend is important to you.
First, say why the friend is important. Next, say the friend's name. Last, say what the friend likes.
First, say what the friend likes. Next, say why the friend is important. Last, say the friend's name.
First, say the friend's name. Next, say why the friend is important. Last, say what the friend likes.
hints: Start by introducing the friend.
End with why the friend is special.
questions.explanation: Introducing the friend first, then their likes, and ending with why they are important is logical.
questions.misconception: A presentation is just saying random facts about a topic.

questions.stem: A pupil says: 'I want to be a doctor. I like helping people. I want to be important for helping sick people.' Is this in a logical order?
options: Yes, because it starts with what they want to be and ends with why.
No, because it starts with the reason.
No, because it has too many sentences.
hints: The order starts with the job, then the reason, then the importance.
This is a logical flow.
questions.explanation: It is logical because it goes from the job (doctor) to the reason (likes helping) to the importance (helping sick people).
questions.misconception: The end of a presentation does not need to connect to the beginning.

questions.stem: A pupil says: 'I want to be a teacher because I want to help children learn.' What is the reason given?
hints: The reason comes after 'because'.
It tells why the pupil wants to be a teacher.
questions.explanation: The reason is 'to help children learn' because it comes after 'because'.
questions.misconception: You don't need to explain why someone or something is important.

questions.stem: Why is a farmer important? Which is the best reason?
options: Farmers grow food that we eat.
hints: The reason should explain how farmers help the community.
They provide food.
questions.explanation: Farmers are important because they grow food that we eat, which is a clear reason.
questions.misconception: A presentation is just saying random facts about a topic.

questions.stem: A pupil presents: 'My mother is important. She is a nurse. She helps sick people.' Is this in a logical order?
options: Yes, because it moves from who she is to what she does to why she is important.
No, because it starts with why she is important.
No, because it is too short.
Yes, because it uses short sentences.
hints: Check the order: who, what, why.
This presentation follows that order.
questions.explanation: It is logical because it presents the person, her job, and why she is important in that order.
questions.misconception: Any order of speaking is fine; the listener will understand.

questions.stem: A pupil presents: 'I want to help people. My name is Kofi. I want to be a doctor.' What is the best improvement?
options: Start with 'My name is Kofi', then say what he wants to be, then why.
Remove the part about helping people.
hints: The order should be: who, what, why.
The first sentence should introduce the person.
questions.explanation: The best improvement is to start with the name, then say the ambition, then the reason.
questions.misconception: The end of a presentation does not need to connect to the beginning.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B3.1.10.1: Plan and present information and ideas for a variety of purposes
indicator.objective: Use appropriate verbal and non-verbal cues to convey meaning while speaking, e.g. smiling, using gestures, etc

skills.description: Recognise non-verbal cues such as facial expression, eye contact, posture, nodding, smiling and crossed arms.
Match specific cues to their meanings.
Demonstrate appropriate posture, eye contact and gestures while giving a short talk.
Adjust verbal and non-verbal cues depending on who they are talking to.
Observe a peer's presentation and give simple feedback on the verbal and non-verbal cues used.
Explain why non-verbal cues are important when speaking to an audience.

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 questions at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4.
misconceptions: Only the words you say matter when presenting.
Smiling all the time is the best way to present.
Looking at the floor is fine as long as you speak loudly.
Crossed arms always mean you are cold.
Gestures should be big and fast to keep attention.

questions.stem: Which of these is a non-verbal cue?
hints: Non-verbal means without words.
Smiling uses the face, not words.
questions.explanation: Smiling is a non-verbal cue because it communicates without using words.
questions.misconception: Only the words you say matter when presenting.

questions.stem: What does nodding your head usually mean?
hints: Nodding is moving your head up and down.
It often shows you are listening and agree.
questions.explanation: Nodding the head up and down usually means you agree or are listening.
questions.misconception: Only the words you say matter when presenting.

questions.stem: A pupil stands up straight and looks at the audience while speaking. Which non-verbal cues is the pupil using?
hints: Standing straight is posture.
Looking at the audience is eye contact.
questions.explanation: The pupil is using good posture (standing straight) and eye contact (looking at the audience).
questions.misconception: Looking at the floor is fine as long as you speak loudly.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a non-verbal cue?
hints: Non-verbal means without words.
Saying words is verbal.
questions.explanation: Saying 'good morning' uses words, so it is a verbal cue, not non-verbal.
questions.misconception: Only the words you say matter when presenting.

questions.stem: What does a smile usually show?
hints: A smile is when your mouth turns up.
It usually shows you are happy.
questions.explanation: A smile usually shows happiness or approval.
questions.misconception: Smiling all the time is the best way to present.

questions.stem: What does crossing your arms often show?
hints: Crossing arms can be a sign of anger or disagreement.
Sometimes it just means you are cold.
questions.explanation: Crossing arms often shows anger or disagreement, but it can also mean you are cold. In presentations, it may send a negative message.
questions.misconception: Crossed arms always mean you are cold.

questions.stem: A pupil looks at the floor while speaking. What might this cue mean?
hints: Looking down often shows you are not confident.
It can mean you are shy or nervous.
questions.explanation: Looking at the floor may show shyness or nervousness, and it can make it hard for the audience to hear you.
questions.misconception: Looking at the floor is fine as long as you speak loudly.

questions.stem: Which pair correctly matches a non-verbal cue to its meaning?
hints: Nodding your head up and down usually means you agree.
Think about what each cue shows.
questions.explanation: Nodding is a non-verbal cue that shows agreement.
questions.misconception: Gestures should be big and fast to keep attention.

questions.stem: When speaking to a teacher, which non-verbal cue is most appropriate?
options: Standing up straight and making eye contact
hints: Show respect to the teacher.
Good posture and eye contact show respect.
questions.explanation: Standing straight and making eye contact shows respect when speaking to a teacher.
questions.misconception: Looking at the floor is fine as long as you speak loudly.

questions.stem: When telling a funny story to your friends, which cue is best?
hints: A funny story should make people laugh.
A smile and lively gestures fit the mood.
questions.explanation: A smile and lively gestures match the happy mood of a funny story.
questions.misconception: Only the words you say matter when presenting.

questions.stem: You are presenting to the whole school at assembly. How should your cues be different from when you are talking to a friend?
options: You should be louder and more formal, with good posture.
You should whisper and look down.
You should use big, wild gestures and shout.
You should turn your back to the audience.
hints: Assembly is a formal occasion.
You need to speak clearly and stand properly.
questions.explanation: At assembly, you need to project your voice and use formal, respectful cues, unlike a casual chat with a friend.
questions.misconception: Smiling all the time is the best way to present.

questions.stem: Why are non-verbal cues important when speaking?
options: They help the audience understand your message better.
hints: Non-verbal cues like smiling and gestures help show what you mean.
They add meaning to your words.
questions.explanation: Non-verbal cues help the audience understand your feelings and message better.
questions.misconception: Only the words you say matter when presenting.

questions.stem: Which sentence best explains why you should make eye contact when speaking?
options: It shows you are confident and interested in the audience.
It helps you read your notes.
hints: Eye contact connects you with the audience.
It shows you are paying attention to them.
questions.explanation: Making eye contact shows confidence and helps the audience feel involved.
questions.misconception: Looking at the floor is fine as long as you speak loudly.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B3.1.2.1: Appreciate a variety of literary pieces
indicator.objective: Compose short rhymes and tongue-twisters and recite them

skills.description: Recognise and pick out words that rhyme in a given rhyme or tongue-twister.
Recite a short rhyme or tongue-twister with clear words and suitable actions/gestures.
Make a short parallel rhyme by changing words while keeping the rhyme pattern.
Create a short tongue-twister using repeated initial sounds.
Recite a composed rhyme in a group with rhythm, clarity and actions.

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 questions at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4.
misconceptions: Words that start with the same letter always rhyme.
A rhyme must be funny to be good.
Tongue-twisters are just nonsense; they have no pattern.
Any two lines can be a rhyme even if the ending sounds do not match.
Reciting means shouting the words.

questions.stem: Which word rhymes with 'cat'?
hints: Say both words aloud. Do they end with the same sound?
The ending sound should be the same.
questions.explanation: Cat and hat both end with the -at sound, so they rhyme.
questions.misconception: Words that start with the same letter always rhyme.

questions.stem: Which pair of words rhymes?
hints: Say each pair aloud.
The ending sounds must match.
questions.explanation: Sun and fun both end with the -un sound.
questions.misconception: Any two lines can be a rhyme even if the ending sounds do not match.

questions.stem: Which word rhymes with 'boy'?
hints: Say the word 'boy' and listen to the ending sound.
The ending sound is -oy.
questions.explanation: Boy and toy both end with the -oy sound.
questions.misconception: Words that start with the same letter always rhyme.

questions.stem: Which word does NOT rhyme with 'make'?
hints: Say each word after 'make'.
Three of the words end with the -ake sound.
questions.explanation: Cake, lake and take all end with -ake. Book ends with a different sound.
questions.misconception: Words that start with the same letter always rhyme.

questions.stem: In the rhyme 'Twinkle, twinkle, little star, / How I wonder what you are,' which word rhymes with 'star'?
hints: Read the last word of each line aloud.
The rhyming words are at the ends of the lines.
questions.explanation: Star and are both end with the -ar sound in this rhyme.
questions.misconception: Any two lines can be a rhyme even if the ending sounds do not match.

questions.stem: Complete the rhyme: 'The cat sat on the ___.'
hints: The word must rhyme with 'cat'.
Cat and mat have the same ending sound.
questions.explanation: The cat sat on the mat. Cat and mat rhyme with the -at sound.
questions.misconception: Any two lines can be a rhyme even if the ending sounds do not match.

questions.stem: Complete the rhyme: 'I saw a dog, sitting on a ___.'
hints: The word must rhyme with 'dog'.
Dog and log share the -og sound.
questions.explanation: I saw a dog, sitting on a log. Dog and log rhyme with the -og sound.
questions.misconception: Any two lines can be a rhyme even if the ending sounds do not match.

questions.stem: Which word completes the rhyme? 'The little boy went to the shop, / He wanted to buy a spinning ___.'
hints: Find the word that rhymes with 'shop'.
Shop and top both end with the -op sound.
questions.explanation: Shop and top rhyme, so 'spinning top' completes the rhyme.
questions.misconception: Any two lines can be a rhyme even if the ending sounds do not match.

questions.stem: Change the rhyme 'The cat sat on the mat' to make a new rhyme about a dog. Which is the best new rhyme?
options: The dog sat on the log.
The dog ran to the cat.
hints: The new rhyme must keep the same pattern.
The last word of each line should rhyme.
questions.explanation: 'The dog sat on the log' follows the same pattern and rhymes (dog/log), so it is a parallel rhyme.
questions.misconception: Any two lines can be a rhyme even if the ending sounds do not match.

questions.stem: Which of these is a tongue-twister?
options: 'She sells sea shells by the sea shore.'
hints: A tongue-twister repeats the same sound many times.
Listen for the repeated /s/ sound.
questions.explanation: 'She sells sea shells' repeats the /s/ and /sh/ sounds, making it a tongue-twister.
questions.misconception: Tongue-twisters are just nonsense; they have no pattern.

questions.stem: A tongue-twister uses words that...
hints: Think of 'She sells sea shells'.
The /s/ sound is repeated.
questions.explanation: A tongue-twister repeats the same sound, usually at the start of words, to make it tricky to say.
questions.misconception: Tongue-twisters are just nonsense; they have no pattern.

questions.stem: Which is the best tongue-twister using the /s/ sound?
hints: Look for words that start with /s/.
Count how many /s/ words are in each sentence.
questions.explanation: 'Silly Sam saw six snakes' repeats the /s/ sound in almost every word, making it a good tongue-twister.
questions.misconception: Tongue-twisters are just nonsense; they have no pattern.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B3.1.4.1: Respond to stories
indicator.objective: Respond to and ask questions based on stories heard

skills.description: Name characters, setting and main events in a story heard.
Form simple, relevant questions about a story.
Answer factual and simple inferential questions about a story heard.
Say which part of the story they liked or disliked and give a simple reason.
Summarise the main events in the correct order.

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 questions at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4.
misconceptions: Any question is fine even if it is not about the story.
Only the teacher can ask questions.
A story has only one correct feeling about it.
Retelling means saying every word again.

questions.stem: Who is the main character in the story?
hints: The main character is the person the story is mostly about.
Who went to the market?
questions.explanation: Ama is the main character because the story follows her actions from start to finish.
questions.misconception: Only the teacher can ask questions.

questions.stem: Where did Ama see the goat?
options: On her way to the market
hints: Ama had not reached the market yet.
The story says 'on her way'.
questions.explanation: The story says Ama saw the goat on her way to the market.
questions.misconception: A story has only one correct feeling about it.

questions.stem: What did Ama see on her way to the market?
hints: It was an animal.
It was caught in a fence.
questions.explanation: The story says Ama saw a small goat caught in a fence.
questions.misconception: Retelling means saying every word again.

questions.stem: What happened first in the story?
options: Ama helped the goat get free
Grandmother sent Ama to the market
hints: Look for the event that started everything.
Who sent Ama out?
questions.explanation: The story begins with Grandmother sending Ama to the market.
questions.misconception: Retelling means saying every word again.

questions.stem: Which sentence gives the best reason for liking this story?
options: I liked it because Ama helped a goat in need.
I liked it because Ama was late to the market.
I liked it because Grandmother was angry.
I liked it because the goat ran away.
hints: Think about what makes the story happy.
Ama did something kind.
questions.explanation: The story is likable because Ama showed kindness by helping the goat.
questions.misconception: A story has only one correct feeling about it.

questions.stem: What did Grandmother ask Ama when she got home?
options: What she bought at the market
Who she met on the way
hints: Grandmother noticed Ama came home late.
She wanted to know the reason.
questions.explanation: Grandmother asked Ama why she was late because Ama did not get to the market on time.
questions.misconception: Any question is fine even if it is not about the story.

questions.stem: Which is the best question to ask about the story?
options: How many tomatoes did Ama buy?
hints: The question must be answered by the story.
The story says the goat was crying.
questions.explanation: The goat was crying because it was caught in a fence, so 'Why was the goat crying?' is a good question about the story.
questions.misconception: Any question is fine even if it is not about the story.

questions.stem: Why was the goat crying?
options: It was caught in a fence
hints: The goat could not move.
Something was holding the goat.
questions.explanation: The story says the goat was caught in a fence, so it was crying for help.
questions.misconception: Retelling means saying every word again.

questions.stem: How did Ama help the goat?
options: She helped it get free from the fence
hints: The goat was stuck.
Ama stopped and did something.
questions.explanation: Ama stopped and helped the goat get free from the fence.
questions.misconception: Retelling means saying every word again.

questions.stem: Which part of the story shows that Ama is kind?
options: When she was late to the market
When she helped the goat get free
When she went to buy tomatoes
When she told Grandmother the story
hints: Kindness means helping others.
Ama stopped to help an animal in trouble.
questions.explanation: Ama showed kindness by stopping to help the goat even though she was in a hurry.
questions.misconception: A story has only one correct feeling about it.

questions.stem: Put these events in the correct order: (1) Ama helped the goat get free, (2) Grandmother sent Ama to the market, (3) Ama told Grandmother what happened, (4) Ama saw a goat caught in a fence.
hints: Start with Grandmother sending Ama.
Ama saw the goat before she helped it.
questions.explanation: The correct order is: Grandmother sent Ama (2), Ama saw the goat (4), Ama helped the goat (1), Ama told Grandmother (3).
questions.misconception: Retelling means saying every word again.

questions.stem: What happened at the end of the story?
options: Grandmother smiled and said Ama did the right thing
hints: Think about Grandmother's reaction.
She was not angry with Ama.
questions.explanation: At the end, Grandmother smiled and told Ama she did the right thing.
questions.misconception: Retelling means saying every word again.

questions.stem: Why was Grandmother happy with Ama?
options: Because Ama helped a goat in need
hints: Grandmother heard the whole story.
Ama did something kind.
questions.explanation: Grandmother was happy because Ama stopped to help a goat that was in trouble.
questions.misconception: A story has only one correct feeling about it.

questions.stem: Do you think Ama did the right thing? Why?
options: Yes, because helping others is good.
No, because the goat was not hers.
hints: Helping someone in need is usually good.
Grandmother said Ama did the right thing.
questions.explanation: Ama did the right thing because she helped a goat in need, and Grandmother agreed.
questions.misconception: A story has only one correct feeling about it.

questions.stem: Ama was late to the market, but she was happy. Explain why.
options: Because she helped someone in need
Because she played on the way
hints: Ama's happiness was not about the market.
She did something good for the goat.
questions.explanation: Ama was happy because she helped a goat in need, even though it made her late.
questions.misconception: A story has only one correct feeling about it.

questions.stem: Two pupils give their opinions about Ama. Pupil A says: 'Ama was kind because she helped the goat.' Pupil B says: 'Ama was wrong because she made her grandmother wait.' Whose opinion is better supported by the story?
options: Pupil A, because the story shows Ama helping the goat and Grandmother praising her
Pupil B, because Ama was late
Neither opinion is supported by the story
hints: What did Grandmother say at the end?
The story shows kindness being rewarded.
questions.explanation: Pupil A's opinion is better supported because the story shows Ama helping the goat and Grandmother praising her for it.
questions.misconception: A story has only one correct feeling about it.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B3.1.4.1: Respond to stories
indicator.objective: Tell parallel stories

skills.description: Recognise the beginning, middle and ending of a story heard.
Make a new story that follows the same pattern but changes characters, setting or minor details.
Narrate the parallel story in a clear sequence with suitable expression.
Say one way the parallel story is like the original and one way it is different.

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 questions at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4.
misconceptions: A parallel story must copy the original exactly.
Any new story is a parallel story.
The order of events does not matter.
Only the characters need to change.

questions.stem: What happens at the beginning of the story?
options: Grandmother sends Ama to the market
The goat runs to its mother
hints: The beginning is where the story starts.
Someone is given a task.
questions.explanation: The story begins with Grandmother sending Ama to the market to buy tomatoes.
questions.misconception: The order of events does not matter.

questions.stem: What happens in the middle of the story?
options: Grandmother sends Ama to the market
Grandmother says 'You did the right thing'
Ama helps a goat caught in a fence
hints: The middle is where the main action happens.
Ama meets an animal in trouble.
questions.explanation: In the middle, Ama sees a goat caught in a fence and helps it get free.
questions.misconception: The order of events does not matter.

questions.stem: What happens at the end of the story?
hints: The ending is how the story finishes.
Grandmother is happy with Ama.
questions.explanation: At the end, Grandmother smiles and tells Ama she did the right thing.
questions.misconception: The order of events does not matter.

questions.stem: Which event belongs to the middle of the story?
options: Grandmother sends Ama to the market
Ama frees the goat from the fence
hints: The middle is the main action.
Ama is on her way to the market.
questions.explanation: Ama freeing the goat from the fence is the main action in the middle of the story.
questions.misconception: The order of events does not matter.

questions.stem: Which part of the story tells us how the story finishes?
options: Ama's grandmother sent her to the market
Ama saw a goat caught in a fence
Grandmother smiled and said Ama did the right thing
Ama helped the goat get free
hints: Look for the last thing that happens.
Grandmother gives her response.
questions.explanation: Grandmother smiling and praising Ama is the ending of the story.
questions.misconception: The order of events does not matter.

questions.stem: A parallel story follows the same pattern but changes some details. Which change makes a good parallel story?
options: Change the characters and setting but keep the same pattern
Copy the story word for word
Tell a story about something else entirely
hints: Parallel means following the same pattern.
The main events stay similar but the details change.
questions.explanation: A parallel story keeps the same pattern of events but changes characters, setting or minor details.
questions.misconception: Any new story is a parallel story.

questions.stem: Which is the best parallel story for 'The Lost Goat'?
options: A story about a boy who helps a lost chicken on his way to school, then his mother praises him
A story about a girl who goes to the market and buys tomatoes
A story about a goat that runs away and never returns
A story about Grandmother going to the market
hints: The parallel story must follow the same pattern: someone is sent on an errand, helps an animal, is late, and is praised.
The characters can change but the events must match.
questions.explanation: The story about the boy follows the same pattern: sent on an errand, sees an animal in trouble, helps it, is late, and is praised.
questions.misconception: Any new story is a parallel story.

questions.stem: Kofi is sent to the market to buy fish. On the way, he sees a small chicken caught under a basket. He helps it get free. He is late but his mother says, 'You did the right thing.' Which story is this?
options: A story that is not related at all
hints: Compare this story to The Lost Goat.
Same pattern, different details.
questions.explanation: This is a parallel story because it follows the same pattern as The Lost Goat but with different characters and details.
questions.misconception: Any new story is a parallel story.

questions.stem: Which detail should you change to make a parallel story for The Lost Goat?
options: Change Ama's name and the animal she helps
Change the lesson at the end
hints: The pattern must stay the same.
Only the details should change.
questions.explanation: In a parallel story, you change the characters and some details but keep the same pattern and lesson.
questions.misconception: Only the characters need to change.

questions.stem: A pupil writes: 'One morning, Kwame's father sent him to the farm. On the way, Kwame saw a dog caught in a hole. He helped the dog get out. Kwame was late but his father praised him.' Which part of this parallel story is different from The Lost Goat?
options: The person who sent the child
The person and the animal both changed
hints: Look at who is in the story.
Compare the characters in both stories.
questions.explanation: Both the main character (Kwame instead of Ama) and the animal (dog instead of goat) have changed, making it a parallel story.
questions.misconception: Only the characters need to change.

questions.stem: Which of these would NOT be a good parallel story for The Lost Goat?
options: A girl who helps a kitten and is praised by her father
A boy who helps a calf and is praised by his mother
A story about a goat that runs away and never comes back
A girl who helps a duckling and is praised by her aunt
hints: A parallel story must have the same pattern of kindness being rewarded.
One story does not have the same pattern.
questions.explanation: A story about a goat that runs away and never comes back does not follow the pattern of helping an animal and being praised, so it is not a good parallel story.
questions.misconception: Any new story is a parallel story.

questions.stem: How is the parallel story about Kofi like The Lost Goat?
options: Both are about a child helping an animal
Both happen at the same place
Both have the same ending words
hints: Look at the main action in both stories.
Both children help an animal in trouble.
questions.explanation: Both stories follow the same pattern: a child helps an animal in trouble and is praised.
questions.misconception: Only the characters need to change.

questions.stem: How is the parallel story about Kofi different from The Lost Goat?
options: The child has a different name and helps a different animal
The order of events is different
hints: Look at the names and animals in each story.
The pattern stays the same but the details change.
questions.explanation: The parallel story uses a different character (Kofi instead of Ama) and a different animal (chicken instead of goat).
questions.misconception: Only the characters need to change.

questions.stem: Which of these is a difference between The Lost Goat and a parallel story about a boy who helps a chicken?
options: The boy helps a chicken, Ama helps a goat
Both stories have the same beginning pattern
hints: Look for a detail that changed.
The animals are different.
questions.explanation: The animal each child helps is different: Ama helps a goat, and the boy helps a chicken.
questions.misconception: A parallel story must copy the original exactly.

questions.stem: Pupil A says: 'The Lost Goat and the parallel story are the same because both children help an animal.' Pupil B says: 'They are different because the children have different names.' Which pupil is correct?
hints: Pupil A talks about the pattern.
Pupil B talks about the details.
questions.explanation: Both pupils are correct: the stories share the same pattern (Pupil A), but the details differ (Pupil B).
questions.misconception: Only the characters need to change.

questions.stem: Which sentence best compares The Lost Goat and a parallel story about a boy who helps a chicken?
options: They follow the same pattern but have different characters and animals.
The parallel story is not a real story.
hints: Think about what stayed the same and what changed.
The pattern is the same; the details are different.
questions.explanation: A good comparison says the stories follow the same pattern but use different characters and animals.
questions.misconception: A parallel story must copy the original exactly.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B3.1.4.1: Respond to stories
indicator.objective: Create own events to extend stories heard

skills.description: Add new events that make sense with the original story.
Keep the characters acting in ways that fit their original traits.
Put the new events in a sensible order.
Present the extended story orally or in writing.

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 questions at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4.
misconceptions: Any new event is fine even if it does not make sense.
The extension must change the original ending completely.
Characters can act in any way in the new part.
Only the teacher can add events to a story.

questions.stem: What is this story mostly about?
options: Two children walking in the rain
Two children going to the market
hints: Look at what happens at the beginning.
It rained and they had no umbrella.
questions.explanation: The story is about Ama and Kojo walking home after the rain.
questions.misconception: Only the teacher can add events to a story.

questions.stem: Who are the two children in the story?
hints: The story mentions their names in the first line.
One is a girl and one is a boy.
questions.explanation: The story names Ama and her brother, Kojo.
questions.misconception: Characters can act in any way in the new part.

questions.stem: What did Ama and Kojo do when it started to rain?
hints: They did not have an umbrella.
They found shelter.
questions.explanation: The story says they waited under a big tree until the rain stopped.
questions.misconception: Any new event is fine even if it does not make sense.

questions.stem: What happened at the end of the story?
hints: Think about the last sentence of the story.
They walked home after the rain stopped.
questions.explanation: The story ends with Ama and Kojo walking home quickly.
questions.misconception: The extension must change the original ending completely.

questions.stem: If you extend the story, what is a good next event to add after they walk home quickly?
options: They arrive home and tell their mother about the rain.
They go back to school to play.
hints: Think about what happens after children walk home.
The new event should make sense with the story.
questions.explanation: Arriving home and telling their mother is a logical next event after walking home.
questions.misconception: Any new event is fine even if it does not make sense.

questions.stem: Which of these new events makes sense to add to the story?
options: Ama and Kojo find a lost puppy on their way home.
Ama and Kojo become birds and fly away.
Ama and Kojo build a tall building.
Ama and Kojo go to the moon.
hints: The story is about everyday life.
Choose an event that could really happen.
questions.explanation: Finding a lost puppy is a logical event that fits the everyday setting of the story.
questions.misconception: Any new event is fine even if it does not make sense.

questions.stem: In the story, Ama and Kojo do not have an umbrella. If you add a new event where they find a coin, what would they likely do?
hints: They are good children.
What would a kind child do?
questions.explanation: Ama and Kojo are good children, so they would likely look for the owner of the coin.
questions.misconception: Characters can act in any way in the new part.

questions.stem: Where should you add the new event of 'Ama and Kojo arriving home'?
hints: They are walking home at the end of the original story.
Arriving home happens after walking home.
questions.explanation: Arriving home comes after they walk home, so it should be added at the end of the story.
questions.misconception: The extension must change the original ending completely.

questions.stem: Which sentence best extends the story in a logical way?
options: They got home and changed their wet clothes.
They got home and ate a bowl of stones.
They got home and sang like elephants.
They got home and flew to the sky.
hints: Their clothes are wet from the rain.
What would you do if you were caught in the rain?
questions.explanation: Changing wet clothes is a logical thing to do after walking home in the rain.
questions.misconception: Any new event is fine even if it does not make sense.

questions.stem: If you extend the story, which action fits Ama and Kojo's character?
options: They help their mother carry the water.
They refuse to greet their mother.
They steal food from the kitchen.
hints: They are well-behaved children.
Good children help at home.
questions.explanation: Helping their mother carry water fits the character of good and obedient children.
questions.misconception: Characters can act in any way in the new part.

questions.stem: What makes a good extension to a story?
options: It must make sense with what already happened.
It must be completely different from the original.
It must change the characters' names.
hints: An extension continues the story.
It should fit naturally with the original events.
questions.explanation: A good extension adds new events that make sense with the original story.
questions.misconception: The extension must change the original ending completely.

questions.stem: If you add two new events—(1) Ama helps her mother cook, and (2) they arrive home—which comes first?
options: They happen at the same time
hints: You cannot help cook before you get home.
Arriving home must happen first.
questions.explanation: You must arrive home before you can help your mother cook, so arriving home comes first.
questions.misconception: The extension must change the original ending completely.

questions.stem: Read this new event: 'The rain started again, and Ama and Kojo got wet.' Where is the BEST place to add this event?
options: Between waiting under the tree and walking home
hints: They were walking home after the rain stopped.
The new rain should happen before they reach home.
questions.explanation: The new rain happens after they leave the tree but before they arrive home, so it fits between the two events.
questions.misconception: Any new event is fine even if it does not make sense.

questions.stem: A pupil writes: 'Ama and Kojo got home. They were angry at their mother and shouted at her.' Why does this NOT fit the story?
options: Ama and Kojo are good children, so they would not shout at their mother.
It does not mention the rain.
hints: Think about how Ama and Kojo behaved in the original story.
They are polite children.
questions.explanation: This new event does not fit the characters because the original story shows them as well-behaved children.
questions.misconception: Characters can act in any way in the new part.

questions.stem: Why is it important to keep Ama and Kojo acting the same way in your extension?
options: So the story makes sense and feels real.
So the teacher will be happy.
So they can be the main characters.
hints: If a character changes completely, the story feels strange.
Consistency makes the story believable.
questions.explanation: Keeping characters consistent makes the extended story believable and easy to follow.
questions.misconception: Characters can act in any way in the new part.

questions.stem: Which is the most sensible order for these events? (1) Ama and Kojo walk home, (2) It rains heavily, (3) They wait under a tree, (4) They arrive home.
hints: The rain causes them to wait.
They walk home after the rain stops.
questions.explanation: The correct order is: it rains (2), they wait under a tree (3), they walk home (1), and they arrive home (4).
questions.misconception: The extension must change the original ending completely.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B3.1.5.1: Perform stories
indicator.objective: Dramatise and role-play stories heard and read

skills.description: Name the characters in a story heard or read and say what they do.
Assign suitable roles to pupils based on character traits and actions.
Act out a character's words and actions with suitable expression, gestures and movement.
Say what was good about a dramatisation and give one suggestion for improvement.
State the moral lesson or value shown in the dramatised story.

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 questions at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4.
misconceptions: Role-play means just reading the words aloud.
Any pupil can play any role without thinking about the character.
Only the main character matters in a drama.
A drama has no moral lesson.
Actions and gestures are not important in role-play.

questions.stem: Who are the two characters in the story?
hints: One animal is big and one is small.
The story is about a hungry animal and a clever animal.
questions.explanation: The two characters in the story are the lion and the tortoise.
questions.misconception: Only the main character matters in a drama.

questions.stem: What did the lion want to do to the tortoise?
hints: The lion was hungry.
He said, 'I will eat you!'
questions.explanation: The hungry lion wanted to eat the tortoise.
questions.misconception: Any pupil can play any role without thinking about the character.

questions.stem: What did the tortoise do to the lion?
options: Tricked the lion into a pit
hints: The tortoise said the king was in a pit.
The lion jumped in and could not get out.
questions.explanation: The tortoise tricked the lion by telling him the king was in the pit. The lion jumped in and was trapped.
questions.misconception: Role-play means just reading the words aloud.

questions.stem: Which words describe the tortoise in the story?
hints: The tortoise used his brain to escape.
He thought of a plan.
questions.explanation: The tortoise is clever and quick-thinking because he tricked the lion into the pit.
questions.misconception: Any pupil can play any role without thinking about the character.

questions.stem: Which pupil should play the lion in a role-play?
options: A pupil who can speak slowly and walk fast
A pupil who can roar loudly and act angry
A pupil who is very quiet and shy
A pupil who likes to sing
hints: The lion is hungry and angry.
What kind of voice and actions fit a lion?
questions.explanation: A pupil who can roar loudly and act angry is best for the role of the lion because the lion is a fierce, hungry character.
questions.misconception: Any pupil can play any role without thinking about the character.

questions.stem: Which pupil should play the tortoise in a role-play?
options: A pupil who can speak slowly and look calm
A pupil who is very loud
A pupil who can jump high
A pupil who likes to fight
hints: The tortoise speaks calmly and thinks before acting.
The tortoise is small and slow.
questions.explanation: The tortoise is calm and clever. A pupil who can speak slowly and look calm fits the role well.
questions.misconception: Role-play means just reading the words aloud.

questions.stem: In a role-play, the tortoise must say 'The king is down there' with a calm face. Which pupil is best for this line?
options: A pupil who can keep a straight face and speak softly
A pupil who shouts every word
A pupil who runs around the stage
hints: The tortoise is tricking the lion.
He must not show that he is lying.
questions.explanation: A pupil who can keep a straight face and speak softly fits the tortoise because the tortoise is calm and clever, not loud.
questions.misconception: Actions and gestures are not important in role-play.

questions.stem: Why should the pupil playing the lion show anger and hunger in his actions?
options: Because the lion is the biggest animal in the forest
Because the lion wants to eat the tortoise and is fierce
Because the lion likes to dance
hints: Think about what kind of animal the lion is.
The lion is looking for food.
questions.explanation: The lion shows anger and hunger because he is a fierce animal looking for food.
questions.misconception: Only the main character matters in a drama.

questions.stem: After a role-play, what is one good thing to say?
options: You spoke clearly and used good actions.
hints: Feedback should be helpful and kind.
Say something the actor did well.
questions.explanation: Saying 'You spoke clearly and used good actions' is helpful feedback because it praises what the actor did well.
questions.misconception: A drama has no moral lesson.

questions.stem: A pupil played the lion but forgot to look angry. What is the best suggestion?
options: Try to show anger with your face and voice next time.
hints: Suggestions should help the actor improve.
The lion is an angry character.
questions.explanation: A helpful suggestion is to try to show anger with your face and voice next time, because the lion is an angry character.
questions.misconception: Only the main character matters in a drama.

questions.stem: Which is a good suggestion for a pupil who speaks too softly during a role-play?
options: Speak louder so everyone can hear.
Let someone else play the part.
hints: The audience needs to hear the words.
The suggestion should fix the problem.
questions.explanation: Speaking louder helps the audience hear the actor, so it is a good suggestion.
questions.misconception: Role-play means just reading the words aloud.

questions.stem: A group performs a role-play. One pupil says: 'The tortoise was very good because he spoke calmly and used a clever face.' Another says: 'The lion was too quiet when he should have been loud.' Which feedback is better and why?
options: The first, because it gives a positive comment about the tortoise.
The second, because it gives a specific suggestion to improve the lion.
hints: Good feedback can be both praise and a suggestion.
Both comments point to something true about the performance.
questions.explanation: Both comments are helpful: one praises the tortoise, and one gives a specific suggestion for the lion. Both are useful for improving the drama.
questions.misconception: A drama has no moral lesson.

questions.stem: After a role-play, a pupil says: 'I liked the tortoise because he walked slowly and looked calm.' What part of the performance is this pupil commenting on?
options: The moral lesson of the story
The actions and expression of the tortoise
hints: Walking slowly and looking calm are actions.
The pupil is not talking about the lesson or the setting.
questions.explanation: The pupil is commenting on the actions and expression of the actor playing the tortoise.
questions.misconception: Actions and gestures are not important in role-play.

questions.stem: What is the moral lesson of the story?
options: Cleverness can help you escape danger.
hints: The tortoise used his brain to escape.
The small tortoise escaped the big lion.
questions.explanation: The moral lesson is that cleverness can help you escape danger. The tortoise used his cleverness to trick the lion.
questions.misconception: A drama has no moral lesson.

questions.stem: Which value did the tortoise show in the story?
hints: The tortoise used his brain.
He tricked the lion.
questions.explanation: The tortoise showed cleverness by tricking the lion into the pit.
questions.misconception: A drama has no moral lesson.

questions.stem: A pupil says: 'The tortoise was wrong to trick the lion. He should have said sorry.' Do you agree with this pupil? Why?
options: Yes, because the tortoise should always be polite.
No, because the tortoise was protecting himself from being eaten.
Yes, because the lion was kind.
No, because the tortoise wanted to be eaten.
hints: The lion wanted to eat the tortoise.
The tortoise was in danger.
questions.explanation: The tortoise was protecting himself from being eaten, so his trick was a clever way to escape danger.
questions.misconception: A drama has no moral lesson.

questions.stem: Which of these is another moral lesson we can learn from the story?
options: Thinking before you act can save you.
Running fast is the best way to escape.
hints: The tortoise thought of a plan before acting.
He used his brain, not his speed.
questions.explanation: Another moral lesson is that thinking before you act can save you. The tortoise thought of a plan and escaped.
questions.misconception: Only the main character matters in a drama.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.sub_strand: Sub-Strand 6: Conversation - Talking about Oneself, Family, People, Places, Greetings, Customs, Events, Social/ Cultural Values, Manners and other Themes
indicator.content_standard: B3.1.6.1: Explore using certain culturally acceptable language for communication
indicator.objective: Use appropriate greetings for special occasions

skills.description: Recognise special occasions such as birthdays, anniversaries and festivals.
Choose the correct greeting and response for a given special occasion.
Use an appropriate greeting and response in a simple conversation about a special occasion.
Say why greetings are important on special occasions.
Take turns to demonstrate greetings for a special occasion.

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 questions at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4.
misconceptions: Any greeting is fine for any occasion.
Only words matter; tone and actions do not.
Greetings are only for adults.
You do not need to respond to a greeting.

questions.stem: Which of these is a special occasion?
hints: Special occasions are days we celebrate.
People often wear new clothes and eat special food.
questions.explanation: A birthday is a special occasion because it is a day people celebrate.
questions.misconception: Greetings are only for adults.

questions.stem: Which of these is a festival celebrated in Ghana?
hints: A festival is a special celebration.
The Ga people celebrate Homowo.
questions.explanation: Homowo is a festival celebrated by the Ga people in Ghana, so it is a special occasion.
questions.misconception: Any greeting is fine for any occasion.

questions.stem: When a married couple celebrates how many years they have been married, what is this called?
hints: It happens every year after the wedding.
The word starts with 'anni-'.
questions.explanation: An anniversary is the yearly celebration of a wedding or another important event.
questions.misconception: Greetings are only for adults.

questions.stem: What do you say to someone on their birthday?
hints: It is a day of celebration for the person.
The greeting includes the word 'birthday'.
questions.explanation: 'Happy birthday!' is the correct greeting for someone celebrating their birthday.
questions.misconception: Any greeting is fine for any occasion.

questions.stem: What do you say to someone who has just gotten married?
hints: It is a happy and important event.
You are showing joy for them.
questions.explanation: 'Congratulations!' is the correct greeting for a wedding because it shows joy for the couple.
questions.misconception: Any greeting is fine for any occasion.

questions.stem: A friend says, 'Happy New Year!' What is the best response?
options: Happy New Year to you too!
hints: The response should match the greeting.
It is also a new year for you.
questions.explanation: 'Happy New Year to you too!' is the best response because it matches the greeting.
questions.misconception: You do not need to respond to a greeting.

questions.stem: A person says, 'Merry Christmas!' What is the best response?
hints: The response should match the greeting.
'Same to you' means you wish them the same.
questions.explanation: 'Same to you!' is the best response to 'Merry Christmas!'
questions.misconception: You do not need to respond to a greeting.

questions.stem: At a naming ceremony, what might you say to the parents?
options: I am sorry for your loss.
hints: A naming ceremony is for a new baby.
The greeting should show joy.
questions.explanation: 'Congratulations on your new baby!' is the right greeting for a naming ceremony.
questions.misconception: Any greeting is fine for any occasion.

questions.stem: During a funeral, what is the best thing to say to the family?
hints: A funeral is a sad occasion.
The family is grieving.
questions.explanation: 'Sorry for your loss' is the right thing to say to a grieving family at a funeral.
questions.misconception: Any greeting is fine for any occasion.

questions.stem: Which greeting is NOT suitable for a festival?
hints: A festival is a happy occasion.
One greeting is for a sad occasion.
questions.explanation: 'Sorry for your loss' is for a funeral, not a festival.
questions.misconception: Any greeting is fine for any occasion.

questions.stem: Your teacher says, 'Good morning, class.' What should you say?
hints: The teacher greeted you.
Greet the teacher in the same way.
questions.explanation: 'Good morning, teacher' is the correct response because it matches the greeting.
questions.misconception: You do not need to respond to a greeting.

questions.stem: Your neighbour says, 'Happy New Year!' What is the best response?
options: Happy New Year to you too!
I am going to the market.
hints: The neighbour greeted you with a special greeting.
Respond with a similar greeting.
questions.explanation: 'Happy New Year to you too!' is the best response because it matches the special occasion greeting.
questions.misconception: You do not need to respond to a greeting.

questions.stem: You are at a wedding. What is the best thing to say to the bride and groom?
hints: A wedding is a happy occasion.
The greeting should show joy for the couple.
questions.explanation: 'Congratulations and best wishes!' is the best thing to say at a wedding.
questions.misconception: Any greeting is fine for any occasion.

questions.stem: Why is it good to greet people on special occasions?
options: It shows respect and makes them happy.
It is a waste of time.
hints: Greetings show kindness.
People feel good when they are greeted.
questions.explanation: Greetings show respect and make people feel happy on their special day.
questions.misconception: Only words matter; tone and actions do not.

questions.stem: Why should you use the right greeting for the right occasion?
options: Because wrong greetings can hurt or confuse people
Because it does not matter what you say
Because only the teacher should greet people
Because all greetings are the same
hints: A funeral greeting is different from a birthday greeting.
Saying 'Happy birthday' at a funeral would hurt people.
questions.explanation: Using the right greeting shows respect and care. A wrong greeting can hurt or confuse people.
questions.misconception: Any greeting is fine for any occasion.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.sub_strand: Sub-Strand 6: Conversation - Talking about Oneself, Family, People, Places, Greetings, Customs, Events, Social/ Cultural Values, Manners and other Themes
indicator.content_standard: B3.1.6.1: Explore using certain culturally acceptable language for communication
indicator.objective: Talk about events in the community

skills.description: Identify common events in the community.
Describe what happens at a community event in simple sentences.
Say which community event they like most and give a simple reason.
Act out a simple scene from a community event.
Ask and answer simple questions about community events.
Say why a community event is important to the people.

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 questions at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4.
misconceptions: All community events are the same.
Only festivals are community events.
A community event has no importance.
You cannot ask questions about an event you have not attended.

questions.stem: Which of these is a community event?
hints: A community event brings many people in the town together.
It often involves a chief or a big celebration.
questions.explanation: A durbar is a community event where people gather to meet the chief and celebrate.
questions.misconception: Only festivals are community events.

questions.stem: What is the name of the festival celebrated by the Ga people in Ghana?
hints: It is a harvest festival celebrated in Accra.
The word means 'hooting at hunger'.
questions.explanation: Homowo is a famous community festival celebrated by the Ga people in Ghana.
questions.misconception: All community events are the same.

questions.stem: Which of these best describes what happens at a naming ceremony?
options: People sing and dance for a new baby.
People cook fufu for a wedding.
hints: A naming ceremony is for a new baby.
People are happy and celebrate the baby.
questions.explanation: At a naming ceremony, people gather to sing, dance, and celebrate the arrival of a new baby.
questions.misconception: All community events are the same.

questions.stem: Why do people in a community celebrate festivals?
options: To bring people together and have fun
hints: Festivals are happy times.
They help people in the town meet and enjoy together.
questions.explanation: Festivals are important because they bring people together to have fun and share their culture.
questions.misconception: A community event has no importance.

questions.stem: Which community event would you prefer to watch if you like drumming and dancing?
hints: Look for the event that involves music and dancing.
A durbar is a traditional gathering with drumming.
questions.explanation: A durbar is a community event where there is often drumming, dancing, and cultural display.
questions.misconception: Only festivals are community events.

questions.stem: Which event happens when a baby is given a name?
hints: The event is about giving a name.
It is a special family and community event.
questions.explanation: A naming ceremony is the event where a new baby is officially given a name.
questions.misconception: All community events are the same.

questions.stem: At a durbar, the chief often sits under a large umbrella. What else happens at a durbar?
options: People drum, dance, and greet the chief.
hints: A durbar is a traditional community gathering.
People come to show respect and celebrate.
questions.explanation: At a durbar, people drum, dance, and greet the chief to show respect and celebrate together.
questions.misconception: Only festivals are community events.

questions.stem: A friend asks, 'What happens at a festival?' What is the best answer?
options: People drum, dance, and eat together.
hints: A festival is a happy celebration.
Think about music, food, and people gathering.
questions.explanation: The best answer is that people drum, dance, and eat together, because a festival is a joyful community event.
questions.misconception: A community event has no importance.

questions.stem: You want to know when a community event will start. Which question is best to ask?
options: What time will the durbar start?
hints: The question should ask about the time.
Use the word 'when' or 'what time'.
questions.explanation: 'What time will the durbar start?' is the best question because it directly asks about the time of the community event.
questions.misconception: You cannot ask questions about an event you have not attended.

questions.stem: Why might a child prefer a naming ceremony to a funeral?
options: Because a naming ceremony is a happy occasion for a new baby.
hints: A naming ceremony is a joyful event.
Think about the feelings at a naming ceremony.
questions.explanation: A child might prefer a naming ceremony because it is a happy occasion that welcomes a new baby.
questions.misconception: All community events are the same.

questions.stem: What do people often wear to a festival?
hints: Festivals are special occasions.
People wear their best cultural clothes.
questions.explanation: People often wear beautiful traditional clothes like kente to festivals to celebrate their culture.
questions.misconception: Only festivals are community events.

questions.stem: Why is a durbar important to a community?
options: It allows the people to meet the chief and share ideas.
hints: A durbar brings the chief and the people together.
It is a time for talking and sharing.
questions.explanation: A durbar is important because it allows the people to meet their chief, share ideas, and discuss community matters.
questions.misconception: A community event has no importance.

questions.stem: A pupil is describing a festival to a friend. Which sentence best describes what happens?
options: At the festival, the chief sits under a big umbrella and people drum and dance.
At the festival, we read books quietly.
At the festival, we clean the classroom.
hints: A festival is a lively community event.
Think about the sights and sounds of a festival.
questions.explanation: The sentence describes the key activities of a festival: the chief's presence and the drumming and dancing.
questions.misconception: All community events are the same.

questions.stem: Explain why a naming ceremony is important.
options: It welcomes a new baby into the family and community.
It teaches the baby to read.
It is a time to buy new clothes.
hints: A naming ceremony is about a new baby.
It is a special event for the whole family and community.
questions.explanation: A naming ceremony is important because it officially welcomes a new baby into the family and the community.
questions.misconception: A community event has no importance.

questions.stem: Two pupils are talking. Kofi says he likes a durbar best. Ama says she likes a naming ceremony best. Which sentence gives the best reason for Ama's choice?
options: Ama likes naming ceremonies because she can sleep.
Ama likes naming ceremonies because they are loud.
Ama likes naming ceremonies because they welcome a new baby.
Ama likes naming ceremonies because she can run.
hints: A naming ceremony is about a baby.
Think about the main purpose of the event.
questions.explanation: The best reason for choosing a naming ceremony is that it welcomes a new baby into the family and community.
questions.misconception: All community events are the same.

questions.stem: Compare a durbar and a naming ceremony. Which sentence describes a difference between them?
options: A durbar is for the whole community, while a naming ceremony is mainly for a family.
A durbar is for one person, while a naming ceremony is for everyone.
hints: A durbar involves the chief and many people.
A naming ceremony is usually for a family and their friends.
questions.explanation: The main difference is that a durbar is for the whole community, while a naming ceremony is mainly for the baby's family.
questions.misconception: All community events are the same.

questions.stem: Which of these is the best reason to prefer one community event over another?
options: Because I do not like the other event.
Because it is my favourite and it brings people together.
hints: The reason should show why the event is important to you.
It should be a positive reason.
questions.explanation: The best reason is that the event is your favourite and it brings people together, which shows you value the community aspect.
questions.misconception: A community event has no importance.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.sub_strand: Sub-Strand 6: Conversation - Talking about Oneself, Family, People, Places, Greetings, Customs, Events, Social/ Cultural Values, Manners and other Themes
indicator.content_standard: B3.1.6.1: Explore using certain culturally acceptable language for communication
indicator.objective: Use a wider variety of words to talk about different customs and cultural values

skills.description: Name customs and cultural practices.
Use a wider variety of words to describe customs and cultural values.
Describe a custom or cultural value in two or three sentences.
Role-play a simple custom or cultural practice.
Say what value a custom teaches.
Compare two customs and say how they are alike or different.

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 questions at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4.
misconceptions: Customs are the same for all Ghanaian communities.
Any word can describe a custom.
Customs have no value.
Only old people can talk about customs.

questions.stem: Which of these is a custom in many Ghanaian communities?
hints: A custom is a traditional practice passed down over time.
It often involves elders and prayers.
questions.explanation: Pouring libation is a traditional custom practised in many Ghanaian communities to honour ancestors and ask for blessings.
questions.misconception: Customs are the same for all Ghanaian communities.

questions.stem: Which of these is a cultural value?
hints: A value is a belief about what is right or important.
It is about how we treat other people.
questions.explanation: Respect for elders is a cultural value because it is a belief about how young people should treat older people.
questions.misconception: Customs have no value.

questions.stem: What is a naming ceremony?
options: A custom where a new baby is given a name
A custom where people go to the farm
A custom where people build a house
A custom where people buy a car
hints: The event is about a name.
It happens when a baby is born.
questions.explanation: A naming ceremony is a custom where a new baby is officially given a name in the community.
questions.misconception: Only old people can talk about customs.

questions.stem: What value does respecting elders teach?
hints: The word 'respect' is in the name.
It is about honouring people.
questions.explanation: Respecting elders teaches the value of respect, which is important in Ghanaian culture.
questions.misconception: Customs have no value.

questions.stem: Which sentence best describes a naming ceremony?
options: People gather to give a new baby a name.
People gather to buy a new car.
hints: The event is about a baby.
A name is given.
questions.explanation: At a naming ceremony, family and friends gather to officially give a new baby a name.
questions.misconception: Customs are the same for all Ghanaian communities.

questions.stem: Which word best describes a custom that has been passed down for many years?
hints: It comes from the past.
It belongs to the culture.
questions.explanation: Traditional means belonging to a culture and passed down over many years.
questions.misconception: Any word can describe a custom.

questions.stem: What is the best word for 'the way of life of a group of people'?
hints: It includes customs, food, and values.
It is about a group's way of life.
questions.explanation: Culture is the way of life of a group of people, including their customs, values, and traditions.
questions.misconception: Any word can describe a custom.

questions.stem: Which word means 'to show honour to someone'?
hints: It is a value about how we treat others.
It is the opposite of being rude.
questions.explanation: To respect someone means to show honour and good treatment towards them.
questions.misconception: Customs have no value.

questions.stem: Which sentence best describes pouring libation?
options: An elder pours a drink on the ground and prays to the ancestors.
A teacher writes on the board.
A child plays with a ball.
hints: It is a custom involving elders and prayers.
A drink is poured as an offering.
questions.explanation: Pouring libation is a custom where an elder pours a drink on the ground and prays to the ancestors.
questions.misconception: Customs are the same for all Ghanaian communities.

questions.stem: What happens during a traditional marriage ceremony?
options: The families meet, give gifts, and celebrate the couple.
hints: A marriage ceremony involves two families.
It is a celebration of love and unity.
questions.explanation: During a traditional marriage ceremony, the families of the bride and groom meet, exchange gifts, and celebrate the couple.
questions.misconception: Customs are the same for all Ghanaian communities.

questions.stem: What value is shown when a community comes together to celebrate a festival?
hints: Coming together shows togetherness.
It is about people being one.
questions.explanation: When a community comes together to celebrate, it shows the value of unity.
questions.misconception: Customs have no value.

questions.stem: How are a naming ceremony and a traditional wedding alike?
options: Both bring family and friends together to celebrate.
hints: Think about who attends these events.
Both are family celebrations.
questions.explanation: A naming ceremony and a traditional wedding are alike because both bring family and friends together to celebrate an important event.
questions.misconception: Customs are the same for all Ghanaian communities.

questions.stem: Which word describes a custom that is special to one ethnic group but not practised by all Ghanaians?
hints: It is about a particular group of people.
It belongs to one tribe or people.
questions.explanation: An ethnic custom belongs to a particular ethnic group and may not be practised by all Ghanaians.
questions.misconception: Customs are the same for all Ghanaian communities.

questions.stem: A pupil says: 'The festival is a time of joy and togetherness.' Which two words best describe the value shown?
hints: The pupil names the values directly.
Festivals are happy and unifying.
questions.explanation: The pupil describes the festival with the words 'joy' and 'togetherness', which are the values shown.
questions.misconception: Customs have no value.

questions.stem: Why is the custom of helping neighbours important?
options: It shows kindness and builds community spirit.
hints: Helping others is a good behaviour.
It brings people together.
questions.explanation: Helping neighbours shows kindness and builds community spirit, which are important values.
questions.misconception: Customs have no value.

questions.stem: How is pouring libation different from a naming ceremony?
options: Pouring libation is a prayer to ancestors, while a naming ceremony is for naming a baby.
Both are for praying to ancestors.
hints: Think about the purpose of each custom.
One is about prayers, and one is about a baby.
questions.explanation: Pouring libation is a prayer to ancestors, while a naming ceremony is specifically for giving a name to a new baby.
questions.misconception: Customs are the same for all Ghanaian communities.

questions.stem: A pupil writes: 'Our custom is very important because it teaches us to be kind, honest, and respectful.' Which words are the VALUE words in this sentence?
hints: Values are about good behaviour.
Look for words that describe good character.
questions.explanation: Kind, honest, and respectful are value words because they describe good behaviour and character.
questions.misconception: Customs have no value.

questions.stem: Pupil A says: 'Naming ceremonies and traditional weddings are the same.' Pupil B says: 'They are different.' Who is correct and why?
options: Pupil B, because a naming ceremony is for a baby and a wedding is for a couple.
Pupil A, because both are for babies.
Pupil A, because both are for couples.
Pupil B, because neither is a custom.
hints: Think about who the ceremony is for.
A baby and a couple are not the same.
questions.explanation: Pupil B is correct because a naming ceremony is for a new baby, while a traditional wedding is for a couple getting married.
questions.misconception: Customs are the same for all Ghanaian communities.

indicator.subject: English Language
