indicator.sub_strand: Sub-Strand 6: Conversation - Talking about Oneself, Family, People, Places, Greetings, Customs, Events, Social/ Cultural Values, Manners and other Themes
indicator.content_standard: B3.1.6.2: Apply knowledge of language and communicative skills to participate in conversation
indicator.objective: Demonstrate turn-taking in conversation in different topics

skills.description: State simple rules of turn-taking.
Take turns correctly in a short group conversation.
Identify familiar/interesting topics for discussion.
Give a simple scenario from a chosen topic.
Keep a conversation going by listening and responding appropriately.
Say whether turn-taking was good in a conversation and why.

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 questions at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4.
misconceptions: Talking the most is the best way to take part.
You can interrupt if you have a good point.
Only the teacher can choose topics.
Listening is not part of conversation.

questions.stem: What is the best rule for taking turns in a conversation?
options: Wait until the other person stops speaking.
Interrupt if you have a good idea.
Only speak if you are the teacher.
hints: Good conversation requires listening.
Do not cut off the person talking.
questions.explanation: Waiting until the other person stops speaking is the correct rule for turn-taking.
questions.misconception: You can interrupt if you have a good point.

questions.stem: When someone else is speaking, what should you do?
hints: Listening is a very important part of a conversation.
You need to hear what they say to respond correctly.
questions.explanation: Listening carefully is the right thing to do when someone else is speaking.
questions.misconception: Listening is not part of conversation.

questions.stem: Why is it important to take turns in a conversation?
options: So everyone gets a chance to speak.
hints: Think about fairness.
If one person talks all the time, others cannot share their ideas.
questions.explanation: Taking turns ensures everyone gets a chance to speak and share their ideas.
questions.misconception: Talking the most is the best way to take part.

questions.stem: Which of these is a good topic for a class conversation?
options: What I ate for dinner last year
The price of a pencil in 1990
hints: A good topic is interesting and familiar to everyone.
It should be something everyone can talk about.
questions.explanation: Keeping the school clean is a good topic because it affects all pupils and everyone can share ideas.
questions.misconception: Only the teacher can choose topics.

questions.stem: Which topic is best for a group discussion about the community?
options: How to stop littering in the town
What is inside my school bag
hints: Community topics should affect everyone in the area.
Littering is a problem for the whole town.
questions.explanation: How to stop littering is a community topic because it affects everyone in the town.
questions.misconception: Only the teacher can choose topics.

questions.stem: A group wants to discuss a school problem. Which topic is best?
options: How to stop bullying in the school
What the moon is made of
hints: The topic should be about a school problem.
Bullying happens in schools and affects pupils.
questions.explanation: Bullying is a school problem, so discussing how to stop it is a good topic for a group discussion.
questions.misconception: Only the teacher can choose topics.

questions.stem: Which scenario matches the topic 'Sanitation'?
options: A pupil drops a wrapper on the school compound.
A pupil wins a football match.
A pupil reads a book under a tree.
hints: Sanitation is about cleanliness.
Dropping a wrapper makes the environment dirty.
questions.explanation: Dropping a wrapper on the compound is a sanitation problem because it makes the area dirty.
questions.misconception: Talking the most is the best way to take part.

questions.stem: Which scenario matches the topic 'Bush Fires'?
options: A farmer burns grass carelessly and the fire spreads.
hints: Bush fires destroy the environment.
Careless burning of grass causes bush fires.
questions.explanation: A farmer burning grass carelessly is a scenario about bush fires because the fire can spread and destroy the bush.
questions.misconception: Listening is not part of conversation.

questions.stem: Which scenario matches the topic 'Flooding'?
options: A pupil throws a plastic bag into a gutter, and it blocks the water.
A pupil buys a new book.
hints: Flooding is caused by blocked waterways.
Throwing waste into gutters can cause flooding.
questions.explanation: Throwing waste into a gutter blocks the water and can cause flooding, making it a good scenario for the topic.
questions.misconception: Talking the most is the best way to take part.

questions.stem: Which scenario matches the topic 'Pollution'?
options: A factory pours dirty water into a river.
A pupil reads a story book.
A teacher writes on the board.
A child plays with a toy car.
hints: Pollution means making the environment dirty or unsafe.
Dirty water in a river harms the environment.
questions.explanation: A factory pouring dirty water into a river is a scenario about pollution because it makes the water unsafe.
questions.misconception: Listening is not part of conversation.

questions.stem: Your friend says, 'I like playing football.' What is the best response to keep the conversation going?
options: I like it too! Which team do you support?
hints: A good response shows you are listening.
Ask a question to keep them talking.
questions.explanation: Saying 'I like it too! Which team do you support?' shows you are listening and keeps the conversation going by asking a question.
questions.misconception: Listening is not part of conversation.

questions.stem: Someone says, 'I went to the market yesterday.' What is a good follow-up question to keep the conversation going?
hints: Ask them for more details about their trip.
A good question starts with 'What' or 'How'.
questions.explanation: Asking 'What did you buy?' is a good follow-up because it invites the speaker to share more about their trip.
questions.misconception: Talking the most is the best way to take part.

questions.stem: A pupil is talking about a book they read. What can you say to show you are listening and keep the conversation going?
options: That sounds interesting, what happened next?
I have not read it, so stop talking.
hints: Show interest in what they are saying.
Ask a question about the story.
questions.explanation: Saying 'That sounds interesting, what happened next?' shows you are listening and encourages the speaker to continue.
questions.misconception: Listening is not part of conversation.

questions.stem: Kofi kept interrupting Ama while she was speaking. Was Kofi taking turns well?
options: Yes, because he had good ideas.
hints: Interrupting means cutting off someone who is speaking.
Is that good turn-taking?
questions.explanation: Kofi was not taking turns well because he kept interrupting Ama, which means he did not wait for his turn to speak.
questions.misconception: You can interrupt if you have a good point.

questions.stem: Group A: everyone shouted at the same time. Group B: pupils raised their hands and waited for their turn. Which group took turns better?
options: Group A, because they were louder.
Group B, because they waited and raised their hands.
hints: Good turn-taking means waiting and not shouting.
Which group showed patience?
questions.explanation: Group B took turns better because they raised their hands and waited for their turn instead of shouting over each other.
questions.misconception: Talking the most is the best way to take part.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.sub_strand: Sub-Strand 6: Conversation - Talking about Oneself, Family, People, Places, Greetings, Customs, Events, Social/ Cultural Values, Manners and other Themes
indicator.content_standard: B3.1.6.2: Apply knowledge of language and communicative skills to participate in conversation
indicator.objective: Ask and answer questions for clarification about what other people say

skills.description: Notice when something said is unclear.
Ask a clear question to get more information.
Answer a clarifying question clearly and simply.
Use clarification questions and answers naturally in a short conversation.
Say why it is good to ask for clarification.
Change a statement to make it clearer after a clarifying question.

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 questions at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4.
misconceptions: Asking for clarification means you were not listening.
Any question is a clarifying question.
You should never admit you do not understand.
Clarifying questions must be long and formal.

questions.stem: Your friend says, 'I went to the place yesterday.' You do not know which place. What is the problem?
options: The friend did not say which place.
The friend used a big word.
hints: The word 'place' is not specific.
You need more information to understand.
questions.explanation: The problem is that your friend did not say which place, so the message is unclear.
questions.misconception: Any question is a clarifying question.

questions.stem: A pupil says, 'Bring the thing tomorrow.' Why do you need to ask for clarification?
options: Because the pupil spoke too softly.
hints: 'The thing' does not tell you what to bring.
You need to know exactly what object is meant.
questions.explanation: You need clarification because 'the thing' is too general; you do not know which object to bring.
questions.misconception: Any question is a clarifying question.

questions.stem: A teacher says, 'Put it there.' You are not sure what 'it' is or where 'there' is. What should you do?
options: Ask the teacher to explain what 'it' and 'there' mean.
Ask a friend to do it for you.
hints: Both 'it' and 'there' are unclear.
Asking for clarification is the best way to understand.
questions.explanation: You should ask the teacher to explain what 'it' and 'there' mean so you can follow the instruction correctly.
questions.misconception: You should never admit you do not understand.

questions.stem: Your friend says, 'I saw him yesterday.' You do not know who 'him' is. What is the best clarifying question?
hints: You need to know the person.
Use the question word 'who'.
questions.explanation: 'Who did you see?' is the best clarifying question because it asks for the identity of the person.
questions.misconception: Any question is a clarifying question.

questions.stem: A pupil says, 'Bring the book tomorrow.' You do not know which book. What is the best clarifying question?
hints: The unclear part is 'the book'.
Ask about the specific book.
questions.explanation: 'Which book should I bring?' is the best clarifying question because it asks for the specific book.
questions.misconception: Clarifying questions must be long and formal.

questions.stem: Someone says, 'I will come at the usual time.' You do not know the usual time. What is the best clarifying question?
options: What time is the usual time?
hints: The unclear part is 'the usual time'.
Ask for the specific time.
questions.explanation: 'What time is the usual time?' is the best clarifying question because it asks for the specific time.
questions.misconception: Asking for clarification means you were not listening.

questions.stem: Your friend asks, 'What do you mean by "the thing"?' You meant the blue bag. What is the best answer?
hints: Answer clearly with the specific object.
Say exactly what you meant.
questions.explanation: The best answer is 'I mean the blue bag' because it clearly explains what 'the thing' refers to.
questions.misconception: You should never admit you do not understand.

questions.stem: A pupil asks, 'Which book should I bring?' You meant the English textbook. What is the best answer?
hints: Answer with the specific book.
Be clear and direct.
questions.explanation: The best answer is 'The English textbook' because it clearly identifies the specific book.
questions.misconception: Asking for clarification means you were not listening.

questions.stem: Your teacher asks, 'What do you mean by "later"?' You meant after break time. What is the best answer?
hints: Give the specific time.
Be clear and direct.
questions.explanation: The best answer is 'After break time' because it clearly explains when 'later' is.
questions.misconception: Clarifying questions must be long and formal.

questions.stem: Why is it good to ask for clarification when you do not understand?
options: It is not allowed in class.
hints: Clarification helps you learn.
It clears up confusion.
questions.explanation: Asking for clarification helps you understand better because it clears up confusion.
questions.misconception: Asking for clarification means you were not listening.

questions.stem: Why should you never be afraid to ask for clarification?
options: Because it shows you are listening and want to understand.
Because it means you were not listening.
Because it is a sign of weakness.
Because the teacher will be angry.
hints: Asking for clarification is a sign of active listening.
It shows you care about understanding correctly.
questions.explanation: You should never be afraid to ask for clarification because it shows you are listening and want to understand correctly.
questions.misconception: Asking for clarification means you were not listening.

questions.stem: Your friend asks, 'Do you mean the red ball?' You meant the blue ball. What should you say?
options: No, I mean the blue ball.
hints: Correct the misunderstanding clearly.
Say 'No' and then give the correct information.
questions.explanation: You should say 'No, I mean the blue ball' to correct the misunderstanding.
questions.misconception: Any question is a clarifying question.

questions.stem: A pupil asks, 'Are we meeting at 10 o'clock?' You meant 2 o'clock. What is the best response?
options: No, we are meeting at 2 o'clock.
hints: Correct the time clearly.
Say 'No' and give the right time.
questions.explanation: The best response is 'No, we are meeting at 2 o'clock' because it corrects the misunderstanding about the time.
questions.misconception: Clarifying questions must be long and formal.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.sub_strand: Sub-Strand 6: Conversation - Talking about Oneself, Family, People, Places, Greetings, Customs, Events, Social/ Cultural Values, Manners and other Themes
indicator.content_standard: B3.1.6.2: Apply knowledge of language and communicative skills to participate in conversation
indicator.objective: Participate in communication, using more varied and more accurate language

skills.description: Choose a range of words rather than repeating the same basic words.
Use correct simple sentence structures when speaking.
Contribute ideas in a group discussion on a poster or topic.
Give an accurate response to a question or comment.
Improve a weak sentence by choosing better words or correcting grammar.
Say why one word or sentence is more accurate than another.

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 questions at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4.
misconceptions: Big words are always better.
Any word with the same general meaning is equally accurate.
Grammar does not matter when speaking.
Repeating the same word makes speech clear.

questions.stem: A pupil says: 'I like rice. I like beans. I like fufu.' Which sentence uses more varied vocabulary?
options: I like rice, beans, and fufu.
I like rice. I like beans. I like fufu.
I like rice and I like beans and I like fufu.
hints: Varied vocabulary means using different words, not repeating the same ones.
Which sentence avoids repeating 'I like' three times?
questions.explanation: 'I like rice, beans, and fufu' is more varied because it lists items without repeating 'I like' each time.
questions.misconception: Repeating the same word makes speech clear.

questions.stem: Which word is a better choice than 'nice' to describe a delicious meal?
hints: Choose a word that specifically describes tasty food.
'Delicious' means very tasty.
questions.explanation: 'Delicious' is more accurate than 'nice' for describing a tasty meal.
questions.misconception: Any word with the same general meaning is equally accurate.

questions.stem: Instead of saying 'The big house' every time, which sentence uses a more varied vocabulary?
hints: 'Enormous' means very big.
Varied vocabulary means using a different word for the same idea.
questions.explanation: 'The enormous house' uses a different word (enormous) instead of repeating 'big', making the language more varied.
questions.misconception: Repeating the same word makes speech clear.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses more accurate and varied language?
options: The tiny ant crawled slowly across the rough ground.
The small thing went across the thing.
hints: Look for specific describing words.
'Tiny', 'crawled', and 'rough' are specific and accurate.
questions.explanation: 'The tiny ant crawled slowly across the rough ground' uses specific, varied words that give a clear picture.
questions.misconception: Big words are always better.

questions.stem: A pupil keeps saying 'good' to describe everything: 'The food is good. The film is good. The book is good.' Which is the best way to improve this?
options: Use different words like delicious, exciting, and interesting.
Keep saying 'good' so it is clear.
hints: Using the same word for everything is not varied.
Choose a specific word for each thing.
questions.explanation: Using different words like delicious, exciting, and interesting makes the language more varied and accurate.
questions.misconception: Repeating the same word makes speech clear.

questions.stem: Which sentence is grammatically correct?
options: She go to school every day.
She goes to school every day.
She going to school every day.
She gone to school every day.
hints: With 'she', the verb needs an 's' in the simple present.
Subject and verb must agree.
questions.explanation: 'She goes to school every day' is correct because the verb 'go' needs an 's' with 'she' in the simple present tense.
questions.misconception: Grammar does not matter when speaking.

questions.stem: Which sentence has correct grammar?
hints: With 'they', use 'are' in the present continuous.
The subject 'they' is plural.
questions.explanation: 'They are playing football' is correct because 'they' takes 'are' in the present continuous tense.
questions.misconception: Grammar does not matter when speaking.

questions.stem: Which sentence is grammatically correct?
hints: With 'he', use 'doesn't' for the negative.
Subject-verb agreement matters.
questions.explanation: 'He doesn't like mangoes' is correct because 'he' takes 'doesn't' in the negative simple present.
questions.misconception: Grammar does not matter when speaking.

questions.stem: Which sentence is grammatically correct?
options: The children was playing in the park.
The children were playing in the park.
The children is playing in the park.
The children be playing in the park.
hints: 'Children' is plural.
Use 'were' with plural subjects in the past continuous.
questions.explanation: 'The children were playing in the park' is correct because 'children' is plural and takes 'were'.
questions.misconception: Grammar does not matter when speaking.

questions.stem: A friend asks, 'What did you do at the market?' Which is the most accurate response?
hints: The most accurate answer gives specific details.
What did you actually do?
questions.explanation: 'I bought tomatoes and onions' is the most accurate response because it gives specific details about what happened.
questions.misconception: Any word with the same general meaning is equally accurate.

questions.stem: A pupil says: 'The weather is nice today.' What is the most accurate response?
options: Yes, it is sunny and warm.
hints: Give specific details about the weather.
Mention what makes it nice.
questions.explanation: 'Yes, it is sunny and warm' is the most accurate response because it gives specific details about the weather.
questions.misconception: Repeating the same word makes speech clear.

questions.stem: Someone asks: 'How was the football match?' Which is the most accurate response?
options: It was exciting. Our team scored two goals.
hints: Give details about what happened.
Say why it was exciting.
questions.explanation: 'It was exciting. Our team scored two goals' is the most accurate because it gives specific details about the match.
questions.misconception: Grammar does not matter when speaking.

questions.stem: Which sentence is better and more accurate?
options: The dog ran quickly across the field.
The dog went across the field.
hints: Look for specific verbs and adverbs.
'Ran quickly' is more specific than 'went'.
questions.explanation: 'The dog ran quickly across the field' is more accurate because 'ran quickly' is more specific than 'went'.
questions.misconception: Any word with the same general meaning is equally accurate.

questions.stem: Improve this sentence: 'The girl ate the food.' Which is the best improvement?
options: The hungry girl ate the delicious food quickly.
The girl ate the food fast.
hints: Add descriptive words to make it more accurate.
Describe the girl and the food.
questions.explanation: 'The hungry girl ate the delicious food quickly' is the best improvement because it adds details that make the sentence clearer and more accurate.
questions.misconception: Big words are always better.

questions.stem: Why is 'The eagle soared high in the sky' better than 'The bird went up'?
options: Because it uses specific and accurate words like 'soared' and 'high'.
hints: Look at the describing words.
'Soared' is more specific than 'went'.
questions.explanation: 'The eagle soared high in the sky' is better because it uses specific, accurate words that create a clear picture.
questions.misconception: Big words are always better.

questions.stem: Which sentence is more accurate and why? A: 'The puppy sprinted across the yard.' B: 'The puppy ran across the yard.'
options: Sentence A, because 'sprinted' is more specific than 'ran'.
Sentence B, because it is simpler.
Sentence A, because it is longer.
hints: 'Sprinted' means running very fast.
Which word gives a clearer picture?
questions.explanation: Sentence A is more accurate because 'sprinted' is a more specific and descriptive verb than 'ran'.
questions.misconception: Any word with the same general meaning is equally accurate.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.sub_strand: Sub-Strand 6: Conversation - Talking about Oneself, Family, People, Places, Greetings, Customs, Events, Social/ Cultural Values, Manners and other Themes
indicator.content_standard: B3.1.6.2: Apply knowledge of language and communicative skills to participate in conversation
indicator.objective: Express a greater variety of communicative meaning (e.g. apologising, agreeing or disagreeing)

skills.description: Recognise apologising, agreeing, disagreeing and expressing feelings.
Select the right expression for a situation.
Express agreement, disagreement or apology politely.
Act out a short situation using the right expressions.
Say why it is important to express meaning politely.
Respond appropriately to an apology, agreement or disagreement.

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 questions at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4.
misconceptions: Disagreeing means being rude.
Any apology works in any situation.
Only words matter; tone does not.
You should hide your feelings in conversation.

questions.stem: Which expression shows apologising?
hints: Apologising means saying sorry.
Which expression shows you regret something?
questions.explanation: 'I am sorry' is an apology because it shows you regret what happened.
questions.misconception: Disagreeing means being rude.

questions.stem: Which expression shows agreeing?
hints: Agreeing means you think the other person is correct.
Which expression shows you share the same opinion?
questions.explanation: 'You are right' shows agreement because you are saying the other person is correct.
questions.misconception: Disagreeing means being rude.

questions.stem: Which expression shows disagreeing politely?
options: I see your point, but I think differently.
hints: Disagreeing means having a different opinion.
Which expression is polite and shows a different view?
questions.explanation: 'I see your point, but I think differently' is a polite way to disagree.
questions.misconception: Disagreeing means being rude.

questions.stem: Which is the most polite way to apologise?
options: I am sorry, it was my mistake.
hints: A polite apology takes responsibility.
Which expression shows you admit the mistake?
questions.explanation: 'I am sorry, it was my mistake' is the most polite apology because it takes responsibility.
questions.misconception: Any apology works in any situation.

questions.stem: A friend says, 'I am sorry for breaking your pencil.' What is the best response?
options: That's okay, don't worry about it.
hints: The friend has apologised.
A good response is kind and forgiving.
questions.explanation: 'That's okay, don't worry about it' is the best response because it accepts the apology kindly.
questions.misconception: You should hide your feelings in conversation.

questions.stem: You accidentally step on your friend's foot. What should you say?
options: I am sorry, I did not mean to.
hints: You caused the accident.
You should apologise.
questions.explanation: 'I am sorry, I did not mean to' is the right thing to say because you accidentally hurt your friend.
questions.misconception: Any apology works in any situation.

questions.stem: A friend says, 'I think we should play football.' You want to play a different game. What is the best response?
options: I don't think so. Can we play something else?
hints: Disagree politely.
Suggest another idea.
questions.explanation: 'I don't think so. Can we play something else?' is the best response because it politely disagrees and suggests another game.
questions.misconception: Disagreeing means being rude.

questions.stem: Which is the most polite way to disagree with a teacher?
options: Excuse me, I see it differently. May I explain?
hints: Always be respectful when disagreeing with a teacher.
Use words like 'excuse me' and 'may I'.
questions.explanation: 'Excuse me, I see it differently. May I explain?' is the most polite way to disagree with a teacher.
questions.misconception: Only words matter; tone does not.

questions.stem: A friend says, 'I agree with your idea.' What is the best response?
options: Thank you, I am glad you agree.
I was not talking to you.
hints: The friend has agreed with you.
Respond politely and positively.
questions.explanation: 'Thank you, I am glad you agree' is the best response because it is polite and positive.
questions.misconception: You should hide your feelings in conversation.

questions.stem: A friend says, 'I think the answer is 5.' You think the answer is 7. What is the best response?
options: I think the answer is 7, but let us check together.
You are wrong! The answer is 7.
hints: Disagree politely.
Suggest checking together.
questions.explanation: 'I think the answer is 7, but let us check together' is the best response because it politely disagrees and suggests a solution.
questions.misconception: Disagreeing means being rude.

questions.stem: Your friend gives you a gift you already have. What should you say?
options: Thank you so much! I really appreciate it.
hints: Your friend is being kind.
Show gratitude even if you already have it.
questions.explanation: 'Thank you so much! I really appreciate it' is the best response because it shows gratitude for the kind gesture.
questions.misconception: Only words matter; tone does not.

questions.stem: You need to tell your friend you disagree with their plan. Which is the politest way?
options: I understand your plan, but I have a different idea. Can I share it?
We should not do your plan.
hints: Acknowledge the friend's idea first.
Then politely offer your own idea.
questions.explanation: 'I understand your plan, but I have a different idea. Can I share it?' is the politest way because it respects the friend's idea and asks to share a different one.
questions.misconception: Disagreeing means being rude.

questions.stem: Why is it important to apologise when you do something wrong?
options: It shows respect and helps repair the relationship.
It makes the other person angry.
hints: Apologising shows you care about the other person's feelings.
It helps the other person feel better.
questions.explanation: Apologising is important because it shows respect and helps repair the relationship after a mistake.
questions.misconception: Disagreeing means being rude.

questions.stem: Why is it important to express disagreement politely?
options: It keeps the conversation respectful and avoids hurting feelings.
It makes the other person feel bad.
It helps you win the argument.
It is not important at all.
hints: Politeness keeps relationships strong.
Rude disagreement can hurt people.
questions.explanation: Politely expressing disagreement is important because it keeps the conversation respectful and avoids hurting others' feelings.
questions.misconception: Only words matter; tone does not.

questions.stem: A friend says, 'I am sorry I forgot your birthday.' What is the best response?
options: It's okay, I understand. Thank you for saying sorry.
hints: Your friend has apologised.
Respond with understanding.
questions.explanation: 'It's okay, I understand. Thank you for saying sorry' is the best response because it accepts the apology and is understanding.
questions.misconception: You should hide your feelings in conversation.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B3.1.7.1: Use appropriate skills and strategies to process meaning from texts
indicator.objective: Listen to and interact actively within information texts

skills.description: Say what they already know (K) about the topic of an information text before listening.
Ask simple questions about what they want to know (W) from the text.
Listen carefully and pick out key facts from an information text.
Answer questions they asked before listening and simple factual questions after listening.
Share what they have learned (L) from the information text with a partner or group.
Respond appropriately while listening to an information text.

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 questions at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4.
misconceptions: Listening means hearing the words without thinking.
You cannot ask questions about a text before you hear it.
Only the teacher can share facts after listening.
All information in a text is equally important.

questions.stem: Before listening to the text, what do you already know about malaria?
options: Malaria is caused by a mosquito bite.
Malaria is caused by eating too much rice.
Malaria is caused by sleeping too much.
Malaria is caused by running fast.
hints: Think about what you have heard about malaria.
It has something to do with mosquitoes.
questions.explanation: Many people already know that malaria is connected to mosquito bites.
questions.misconception: You cannot ask questions about a text before you hear it.

questions.stem: Before listening, which question about malaria would you want answered?
options: What is the capital of Ghana?
How do you bake a cake?
What is the weather like today?
hints: Choose a question that is about malaria.
The text is about malaria and mosquitoes.
questions.explanation: 'How does malaria spread?' is a good question to want answered before listening to a text about malaria.
questions.misconception: You cannot ask questions about a text before you hear it.

questions.stem: Which is a good question to ask before listening to a text about malaria?
hints: The question should be about the topic of malaria.
What do you want to learn about malaria?
questions.explanation: 'What causes malaria?' is a good question because it is about the topic and you want to know the answer.
questions.misconception: You cannot ask questions about a text before you hear it.

questions.stem: A pupil says, 'I want to know how to stop mosquitoes from biting me.' Which part of the text will answer this question?
options: The part about the mosquito biting a sick person
hints: Stopping mosquitoes from biting is about prevention.
Look for words like 'prevent' or 'net'.
questions.explanation: The part about prevention will answer the question about stopping mosquito bites.
questions.misconception: All information in a text is equally important.

questions.stem: What causes malaria?
options: A tiny germ called a parasite
hints: The text says malaria is caused by a tiny germ.
It is spread by a mosquito.
questions.explanation: The text says malaria is caused by a tiny germ called a parasite.
questions.misconception: Listening means hearing the words without thinking.

questions.stem: What spreads the germ that causes malaria?
hints: The text mentions a specific insect.
It bites people at night.
questions.explanation: The text says the parasite is spread by the bite of a female mosquito.
questions.misconception: Listening means hearing the words without thinking.

questions.stem: When does a mosquito pass the germ into a person's blood?
options: When it flies near the person
When it lands on the person's food
When it buzzes near the person's ear
hints: The germ enters through a bite.
The text says 'when that mosquito bites another person'.
questions.explanation: The mosquito passes the germ into a person's blood when it bites the person.
questions.misconception: All information in a text is equally important.

questions.stem: How can we prevent malaria, according to the text?
options: By sleeping under mosquito nets and clearing standing water
hints: The text gives two ways to prevent malaria.
One involves a net, and one involves water.
questions.explanation: The text says we should sleep under mosquito nets and clear standing water to prevent malaria.
questions.misconception: All information in a text is equally important.

questions.stem: What is the germ that causes malaria called?
hints: The text says it is a tiny germ.
It is called a parasite.
questions.explanation: The text says the germ that causes malaria is called a parasite.
questions.misconception: Only the teacher can share facts after listening.

questions.stem: How does a mosquito pick up the germ?
options: By biting a person who has malaria
hints: The mosquito bites a person who is sick.
It picks up the germ from the person's blood.
questions.explanation: The mosquito picks up the germ by biting a person who has malaria.
questions.misconception: Listening means hearing the words without thinking.

questions.stem: Why should we clear standing water?
options: Because mosquitoes breed in standing water.
Because standing water is good for drinking.
Because standing water makes the ground wet.
hints: The text connects standing water to mosquitoes.
Mosquitoes lay their eggs in water.
questions.explanation: We should clear standing water because mosquitoes breed in it.
questions.misconception: All information in a text is equally important.

questions.stem: Why is it important to sleep under a mosquito net?
options: Because the net stops mosquitoes from biting you while you sleep.
Because the net keeps you warm at night.
Because the net makes you sleep faster.
hints: Think about what a mosquito net does.
It is a barrier between you and mosquitoes.
questions.explanation: A mosquito net is important because it stops mosquitoes from biting you while you sleep, which prevents malaria.
questions.misconception: All information in a text is equally important.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B3.1.7.1: Use appropriate skills and strategies to process meaning from texts
indicator.objective: Recognise and relate the sequence of events in stories

skills.description: Name the beginning, middle and end of a story heard.
Put events from a story heard in the correct order.
Say how one event leads to another.
Retell the main events of a story in order.
Use words such as first, next, then, last to describe the sequence.

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 questions at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4.
misconceptions: The order of events does not matter in a story.
Any event can be the beginning.
Retelling means saying every word again.
Because and so are not needed when telling a story.

questions.stem: What happened at the beginning of the story?
options: Kofi went to the river to fish
hints: The beginning is where the story starts.
Where did Kofi go first?
questions.explanation: The story begins with Kofi going to the river to fish.
questions.misconception: Any event can be the beginning.

questions.stem: Which event belongs to the middle of the story?
options: Kofi dug for worms and threw his line into the river
Kofi took the fish to his mother
hints: The middle is where the main action happens.
What did Kofi do after going to the river but before catching the fish?
questions.explanation: Digging for worms and throwing the line into the river happen in the middle of the story.
questions.misconception: The order of events does not matter in a story.

questions.stem: What happened at the end of the story?
options: Kofi threw his line into the river
Kofi felt a pull on the line
Kofi took the fish home to his mother
hints: The end is how the story finishes.
What did Kofi do with the fish?
questions.explanation: The story ends with Kofi taking the fish home to his mother.
questions.misconception: Any event can be the beginning.

questions.stem: Which of these is the main event in the middle of the story?
options: Kofi caught a big fish after pulling hard
hints: The main event is the most exciting part.
What was Kofi trying to do at the river?
questions.explanation: Catching the big fish is the main event in the middle of the story because it is the most important action.
questions.misconception: The order of events does not matter in a story.

questions.stem: Put these events in the correct order: (1) Kofi threw his line into the river, (2) Kofi went to the river, (3) Kofi dug for worms.
hints: First, Kofi went to the river.
Then he dug for worms, and after that he threw his line.
questions.explanation: The correct order is: Kofi went to the river (2), he dug for worms (3), and he threw his line into the river (1).
questions.misconception: The order of events does not matter in a story.

questions.stem: What happened right after Kofi dug for worms?
options: He threw his line into the river
hints: After digging for worms, Kofi used them as bait.
What did he do with the line?
questions.explanation: Right after digging for worms, Kofi threw his line into the river.
questions.misconception: Retelling means saying every word again.

questions.stem: What happened just before Kofi caught the big fish?
options: He went home to his mother
He felt a strong pull on the line and pulled hard
He threw his line into the river for the first time
hints: Before catching the fish, something pulled the line.
Kofi had to pull hard.
questions.explanation: Just before catching the fish, Kofi felt a strong pull on the line and pulled hard.
questions.misconception: The order of events does not matter in a story.

questions.stem: Put these four events in the correct order: (1) Kofi felt a strong pull, (2) Kofi went to the river, (3) Kofi took the fish home, (4) Kofi threw his line into the river.
hints: First, Kofi goes to the river (2).
Then he throws his line (4), feels a pull (1), and finally takes the fish home (3).
questions.explanation: The correct order is: went to the river (2), threw the line (4), felt a pull (1), took the fish home (3).
questions.misconception: The order of events does not matter in a story.

questions.stem: A pupil retells the story like this: 'Kofi caught a big fish. Then he went to the river. First, he took the fish home.' What is wrong with this retell?
options: The events are not in the correct order.
The pupil used the wrong names.
The pupil forgot to mention the worms.
hints: Think about the correct order of events.
Kofi cannot catch a fish before going to the river.
questions.explanation: The retell is wrong because the events are not in the correct order. Kofi must go to the river before he can catch a fish.
questions.misconception: The order of events does not matter in a story.

questions.stem: Why did Kofi go to the river?
hints: The story says Kofi went to the river to do something.
He wanted to catch something.
questions.explanation: Kofi went to the river to fish, as stated at the beginning of the story.
questions.misconception: Because and so are not needed when telling a story.

questions.stem: What caused Kofi to pull hard on his line?
options: He saw a big fish jumping
hints: Something happened to the line.
Kofi felt something on the other end.
questions.explanation: Kofi pulled hard because he felt a strong pull on his line, which meant a fish was caught.
questions.misconception: Because and so are not needed when telling a story.

questions.stem: Kofi dug for worms before throwing his line into the river. Why did he do this?
options: Because he wanted to use the worms as bait to catch fish
Because he wanted to play in the mud
Because his mother told him to
hints: Worms are used to catch fish.
Kofi used the worms on his line.
questions.explanation: Kofi dug for worms because he wanted to use them as bait to catch fish.
questions.misconception: Because and so are not needed when telling a story.

questions.stem: Which sentence best explains how one event led to another in the story?
options: Kofi felt a pull, so he pulled hard and caught the fish.
Kofi went to the river because he was hungry.
Kofi took the fish home after he went to sleep.
Kofi dug for worms because he wanted to play.
hints: Look for a cause-and-effect sentence.
One action causes the next action.
questions.explanation: 'Kofi felt a pull, so he pulled hard and caught the fish' best explains how one event led to another because the pull caused Kofi to pull hard and catch the fish.
questions.misconception: Because and so are not needed when telling a story.

questions.stem: Which word can you use to talk about the first event in a story?
hints: It tells you something happens before anything else.
It starts with the letter 'F'.
questions.explanation: 'First' is used to talk about the first event in a story.
questions.misconception: Retelling means saying every word again.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses sequence words correctly to retell the story?
options: First, Kofi caught a fish. Next, he went to the river. Finally, he dug for worms.
First, Kofi went to the river. Next, he dug for worms. Then, he threw his line. Finally, he caught a fish.
Finally, Kofi went to the river. First, he caught a fish.
Kofi went to the river. He caught a fish. He dug for worms.
hints: The order of events must be correct.
First, next, then, and finally should follow the story order.
questions.explanation: 'First, Kofi went to the river. Next, he dug for worms. Then, he threw his line. Finally, he caught a fish' uses sequence words correctly and follows the story order.
questions.misconception: The order of events does not matter in a story.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B3.1.7.1: Use appropriate skills and strategies to process meaning from texts
indicator.objective: Share facts from information texts heard with a partner, groups or the teacher

skills.description: Remember key facts from an information text heard.
Say a fact from the text in a clear, simple sentence.
Tell a partner one or two facts learned from the text.
Share facts with a small group and listen to others' facts.
Report a fact to the teacher accurately.
Recognise a fact from the text and not a personal opinion.

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 questions at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4.
misconceptions: Any sentence about the topic is a fact from the text.
Sharing facts means repeating the whole text.
Only the teacher can decide which facts are important.
A personal opinion is the same as a fact.

questions.stem: According to the text, what do trees give us to breathe?
hints: The text mentions something we need to breathe.
It starts with the letter 'O'.
questions.explanation: The text says trees give us oxygen to breathe.
questions.misconception: Sharing facts means repeating the whole text.

questions.stem: What kind of fruits does the text mention that trees give us?
hints: The text names two specific fruits.
One is yellow and one is orange.
questions.explanation: The text mentions mangoes and oranges as examples of fruits from trees.
questions.misconception: Any sentence about the topic is a fact from the text.

questions.stem: Where do birds build their nests, according to the text?
hints: The text says where birds build their homes.
It is related to the topic of trees.
questions.explanation: The text says birds build their nests in trees.
questions.misconception: Sharing facts means repeating the whole text.

questions.stem: How do trees help the soil?
options: They help hold the soil together so rain does not wash it away.
They cover the soil with leaves.
hints: The text says trees help with rain and soil.
They hold the soil together.
questions.explanation: The text says trees hold the soil together so that rain does not wash it away.
questions.misconception: Any sentence about the topic is a fact from the text.

questions.stem: The text gives several reasons why trees are important. Which of these is NOT a reason given in the text?
options: They give us fruits to eat.
They give us oxygen to breathe.
They give us paper to write on.
hints: Three of these are mentioned in the text.
One is not mentioned in the text.
questions.explanation: The text mentions shade, fruits, and oxygen, but it does not mention paper. So 'They give us paper to write on' is not in the text.
questions.misconception: Any sentence about the topic is a fact from the text.

questions.stem: Which sentence states a fact from the text clearly?
options: Trees are important because they give us shade and oxygen.
hints: The fact must come from the text.
The sentence should be clear and complete.
questions.explanation: 'Trees are important because they give us shade and oxygen' is a clear fact from the text.
questions.misconception: A personal opinion is the same as a fact.

questions.stem: Which sentence is the clearest way to state a fact about trees?
options: Trees give us fruits such as mangoes and oranges.
Trees are things that are very important.
hints: The sentence should be specific and clear.
It should give an example.
questions.explanation: 'Trees give us fruits such as mangoes and oranges' is clear and specific.
questions.misconception: Sharing facts means repeating the whole text.

questions.stem: A pupil says: 'Trees are good for us because they give us oxygen, shade, fruits, and help hold the soil.' Is this a clear way to share facts?
options: Yes, because it gives several clear facts from the text.
No, because it is too long.
No, because it uses big words.
Yes, because it is the pupil's opinion.
hints: A clear sharing of facts includes facts from the text.
The pupil gives several facts in one sentence.
questions.explanation: It is a clear way to share facts because the pupil states several facts from the text clearly.
questions.misconception: Sharing facts means repeating the whole text.

questions.stem: Which of these is a fact from the text?
options: Trees are the prettiest things in the world.
hints: A fact can be proven or found in the text.
An opinion is what someone thinks or feels.
questions.explanation: 'Trees give us oxygen' is a fact from the text because it is stated in the text.
questions.misconception: A personal opinion is the same as a fact.

questions.stem: Which sentence is an OPINION and NOT a fact from the text?
options: Trees provide shade from the hot sun.
Birds build their nests in trees.
Trees are the most beautiful plants in the world.
hints: An opinion cannot be proven true or false.
Beauty is in the eye of the beholder.
questions.explanation: 'Trees are the most beautiful plants in the world' is an opinion because it is what someone thinks, not a fact.
questions.misconception: A personal opinion is the same as a fact.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B3.1.8.1: Demonstrate understanding in asking and answering questions
indicator.objective: Ask and answer questions for clarifications about given topics

skills.description: Choose an interesting topic for discussion from a given list or from own ideas.
Form a clear question to get more information about a topic.
Answer a clarifying question clearly and simply.
Take turns and listen when asking and answering questions in a group.
Use question words correctly when asking for clarification.
Say why asking and answering clarifying questions is useful.

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 questions at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4.
misconceptions: Any question is a clarifying question.
Asking for clarification means you were not listening.
You should never admit you do not understand.
Clarifying questions must be long and formal.
Only the teacher can ask clarifying questions.

questions.stem: Which is the best topic for a class discussion?
options: How to keep our school clean
What I ate for breakfast last year
The colour of my neighbour's car
hints: A good topic is familiar and useful to everyone.
Keeping the school clean affects all pupils.
questions.explanation: Keeping the school clean is a good topic because it is useful and everyone can discuss it.
questions.misconception: Only the teacher can ask clarifying questions.

questions.stem: A group wants to discuss a topic about health. Which is the best topic?
hints: The topic should be about health.
Malaria is a health issue.
questions.explanation: How to prevent malaria is a health topic that everyone can discuss and learn from.
questions.misconception: Any question is a clarifying question.

questions.stem: The teacher asks the class to choose a topic about the community. Which is the best choice?
options: How to stop littering in our town
hints: The topic must be about the community.
Littering affects everyone in the town.
questions.explanation: How to stop littering in our town is a community topic that affects everyone.
questions.misconception: Only the teacher can ask clarifying questions.

questions.stem: Which question word asks about a person?
hints: It starts with 'W' and asks about a person.
Who is used for people.
questions.explanation: 'Who' is the question word used to ask about a person.
questions.misconception: Any question is a clarifying question.

questions.stem: Complete the question: '________ did you go yesterday?'
hints: The question is about a place.
Use the word that asks about a place.
questions.explanation: 'Where' is the correct question word because the question asks about a place.
questions.misconception: Any question is a clarifying question.

questions.stem: Complete the question: '________ are you late?'
hints: The question asks for a reason.
Use the word that asks about a reason.
questions.explanation: 'Why' is the correct question word because the question asks for a reason.
questions.misconception: Any question is a clarifying question.

questions.stem: A pupil says, 'I will bring it tomorrow.' You want to know what 'it' is. Which question word should you use?
hints: You want to know about a thing.
Use the question word for things.
questions.explanation: 'What' is the correct question word because you want to know what the object is.
questions.misconception: Any question is a clarifying question.

questions.stem: A friend says, 'The event will happen soon.' You want to know the exact time. Which is the best clarifying question?
options: When exactly will the event happen?
Who is coming to the event?
hints: The unclear part is the time.
Use the question word 'When'.
questions.explanation: 'When exactly will the event happen?' is the best clarifying question because it asks for the specific time.
questions.misconception: Clarifying questions must be long and formal.

questions.stem: Your friend says, 'I saw him at the market.' You do not know who 'him' is. What is the best clarifying question?
options: Who did you see at the market?
When did you go to the market?
Why did you go to the market?
hints: You need to know the person.
Use the question word 'Who'.
questions.explanation: 'Who did you see at the market?' is the best clarifying question because it asks for the identity of the person.
questions.misconception: Any question is a clarifying question.

questions.stem: A pupil says, 'Bring the book.' You do not know which book. What is the best clarifying question?
hints: The unclear part is the book.
Ask about the specific book.
questions.explanation: 'Which book should I bring?' is the best clarifying question because it asks for the specific book.
questions.misconception: You should never admit you do not understand.

questions.stem: Your teacher says, 'Put it there.' You do not know what 'it' is or where 'there' is. What should you do?
options: Ask the teacher what 'it' is and where 'there' is.
Ask a friend to do it for you.
hints: Both 'it' and 'there' are unclear.
Asking for clarification is the best way to understand.
questions.explanation: You should ask the teacher what 'it' is and where 'there' is so you can follow the instruction correctly.
questions.misconception: Asking for clarification means you were not listening.

questions.stem: Your friend asks, 'What do you mean by "later"?' You meant after break time. What is the best answer?
hints: Give a specific time.
Be clear and direct.
questions.explanation: 'I mean after break time' is the best answer because it clearly explains when 'later' is.
questions.misconception: Asking for clarification means you were not listening.

questions.stem: A pupil asks, 'Which book should I bring?' You meant the English textbook. What is the best answer?
hints: Answer with the specific book.
Be clear and direct.
questions.explanation: 'The English textbook' is the best answer because it clearly identifies the specific book.
questions.misconception: You should never admit you do not understand.

questions.stem: Your teacher asks, 'What do you mean by "the usual time"?' You meant 8 o'clock. What is the best answer?
hints: Give the specific time.
Be clear and direct.
questions.explanation: 'I mean 8 o'clock' is the best answer because it clearly explains the specific time.
questions.misconception: Clarifying questions must be long and formal.

questions.stem: Why is it good to ask clarifying questions?
options: It helps you understand things clearly.
It is not allowed in class.
hints: Clarifying questions clear up confusion.
They help you learn better.
questions.explanation: Asking clarifying questions helps you understand things clearly and learn better.
questions.misconception: Asking for clarification means you were not listening.

questions.stem: Why is it important to answer clarifying questions clearly and simply?
options: So the person asking can understand the answer easily.
So the answer can be as long as possible.
hints: The purpose is to help the other person understand.
A clear answer helps the other person.
questions.explanation: Answering clearly and simply helps the person asking to understand the answer easily, which is the purpose of clarification.
questions.misconception: Asking for clarification means you were not listening.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B3.1.8.1: Demonstrate understanding in asking and answering questions
indicator.objective: Use appropriate pronunciation and intonation in asking and answering the inversion questions

skills.description: Recognise an inversion question.
Change a statement into an inversion question by moving the verb/auxiliary to the front.
Use a rising intonation at the end of an inversion question when speaking.
Answer an inversion question with a falling intonation.
Ask and answer inversion questions in a pair or small group using correct pronunciation and intonation.
Write correct answers to inversion questions.

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 questions at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4.
misconceptions: Any question is an inversion question.
Intonation does not matter in questions.
You can use falling intonation for all questions.
Answers to inversion questions should use rising intonation.
Only the teacher can ask inversion questions.

questions.stem: Which of these is an inversion question?
hints: An inversion question moves the verb to the front.
Look for the question form of 'He is going'.
questions.explanation: The statement 'He is going' becomes the inversion question 'Is he going?' by moving 'is' to the front.
questions.misconception: Any question is an inversion question.

questions.stem: Which question is an inversion question?
hints: The helping word goes before the subject.
Can you swim? is the question form.
questions.explanation: 'Can you swim?' is an inversion question because 'can' comes before the subject 'you'.
questions.misconception: Any question is an inversion question.

questions.stem: Change 'She is happy' to an inversion question.
hints: Move 'is' to the front.
The subject comes after the verb.
questions.explanation: Moving 'is' to the front gives 'Is she happy?'
questions.misconception: You can use falling intonation for all questions.

questions.stem: Change 'They are playing' to an inversion question.
hints: Move 'are' to the front.
The subject 'they' comes after 'are'.
questions.explanation: Moving 'are' to the front gives 'Are they playing?'
questions.misconception: Any question is an inversion question.

questions.stem: Which of these is an inversion question?
hints: Find the question form.
The verb 'is' comes before the subject.
questions.explanation: 'Is the boy tall?' is an inversion question because 'is' comes before 'the boy'.
questions.misconception: Any question is an inversion question.

questions.stem: Change 'He can run fast' to an inversion question.
hints: Move 'can' to the front.
The subject 'he' comes after 'can'.
questions.explanation: Moving 'can' to the front gives 'Can he run fast?'
questions.misconception: You can use falling intonation for all questions.

questions.stem: Change 'She was at school' to an inversion question.
hints: Move 'was' to the front.
The subject 'she' comes after 'was'.
questions.explanation: Moving 'was' to the front gives 'Was she at school?'
questions.misconception: Any question is an inversion question.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.sub_strand: Sub-Strand 9: Giving and Responding to Commands/Instructions/Directions and Making Requests
indicator.content_standard: B3.1.9.1: Demonstrate understanding in commands, instructions, directions and requests
indicator.objective: Give and respond to commands, instructions and directions

skills.description: Recognise and distinguish commands, instructions, and directions.
Perform physical actions based on oral instructions or directions.
Formulate and give clear commands or instructions to peers.
Put steps of an instruction in logical order using words like first, next, then, finally.
Understand and use direction words such as go straight, turn left, turn right.
Respond appropriately with words or actions to commands and instructions.

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 questions at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4.
misconceptions: Commands and requests are the same thing.
Directions and instructions mean exactly the same thing.
You do not need to look at the person giving the instruction.
The order of steps in an instruction does not matter.
Any word can be used to give directions.

questions.stem: Which of these is a command?
hints: A command tells someone to do something.
It usually starts with a verb.
questions.explanation: 'Sit down' is a command because it tells someone to do something.
questions.misconception: Commands and requests are the same thing.

questions.stem: Which of these is an instruction?
options: The book is on the table.
hints: An instruction tells you how to do something step by step.
Look for words like 'first' or 'next'.
questions.explanation: 'First, draw a square' is an instruction because it gives a step to follow.
questions.misconception: Directions and instructions mean exactly the same thing.

questions.stem: Which sentence gives a direction?
hints: A direction tells you where to go or how to move.
Look for words like 'left', 'right', or 'straight'.
questions.explanation: 'Turn left at the corner' is a direction because it tells you which way to go.
questions.misconception: Directions and instructions mean exactly the same thing.

questions.stem: Instruction: 'First draw a circle. Next draw a square inside the circle.' What do you draw first?
hints: The word 'first' tells you which step comes before the other.
The circle is drawn before the square.
questions.explanation: The instruction says 'First draw a circle', so the circle is drawn first.
questions.misconception: The order of steps in an instruction does not matter.

questions.stem: Instruction: 'Draw a square. Draw a triangle inside the square. Draw a circle inside the triangle.' Which shape is in the middle?
hints: The triangle is drawn inside the square.
The circle is drawn inside the triangle.
questions.explanation: The triangle is in the middle because it is inside the square and the circle is inside the triangle.
questions.misconception: The order of steps in an instruction does not matter.

questions.stem: Instruction: 'First, take out your pencil. Next, open your book. Then, write your name.' Which step comes first?
hints: The word 'first' tells you the first step.
Look at the beginning of the instruction.
questions.explanation: The instruction says 'First, take out your pencil', so that is the first step.
questions.misconception: The order of steps in an instruction does not matter.

questions.stem: Instruction: 'First draw a line. Next draw a circle at the end of the line. Then colour the circle red.' Which step comes after drawing the line?
hints: After drawing the line, the next step is to draw a circle.
The colouring comes last.
questions.explanation: After drawing the line, the next step is to draw a circle at the end of the line.
questions.misconception: The order of steps in an instruction does not matter.

questions.stem: Put these instruction steps in the correct order: (A) Cut the paper, (B) Draw a shape on the paper, (C) Colour the shape.
hints: You must draw the shape before you can cut it.
You cut the shape before you colour it.
questions.explanation: The correct order is: draw the shape (B), cut the paper (A), colour the shape (C).
questions.misconception: The order of steps in an instruction does not matter.

questions.stem: Which word tells you to go to the left side?
hints: The word sounds like 'left'.
It is the opposite of 'right'.
questions.explanation: 'Left' is the direction word that tells you to go to the left side.
questions.misconception: Any word can be used to give directions.

questions.stem: You are walking to the market. You turn to your left side. What did you do?
hints: The direction word tells you which way you turned.
You turned left.
questions.explanation: Turning to your left side means you followed the direction 'turn left'.
questions.misconception: Any word can be used to give directions.

questions.stem: The teacher says, 'Go straight, then turn right.' What should you do first?
hints: The word 'then' shows the second step.
The first direction is 'go straight'.
questions.explanation: You should go straight first, then turn right, because the instruction says 'Go straight, then turn right'.
questions.misconception: Directions and instructions mean exactly the same thing.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.sub_strand: Sub-Strand 9: Giving and Responding to Commands/Instructions/Directions and Making Requests
indicator.content_standard: B3.1.9.1: Demonstrate understanding in commands, instructions, directions and requests
indicator.objective: Make and respond to polite requests

skills.description: Recognise polite words and phrases.
Formulate requests using appropriate polite language.
Respond to requests politely using phrases such as 'Yes, of course' or 'I'm sorry I can't'.
Interpret a picture and make the corresponding polite request.
Act out a short situation making and responding to polite requests.
Explain why being polite when asking for things is important.

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 questions at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4.
misconceptions: Adding 'please' to any command makes it a polite request.
You must say yes to every request.
Refusing a request is always rude.
Only adults need to be polite.
Any response is fine as long as you understand the request.

questions.stem: Which word is a polite word used when making a request?
hints: Polite words show respect.
You often say it when asking for something.
questions.explanation: 'Please' is a polite word used when making a request.
questions.misconception: Adding 'please' to any command makes it a polite request.

questions.stem: Which phrase is a polite way to ask for something?
hints: Polite requests use words like 'may' or 'could'.
They sound respectful.
questions.explanation: 'May I have that?' is a polite request because it uses 'may I'.
questions.misconception: Adding 'please' to any command makes it a polite request.

questions.stem: Which response to a request is polite?
hints: A polite response shows willingness and kindness.
It sounds respectful.
questions.explanation: 'Of course, here you are' is a polite response to a request.
questions.misconception: Any response is fine as long as you understand the request.

questions.stem: You want your friend to pass you a pencil. What is the most polite way to ask?
options: Can you pass me a pencil, please?
hints: Use 'please' and a question form.
Start with 'Can you' or 'May I'.
questions.explanation: 'Can you pass me a pencil, please?' is polite because it uses a question form and 'please'.
questions.misconception: Adding 'please' to any command makes it a polite request.

questions.stem: You want to borrow a book from your teacher. Which is the most polite request?
options: May I borrow the book, please?
hints: Use 'May I' and 'please'.
Show respect to the teacher.
questions.explanation: 'May I borrow the book, please?' is polite and respectful.
questions.misconception: Adding 'please' to any command makes it a polite request.

questions.stem: Your friend asks, 'Can I use your pen?' You want to say yes politely. What do you say?
hints: A polite 'yes' shows willingness.
Use words like 'of course' or 'sure'.
questions.explanation: 'Yes, of course' is a polite way to accept a request.
questions.misconception: You must say yes to every request.

questions.stem: A friend asks, 'Can you help me with my homework?' You cannot help right now. What is the most polite way to decline?
options: I'm sorry, I can't right now. Maybe later.
hints: A polite refusal starts with 'I'm sorry'.
Suggest another time if possible.
questions.explanation: 'I'm sorry, I can't right now. Maybe later' is polite because it apologises and offers a future option.
questions.misconception: Refusing a request is always rude.

questions.stem: Picture: A pupil is carrying many books and looks tired. Which is the best polite request?
options: Can you help me carry these books, please?
hints: The picture shows someone who needs help.
The request should be polite.
questions.explanation: The picture shows a pupil needing help with books, so 'Can you help me carry these books, please?' is the best polite request.
questions.misconception: Adding 'please' to any command makes it a polite request.

questions.stem: Picture: A closed door. A pupil wants to enter. Which polite request is most suitable?
hints: The pupil is outside a closed door.
A polite request asks for permission.
questions.explanation: 'May I come in, please?' is the polite request for a closed door.
questions.misconception: Any response is fine as long as you understand the request.

questions.stem: Why is it important to be polite when making a request?
options: It shows respect and makes people more willing to help.
hints: Politeness shows respect.
People like to help those who are polite.
questions.explanation: Being polite shows respect and makes people more willing to help.
questions.misconception: Only adults need to be polite.

questions.stem: Why is it better to say 'Can you help me, please?' than 'Give me that'?
options: Because 'please' and 'can you' show respect and kindness.
hints: Polite words show kindness and respect.
People respond better to polite requests.
questions.explanation: 'Can you help me, please?' is polite and shows respect, which makes people more willing to help.
questions.misconception: Adding 'please' to any command makes it a polite request.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B3.2.2.1: Connect sounds to letters and blend letters/syllables in order to read and write
indicator.objective: Understand the relationship between spelling of words and sounds of speech

skills.description: Recognise the sound represented by individual letters or groups of letters in words.
Say the individual sounds in a simple word.
Use letter-sound knowledge to spell words correctly.
Identify the position of a target sound in a word (beginning, middle, end).
Read simple words by blending the sounds of their letters.
Explain in simple terms that letters stand for sounds in words.

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 questions at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4.
misconceptions: Each letter always makes one sound in every word.
Spelling is just memorising letters; sounds do not help.
The name of a letter is the same as its sound.
You can spell any word correctly just by guessing.
Sounds only appear at the beginning of words.

questions.stem: Which letter makes the first sound in the word 'bag'?
hints: Say the word 'bag' slowly.
Listen to the very first sound.
questions.explanation: The word 'bag' starts with the /b/ sound, which is made by the letter b.
questions.misconception: The name of a letter is the same as its sound.

questions.stem: Which letters spell the word you hear: /b/ /e/ /d/?
hints: Match each sound to a letter.
/b/ is b, /e/ is e, /d/ is d.
questions.explanation: The sounds /b/ /e/ /d/ make the word 'bed'.
questions.misconception: You can spell any word correctly just by guessing.

questions.stem: Where is the /a/ sound in the word 'mat'?
hints: Say 'mat' slowly.
The /a/ sound is the vowel in the middle.
questions.explanation: In 'mat', the /a/ sound is in the middle (m-a-t).
questions.misconception: Sounds only appear at the beginning of words.

questions.stem: Which word is 'm-a-p'?
hints: Blend the sounds together: /m/ /a/ /p/.
The first sound is /m/.
questions.explanation: Blending /m/ /a/ /p/ gives the word 'map'.
questions.misconception: Spelling is just memorising letters; sounds do not help.

questions.stem: Which letter makes the /m/ sound?
hints: Say the sound /m/.
Which letter looks like two humps?
questions.explanation: The letter m makes the /m/ sound.
questions.misconception: Each letter always makes one sound in every word.

questions.stem: Which sounds make the word 'fish'?
hints: Say 'fish' slowly.
The ending sound is /sh/.
questions.explanation: The word 'fish' is made of the sounds /f/ /i/ /sh/.
questions.misconception: Each letter always makes one sound in every word.

questions.stem: Which letters spell the word you hear: /k/ /a/ /t/?
hints: The first sound /k/ can be spelled with c.
The middle sound is /a/.
questions.explanation: The sounds /k/ /a/ /t/ make the word 'cat'.
questions.misconception: You can spell any word correctly just by guessing.

questions.stem: Which is the correct spelling for the word /d/ /o/ /g/?
hints: The middle sound is /o/.
The last sound is /g/.
questions.explanation: The sounds /d/ /o/ /g/ make the word 'dog'.
questions.misconception: Spelling is just memorising letters; sounds do not help.

questions.stem: Where is the /g/ sound in the word 'bag'?
hints: Say 'bag' slowly.
The /g/ sound comes last.
questions.explanation: In 'bag', the /g/ sound is at the end (ba-g).
questions.misconception: Sounds only appear at the beginning of words.

questions.stem: Which word is 's-u-n'?
hints: Blend the sounds: /s/ /u/ /n/.
The middle sound is /u/.
questions.explanation: Blending /s/ /u/ /n/ gives the word 'sun'.
questions.misconception: Each letter always makes one sound in every word.

questions.stem: Which letter makes the middle sound in the word 'cup'?
hints: Say 'cup' slowly.
The middle sound is /u/.
questions.explanation: In 'cup', the middle sound is /u/, made by the letter u.
questions.misconception: Each letter always makes one sound in every word.

questions.stem: Which word has the same middle sound as 'bed'?
hints: Say 'bed' and listen to the middle sound /e/.
Find the word with /e/ in the middle.
questions.explanation: 'Bed' and 'pen' both have the /e/ sound in the middle.
questions.misconception: Each letter always makes one sound in every word.

questions.stem: Which word has the /e/ sound at the beginning?
hints: Say each word and listen to the first sound.
The word 'egg' starts with /e/.
questions.explanation: 'Egg' starts with the /e/ sound.
questions.misconception: Sounds only appear at the beginning of words.

questions.stem: Which word is 'h-o-t'?
hints: Blend the sounds: /h/ /o/ /t/.
The middle sound is /o/.
questions.explanation: Blending /h/ /o/ /t/ gives the word 'hot'.
questions.misconception: Spelling is just memorising letters; sounds do not help.

questions.stem: Why is it important to know the sounds of letters when spelling?
options: It helps you spell words correctly.
hints: Sounds help you match letters to the sounds you hear.
This helps with spelling.
questions.explanation: Knowing letter sounds helps you spell words correctly because you can match each sound to the right letter.
questions.misconception: Spelling is just memorising letters; sounds do not help.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B3.2.2.1: Connect sounds to letters and blend letters/syllables in order to read and write
indicator.objective: Use the alphabetic knowledge to decode unknown words (e.g. consonant blends, consonant digraphs, vowel sounds, vowel digraphs and word patterns)

skills.description: Recognise consonant blends (e.g. bl, br, st, tr, fl, gr) in words.
Recognise common consonant and vowel digraphs (e.g. ch, sh, th, ck, ai, ee, oa, oo).
Use knowledge of blends and digraphs to read unfamiliar words.
Group words according to their blends, digraphs or vowel patterns.
Create new words using a given blend or digraph.
Explain how the blend or digraph helps them read an unknown word.

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 questions at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4.
misconceptions: Each letter in a blend or digraph makes a separate sound (e.g. 'ch' = 'c' + 'h').
Consonant blends and consonant digraphs are the same thing.
Vowel digraphs are read as two separate vowels (e.g. 'ai' = 'a' + 'i').
A blend at the beginning of a word sounds the same as at the end.
Unknown words cannot be read without the teacher's help.

questions.stem: Which word begins with the consonant blend 'st'?
hints: Say the beginning sound of each word.
Look for the word that starts with the /st/ sound.
questions.explanation: The word 'star' begins with the consonant blend 'st'.
questions.misconception: Consonant blends and consonant digraphs are the same thing.

questions.stem: What is the consonant blend at the beginning of the word 'black'?
hints: Listen to the first two sounds in 'black'.
It starts with /b/ and /l/.
questions.explanation: 'Black' starts with the consonant blend 'bl'.
questions.misconception: Each letter in a blend or digraph makes a separate sound.

questions.stem: Which word contains the digraph 'ch'?
hints: Look for the two letters 'c' and 'h' together.
The word 'chair' has 'ch' at the beginning.
questions.explanation: The word 'chair' contains the consonant digraph 'ch'.
questions.misconception: Each letter in a blend or digraph makes a separate sound.

questions.stem: What two letters make the digraph sound at the beginning of 'ship'?
hints: Say 'ship' slowly.
The first sound is /sh/.
questions.explanation: The word 'ship' begins with the digraph 'sh'.
questions.misconception: Vowel digraphs are read as two separate vowels.

questions.stem: Which word is 'tr' + 'ain'?
hints: Blend the blend 'tr' with the vowel digraph 'ai' and the sound /n/.
The word is a vehicle that runs on tracks.
questions.explanation: The blend 'tr' and the digraph 'ai' with 'n' make the word 'train'.
questions.misconception: Unknown words cannot be read without the teacher's help.

questions.stem: Which word has the same vowel digraph as 'rain'?
hints: The word 'rain' has the vowel digraph 'ai'.
Find the word that also has 'ai'.
questions.explanation: 'Rain' and 'main' both have the vowel digraph 'ai'.
questions.misconception: Vowel digraphs are read as two separate vowels.

questions.stem: What is the blend in the word 'brush'?
hints: Listen to the first two sounds of 'brush'.
The blend is at the beginning.
questions.explanation: The word 'brush' begins with the consonant blend 'br'.
questions.misconception: A blend at the beginning of a word sounds the same as at the end.

questions.stem: What is the middle sound in the word 'boat'?
hints: Say 'boat' slowly.
The middle sound is the vowel digraph 'oa'.
questions.explanation: The middle sound in 'boat' is the vowel digraph 'oa'.
questions.misconception: Vowel digraphs are read as two separate vowels.

questions.stem: Which word does NOT belong with 'chop', 'chin', and 'chat'?
hints: Look at the first two letters of each word.
Three words start with 'ch' and one starts with 'sh'.
questions.explanation: 'Chop', 'chin', 'chat', 'chalk', 'chess', and 'chick' all start with 'ch'. 'Ship' starts with 'sh', so it does not belong.
questions.misconception: Each letter in a blend or digraph makes a separate sound.

questions.stem: Which word has the same ending blend as 'jump'?
hints: The ending blend in 'jump' is 'mp'.
Look for a word that ends with 'mp'.

questions.stem: Which word has a consonant blend at the END?

questions.misconception: A blend at the beginning of a word sounds the same as at the end.

questions.misconception: Unknown words cannot be read without the teacher's help.

questions.stem: Why does the word 'shop' start with 'sh' and not 's' and 'h' separately?

questions.stem: A pupil is reading: 'The train goes down the street.' Which word has BOTH a consonant blend and a vowel digraph?

questions.stem: Which word has the diphthong 'ou'?

questions.stem: Which word has the diphthong 'oi'?

questions.explanation: The word 'coin' contains the diphthong 'oi'.

questions.stem: Which word has the diphthong 'ow'?
hints: Look for the letters 'o' and 'w' together.
The word 'cow' has 'ow'.
questions.explanation: The word 'cow' contains the diphthong 'ow'.
questions.misconception: Words with ou and ow always sound completely different.

questions.stem: Which word can you make with the diphthong 'ou'?
