Say 'loud' aloud.
questions.explanation: The word 'loud' is built with the diphthong 'ou'.
questions.misconception: You can spell any diphthong word however it sounds to you.

questions.stem: Complete the word: h__se (a building where people live).

questions.explanation: The word is 'house', completed with the diphthong 'ou'.
questions.misconception: A diphthong is just two separate vowels sounded separately.

questions.stem: Which word has the same diphthong as 'boy'?

questions.stem: Which word can you build with the diphthong 'ai'?

Say 'rain' aloud.
questions.explanation: The word 'rain' is built with the diphthong 'ai'.
questions.misconception: You can spell any diphthong word however it sounds to you.

questions.stem: Which set of words all have the 'ow' diphthong?

questions.misconception: Words with ou and ow always sound completely different.

questions.stem: Which word does NOT have the 'ou' diphthong?

questions.misconception: Any two vowels together make a diphthong.

questions.stem: Sort these words into two groups: 'coin', 'cow', 'boy', 'house'. Which words go with 'coin'?

Find the word with the same diphthong.
questions.explanation: 'Coin' and 'boy' have diphthongs that sound similar ('oi' and 'oy').
questions.misconception: Words with ou and ow always sound completely different.

questions.stem: Complete the word: cl__d (in the sky).
hints: Say the word 'cloud' aloud.
Listen to the vowel sound.
questions.explanation: The word is 'cloud', completed with the diphthong 'ou'.
questions.misconception: A diphthong is just two separate vowels sounded separately.

questions.stem: Complete the word: r__n (water falling from clouds).

Listen to the vowel sound in the middle.
questions.explanation: The word is 'rain', completed with the diphthong 'ai'.
questions.misconception: Any two vowels together make a diphthong.

questions.stem: Which word has BOTH a diphthong and a consonant blend?

questions.misconception: Diphthongs and consonant blends are the same thing.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses a word with a diphthong correctly?

Only one sentence makes sense and uses a diphthong word.
questions.explanation: 'The cow is eating grass' uses 'cow', which has the diphthong 'ow'.
questions.misconception: You can spell any diphthong word however it sounds to you.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence with a word that has a diphthong: 'I can hear the ___ of the dog.'
hints: The word must make sense in the sentence.
'Sound' has the diphthong 'ou'.
questions.explanation: 'Sound' has the diphthong 'ou' and fits the sentence: 'I can hear the sound of the dog.'
questions.misconception: Any two vowels together make a diphthong.

questions.stem: A pupil sorts these words: 'train', 'cloud', 'rain', 'loud'. Which group is correct?
options: Group 1: train, rain (ai); Group 2: cloud, loud (ou)

Group 1: train, loud (ou); Group 2: cloud, rain (ai)
All words have the same diphthong
hints: Look at the vowel pattern in each word.

questions.misconception: Any two vowels together make a diphthong.

questions.stem: Which word has a diphthong and NOT just a single vowel?

'Boy' has the diphthong 'oy'.
questions.explanation: 'Boy' has the diphthong 'oy', while 'cat', 'sit', and 'pen' have single vowels.
questions.misconception: A diphthong is just two separate vowels sounded separately.

questions.stem: Which word has a single vowel sound and NOT a diphthong?
hints: 'House' has 'ou', 'rain' has 'ai', 'boy' has 'oy'.
'Dog' has a single vowel 'o'.
questions.explanation: 'Dog' has a single vowel sound /o/, while the other words contain diphthongs.
questions.misconception: Any two vowels together make a diphthong.

indicator.subject: English Language

indicator.objective: Use consonant blends to build words

skills.description: Recognise consonant blends at the beginning or end of words.
Generate and spell words using a given consonant blend.
Group words according to their initial or final consonant blends.
Fill in the missing consonant blend to complete a word.
Use words containing consonant blends in simple, meaningful sentences.
Tell the difference between a blend where both letters are heard and a digraph where a new sound is made.

misconceptions: Consonant blends and consonant digraphs are the same thing.
Every letter in a blend is pronounced exactly like its alphabet name.
Consonant blends only come at the beginning of a word.
Any two consonants together make a blend.
You can spell any blend word however it sounds to you.

questions.stem: Which word begins with the consonant blend 'br'?
hints: Say the first two sounds of each word.
The word 'bread' starts with /br/.
questions.explanation: The word 'bread' begins with the consonant blend 'br'.
questions.misconception: Consonant blends and consonant digraphs are the same thing.

questions.stem: Which word ends with the consonant blend 'st'?
hints: Listen to the last two sounds of each word.
The word 'nest' ends with /st/.
questions.explanation: The word 'nest' ends with the consonant blend 'st'.
questions.misconception: Consonant blends only come at the beginning of a word.

questions.stem: Which word can you make with the blend 'fl' and the ending 'ower'?
hints: Put 'fl' before 'ower'.
The word is a plant with petals.
questions.explanation: Adding 'fl' to 'ower' makes the word 'flower'.
questions.misconception: You can spell any blend word however it sounds to you.

questions.stem: Complete the word: __ue (a colour).
hints: Say the word 'blue' aloud.
It starts with the /bl/ sound.
questions.explanation: The word is 'blue', completed with the blend 'bl'.
questions.misconception: Every letter in a blend is pronounced exactly like its alphabet name.

questions.stem: In the word 'ship', are the letters 'sh' a blend or a digraph?
hints: In a digraph, two letters make one new sound.
Say 'sh' aloud; it is one sound, not /s/ and /h/.
questions.explanation: 'Sh' is a digraph because the two letters make one new sound (/sh/), not two separate sounds.
questions.misconception: Consonant blends and consonant digraphs are the same thing.

questions.stem: Which word has a consonant blend at the beginning?
hints: Look for two consonants together at the start.
The word 'stop' begins with 'st'.
questions.explanation: The word 'stop' begins with the consonant blend 'st'.
questions.misconception: Consonant blends only come at the beginning of a word.

questions.stem: Which word can you build with the blend 'gr'?

Grass grows on the ground.
questions.explanation: The word 'grass' is built with the blend 'gr'.
questions.misconception: Any two consonants together make a blend.

questions.stem: Which word does NOT begin with the blend 'tr'?
hints: Look at the first two letters of each word.
Three words start with 'tr'. One starts with 'ta'.
questions.explanation: 'Tree', 'train', and 'tray' start with 'tr'. 'Table' starts with 'ta', so it does not belong.
questions.misconception: Any two consonants together make a blend.

questions.stem: Sort these words into two groups: 'stop', 'star', 'skip', 'skin'. Which words have the blend 'st'?
hints: Look for the letters 'st' together.
'Stop' and 'star' both begin with 'st'.
questions.explanation: 'Stop' and 'star' both have the blend 'st'. 'Skip' and 'skin' have the blend 'sk'.

questions.stem: Complete the word: __ue (the opposite of old).

It starts with the blend 'bl'.
questions.explanation: The word is 'blue', completed with the blend 'bl'.
questions.misconception: Every letter in a blend is pronounced exactly like its alphabet name.

It starts with the blend 'st'.
questions.explanation: The word is 'stop', completed with the blend 'st'.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses a word with the blend 'gr'?

Only one sentence uses a word starting with 'gr'.
questions.explanation: 'The grass is green' uses 'grass', which begins with the blend 'gr'.
questions.misconception: Consonant blends and consonant digraphs are the same thing.

questions.stem: Which set of words all have the blend 'st'?

Check each word's first two letters.
questions.explanation: 'Stop', 'star', and 'stone' all have the blend 'st'.
questions.misconception: Any two consonants together make a blend.

questions.stem: Which word can you build with the blend 'sk'?
hints: The word must start with 'sk'.
Skip means to jump lightly.
questions.explanation: The word 'skip' is built with the blend 'sk'.
questions.misconception: Consonant blends only come at the beginning of a word.

questions.stem: Which word has a blend at the END?
hints: Listen to the last two sounds.
The word 'jump' ends with 'mp'.
questions.explanation: The word 'jump' ends with the consonant blend 'mp'.
questions.misconception: Consonant blends only come at the beginning of a word.

questions.stem: Complete the word: __ain (a vehicle that runs on tracks).
hints: The word is 'train'.
It starts with the blend 'tr'.
questions.explanation: The word is 'train', completed with the blend 'tr'.
questions.misconception: You can spell any blend word however it sounds to you.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses a word with the blend 'tr'?
options: The pen is on the table.
hints: 'Train' begins with 'tr'.
Only one sentence uses a word starting with 'tr'.
questions.explanation: 'The train is coming' uses 'train', which begins with the blend 'tr'.
questions.misconception: Consonant blends and consonant digraphs are the same thing.

questions.stem: A pupil is sorting words into two groups: words with 'bl' and words with 'br'. Which word belongs in the 'bl' group?

'Black' starts with 'bl'.
questions.explanation: 'Black' has the blend 'bl'. 'Bread', 'brown', and 'brush' have the blend 'br'.
questions.misconception: Any two consonants together make a blend.

questions.stem: Which of these is a consonant blend (both letters are heard separately) and NOT a digraph?

In 'stop', you hear /s/ and /t/ separately.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B3.2.6.1: Understand word meanings and usage
indicator.objective: Read level-appropriate sight words, understand and use them in meaningful complex sentences

skills.description: Read common sight words automatically.
Show understanding of what a sight word means in context.
Use sight words to form meaningful complex sentences.
Fill in blanks in sentences with the correct sight word.
Find and circle sight words in a short passage.
Identify and fix incorrect use of a sight word in a sentence.

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 questions at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4.
misconceptions: Sight words are only for beginners and can be ignored in Basic 3.
Any word can be used in any sentence.
Complex sentences must be long and difficult.
Sight words and content words are the same.
You can spell sight words however you like because they are common.

questions.stem: Which of these is a sight word?
hints: Sight words are common words you see often.
They are usually short words like 'the', 'and', 'is'.
questions.explanation: 'The' is a common sight word that appears often in reading.
questions.misconception: Sight words are only for beginners and can be ignored in Basic 3.

questions.stem: Which word is a sight word?
hints: Sight words are high-frequency words.
They are often short and common.
questions.explanation: 'And' is a sight word because it is a common word used often in sentences.
questions.misconception: Sight words and content words are the same.

questions.stem: Which word is a sight word?
hints: Sight words are common and often short.
'They' is a pronoun used often.
questions.explanation: 'They' is a sight word because it is a common pronoun.
questions.misconception: Sight words are only for beginners and can be ignored in Basic 3.

questions.stem: What does the word 'because' mean in a sentence?
hints: 'Because' connects a reason to an action.
It answers the question 'why?'.
questions.explanation: 'Because' is a sight word that shows a reason, like in 'I am happy because it is my birthday.'
questions.misconception: Any word can be used in any sentence.

questions.stem: In the sentence 'They played with it in the yard', what does 'it' refer to?
hints: Look at the sentence before.
What did the children have?
questions.explanation: 'It' refers to the new ball mentioned earlier in the passage.
questions.misconception: Sight words and content words are the same.

questions.stem: What does 'when' mean in the sentence 'When it started to rain, they went inside'?
hints: 'When' tells you at what time something happens.
It answers the question 'when?'.
questions.explanation: 'When' is a sight word that shows time, indicating the moment the rain started.
questions.misconception: Any word can be used in any sentence.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence: 'I am happy ___ it is my birthday.'
hints: The sentence gives a reason for being happy.
Use the word that means 'for the reason that'.
questions.explanation: 'Because' is the correct sight word to show the reason for being happy.
questions.misconception: Any word can be used in any sentence.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence: 'She wanted to go out, ___ it was raining.'
hints: The sentence shows a contrast.
Use the word that means 'however'.
questions.explanation: 'But' is the correct sight word to show contrast between wanting to go out and the rain.
questions.misconception: Complex sentences must be long and difficult.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence: 'We stayed inside ___ the rain stopped.'
hints: The sentence shows how long they stayed inside.
Use the word that means 'up to the time when'.
questions.explanation: 'Until' is the correct sight word meaning 'up to the time when' the rain stopped.
questions.misconception: Sight words and content words are the same.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence: '___ they were playing, it started to rain.'
hints: The sentence tells what was happening when the rain started.
Use the word that means 'during the time that'.
questions.explanation: 'While' is the correct sight word meaning 'during the time that' they were playing.
questions.misconception: Complex sentences must be long and difficult.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the sight word 'because' correctly?
options: I like rice because it is tasty.
hints: 'Because' should connect a reason to an action.
It needs a complete idea after it.
questions.explanation: 'I like rice because it is tasty' correctly uses 'because' to give a reason.
questions.misconception: Any word can be used in any sentence.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the sight word 'but' correctly?
options: I wanted to play, but it was raining.
hints: 'But' joins two contrasting ideas.
Both parts of the sentence must be complete.
questions.explanation: 'I wanted to play, but it was raining' correctly uses 'but' to join two contrasting ideas.
questions.misconception: Complex sentences must be long and difficult.

questions.stem: In the passage, which word is a sight word?
hints: Look for a common, short word.
'They' is a pronoun used often.
questions.explanation: 'They' is a sight word because it is a common pronoun.
questions.misconception: Sight words and content words are the same.

questions.stem: Find the mistake: 'I am happy but it is my birthday.'
hints: The sentence gives a reason for being happy.
'But' shows contrast, not reason.
questions.explanation: The correct sentence is 'I am happy because it is my birthday.' 'But' should be 'because'.
questions.misconception: Any word can be used in any sentence.

questions.stem: Find the mistake: 'She wanted to go out because it was raining.'
hints: The sentence shows a contrast: wanting to go out vs. rain.
'Because' shows a reason, not contrast.
questions.explanation: The correct sentence is 'She wanted to go out, but it was raining.' 'Because' should be 'but'.
questions.misconception: Any word can be used in any sentence.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B3.2.6.1: Understand word meanings and usage
indicator.objective: Use knowledge of prefixes and suffixes to interpret unfamiliar words

skills.description: Recognise a prefix at the beginning of a word.
Recognise a suffix at the end of a word.
Explain how a prefix or suffix changes the meaning of a root word.
Use prefix/suffix knowledge to work out the meaning of an unfamiliar word in a sentence.
Create new words by adding a prefix or suffix to a root word.
Match a prefixed or suffixed word to its correct meaning.

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 questions at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4.
misconceptions: A prefix or suffix is a whole word on its own.
Adding a prefix always changes a word to its opposite.
A suffix never changes the meaning of a word.
Any group of letters at the start of a word is a prefix.
You can guess the meaning of a word without looking at its parts.

questions.stem: What is the prefix in the word 'unhappy'?
hints: A prefix comes at the beginning of a word.
Look at the first two letters.
questions.explanation: The prefix in 'unhappy' is 'un-', which changes the meaning of 'happy'.
questions.misconception: A prefix or suffix is a whole word on its own.

questions.stem: What is the prefix in the word 'redo'?
hints: The prefix comes before the root word.
The root word is 'do'.
questions.explanation: The prefix in 'redo' is 're-', meaning 'again'.
questions.misconception: Any group of letters at the start of a word is a prefix.

questions.stem: What is the suffix in the word 'careful'?
hints: A suffix comes at the end of a word.
Look at the last three letters.
questions.explanation: The suffix in 'careful' is '-ful', meaning 'full of care'.
questions.misconception: A suffix never changes the meaning of a word.

questions.stem: What is the suffix in the word 'quickly'?
hints: The suffix is at the end.
It often turns an adjective into an adverb.
questions.explanation: The suffix in 'quickly' is '-ly', which tells us how something is done.
questions.misconception: Any group of letters at the end of a word is a suffix.

questions.stem: How does the prefix 'un-' change the meaning of 'kind'?
options: It does not change the meaning
hints: 'Un-' often means 'not'.
Think of 'unhappy'.
questions.explanation: The prefix 'un-' changes 'kind' to 'unkind', meaning 'not kind'.
questions.misconception: Adding a prefix always changes a word to its opposite.

questions.stem: What does the suffix '-less' do to the word 'hope'?
hints: '-less' means 'without'.
Think of 'careless'.
questions.explanation: The suffix '-less' changes 'hope' to 'hopeless', meaning 'without hope'.
questions.misconception: A suffix never changes the meaning of a word.

questions.stem: What does the word 'disagree' mean?
hints: The prefix 'dis-' often means 'not' or 'opposite'.
Think of 'dislike'.
questions.explanation: The prefix 'dis-' changes 'agree' to 'disagree', meaning 'to not agree'.
questions.misconception: Adding a prefix always changes a word to its opposite.

questions.stem: Read the sentence: 'The teacher asked the pupils to rewrite the sentence.' What does 'rewrite' mean?
hints: The prefix 're-' means 'again'.
So 'rewrite' means to write again.
questions.explanation: 'Rewrite' means to write again, using the prefix 're-' meaning 'again'.
questions.misconception: You can guess the meaning of a word without looking at its parts.

questions.stem: Read: 'The baby was playful and happy.' What does 'playful' mean?
hints: The suffix '-ful' means 'full of'.
So 'playful' means full of play.
questions.explanation: 'Playful' means full of play or fun, using the suffix '-ful' meaning 'full of'.
questions.misconception: A suffix never changes the meaning of a word.

questions.stem: Read: 'The soup was tasteless.' What does 'tasteless' mean?
hints: The suffix '-less' means 'without'.
So 'tasteless' means without taste.
questions.explanation: 'Tasteless' means without taste, using the suffix '-less' meaning 'without'.
questions.misconception: A suffix never changes the meaning of a word.

questions.stem: Add the prefix 'un-' to 'happy' to make a new word. Which word is it?
hints: Put 'un-' before 'happy'.
It means 'not happy'.
questions.explanation: Adding 'un-' to 'happy' makes 'unhappy'.
questions.misconception: A prefix or suffix is a whole word on its own.

questions.stem: Add the suffix '-ful' to 'care' to make a new word. Which word is it?
hints: Put '-ful' after 'care'.
It means 'full of care'.
questions.explanation: Adding '-ful' to 'care' makes 'careful'.
questions.misconception: A suffix never changes the meaning of a word.

questions.stem: Which word means 'not happy'?
hints: Use the prefix 'un-'.
It means 'not'.
questions.explanation: 'Unhappy' means not happy, using the prefix 'un-'.
questions.misconception: A prefix or suffix is a whole word on its own.

questions.stem: Which word means 'full of beauty'?
hints: The suffix '-ful' means 'full of'.
Add '-ful' to 'beauty'.
questions.explanation: 'Beautiful' means full of beauty, using the suffix '-ful'.
questions.misconception: A suffix never changes the meaning of a word.

questions.stem: Which word means 'to not agree'?
hints: Use the prefix 'dis-'.
It means 'not' or 'opposite'.
questions.explanation: 'Disagree' means to not agree, using the prefix 'dis-'.
questions.misconception: Adding a prefix always changes a word to its opposite.

questions.stem: Which word means 'without fear'?
hints: The suffix '-less' means 'without'.
Add '-less' to 'fear'.
questions.explanation: 'Fearless' means without fear, using the suffix '-less'.
questions.misconception: A suffix never changes the meaning of a word.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B3.2.6.1: Understand word meanings and usage
indicator.objective: Understand and use many of the frequently occurring words and chunks in the language, including both content words (nouns, verbs, adjectives and adverbs) and function words (prepositions, articles)

skills.description: Recognise nouns, verbs, adjectives and adverbs in sentences.
Recognise prepositions and articles in sentences.
Use content words correctly in simple sentences.
Use prepositions and articles correctly in simple sentences.
Sort a list of words into content and function words.
Use common word chunks or phrases correctly in sentences.

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 questions at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4.
misconceptions: Function words are not important because they are short.
Adjectives and adverbs are the same thing.
Any preposition can be used in any sentence.
Articles are not real words.
You can leave out prepositions in a sentence and it will still make sense.

questions.stem: Which word in this sentence is a noun? 'The dog is barking.'
hints: A noun names a person, animal, place or thing.
What animal is in the sentence?
questions.explanation: 'Dog' is a noun because it names an animal.
questions.misconception: Function words are not important because they are short.

questions.stem: Which word in this sentence is a verb? 'The children play in the park.'
hints: A verb is an action word.
What are the children doing?
questions.explanation: 'Play' is a verb because it is an action word.
questions.misconception: Adjectives and adverbs are the same thing.

questions.stem: Which word in this sentence is an adjective? 'I saw a big house.'
hints: An adjective describes a noun.
Which word tells you the size of the house?
questions.explanation: 'Big' is an adjective because it describes the size of the house.
questions.misconception: Adjectives and adverbs are the same thing.

questions.stem: Which word in this sentence is a preposition? 'The cat is under the table.'
hints: A preposition shows where something is.
Where is the cat?
questions.explanation: 'Under' is a preposition because it tells us where the cat is.
questions.misconception: You can leave out prepositions in a sentence and it will still make sense.

questions.stem: Which word in this sentence is an article? 'She has a pencil.'
hints: Articles are 'a', 'an', and 'the'.
Which word comes before 'pencil'?
questions.explanation: 'A' is an article because it comes before the noun 'pencil'.
questions.misconception: Articles are not real words.

questions.stem: Which word in this sentence is an adverb? 'He ran quickly to school.'
hints: An adverb describes how an action is done.
How did he run?
questions.explanation: 'Quickly' is an adverb because it tells us how he ran.
questions.misconception: Adjectives and adverbs are the same thing.

questions.stem: Which word in this sentence is a preposition? 'The book is on the desk.'
hints: A preposition shows position or direction.
Where is the book?
questions.explanation: 'On' is a preposition because it shows the position of the book.
questions.misconception: Any preposition can be used in any sentence.

questions.stem: Which word in this sentence is an article? 'The boy is playing with a ball.'
hints: Articles are 'a', 'an', and 'the'.
Which word comes before 'boy'?
questions.explanation: 'The' is an article because it comes before the noun 'boy'.
questions.misconception: Articles are not real words.

questions.stem: Choose the best verb to complete the sentence: 'The bird ___ in the sky.'
hints: A verb is an action word.
What does a bird do in the sky?
questions.explanation: 'Flies' is the correct verb because it shows the action of the bird.
questions.misconception: Function words are not important because they are short.

questions.stem: Choose the best adjective to complete the sentence: 'The ___ elephant is walking.'
hints: An adjective describes a noun.
Which word describes the elephant?
questions.explanation: 'Big' is the correct adjective because it describes the elephant.
questions.misconception: Adjectives and adverbs are the same thing.

questions.stem: Choose the correct preposition: 'The pen is ___ the table.'
hints: A pen usually sits on top of a table.
The preposition 'on' shows position.
questions.explanation: 'On' is the correct preposition because the pen is on top of the table.
questions.misconception: Any preposition can be used in any sentence.

questions.stem: Choose the correct article: 'I saw ___ elephant at the zoo.'
hints: Use 'an' before a word that starts with a vowel sound.
'Elephant' starts with /e/.
questions.explanation: 'An' is the correct article because 'elephant' starts with a vowel sound.
questions.misconception: Articles are not real words.

questions.stem: Choose the correct preposition: 'The pupils are sitting ___ the classroom.'
hints: The pupils are inside the classroom.
Use the preposition that means 'inside'.
questions.explanation: 'In' is the correct preposition because it means the pupils are inside the classroom.
questions.misconception: Any preposition can be used in any sentence.

questions.stem: Which word is a function word?
hints: Function words are short words like prepositions and articles.
'Under' is a preposition.
questions.explanation: 'Under' is a function word because it is a preposition.
questions.misconception: Function words are not important because they are short.

questions.stem: Sort these words: 'table', 'the', 'jump', 'happy', 'on', 'a'. Which group is correct?
options: Content words: table, jump, happy; Function words: the, on, a
Content words: the, on, a; Function words: table, jump, happy
Content words: table, the, on; Function words: jump, happy, a
Content words: table, jump, the; Function words: happy, on, a
hints: Content words include nouns, verbs and adjectives.
Function words include prepositions and articles.
questions.explanation: Content words are 'table' (noun), 'jump' (verb), and 'happy' (adjective). Function words are 'the' (article), 'on' (preposition), and 'a' (article).
questions.misconception: Function words are not important because they are short.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the chunk 'in the morning' correctly?
options: I brush my teeth in the morning.
I brush my teeth on the morning.
I brush my teeth at the morning.
I brush my teeth under the morning.
hints: The correct chunk is 'in the morning'.
Prepositions in chunks are fixed.
questions.explanation: 'In the morning' is the correct chunk. We do not say 'on the morning' or 'at the morning'.
questions.misconception: Any preposition can be used in any sentence.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence with the correct chunk: 'We go to school ___.'
hints: The correct chunk for travelling by vehicle is 'by bus'.
We say 'by car', 'by train', 'by bus'.
questions.explanation: 'By bus' is the correct chunk for travelling by vehicle.
questions.misconception: You can leave out prepositions in a sentence and it will still make sense.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B3.2.6.1: Understand word meanings and usage
indicator.objective: Use dictionaries, glossaries and internet to clarify word meanings

skills.description: Use guide words at the top of a dictionary page to find a word quickly.
Locate and read the meaning of a word in a dictionary.
Use a glossary to find the meaning of a word from a textbook or story.
Choose the meaning that fits the word in a specific sentence when there is more than one meaning.
Create a simple personal glossary with new words and their meanings.
Use a dictionary to check and correct the spelling of a word.

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 questions at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4.
misconceptions: A dictionary shows only one meaning for each word.
Guide words are the first and last words in the whole dictionary.
A glossary is the same as a dictionary.
You can find any word by opening the dictionary at random.
The internet always gives the correct meaning.

questions.stem: What are guide words in a dictionary?
options: The first and last words on a page
hints: Guide words help you find a word quickly.
They are at the top of each page.
questions.explanation: Guide words are the first and last words on a dictionary page.
questions.misconception: Guide words are the first and last words in the whole dictionary.

questions.stem: The guide words on a page are 'apple' and 'ant'. Which word would you find on that page?
hints: The word must come between 'apple' and 'ant' alphabetically.
'Animal' starts with 'an', which is between 'ap' and 'an'.
questions.explanation: 'Animal' comes between 'apple' and 'ant' alphabetically, so it would be on that page.
questions.misconception: You can find any word by opening the dictionary at random.

questions.stem: Guide words: 'book' and 'boot'. Which word is on this page?
hints: The word must come between 'book' and 'boot'.
'Boat' starts with 'boa', which is before 'boo'.
questions.explanation: 'Boat' comes between 'book' and 'boot' alphabetically.
questions.misconception: Guide words are the first and last words in the whole dictionary.

questions.stem: Where do you look to find the meaning of a word?
hints: A dictionary gives word meanings.
It is a reference book.
questions.explanation: A dictionary is used to find the meaning of words.
questions.misconception: A dictionary shows only one meaning for each word.

questions.stem: A dictionary entry for 'bat' shows two meanings: 1. a small animal that flies at night, 2. a wooden stick used in games. Which meaning fits this sentence? 'The boy hit the ball with his bat.'
hints: The sentence is about playing a game.
A bat is used to hit a ball.
questions.explanation: In this sentence, 'bat' means the wooden stick used in games (Meaning 2).
questions.misconception: A dictionary shows only one meaning for each word.

questions.stem: A dictionary entry for 'bank' shows: 1. a place where money is kept, 2. the side of a river. Which meaning fits: 'We sat on the bank of the river.'?
hints: The sentence is about a river.
The side of a river is called a bank.
questions.explanation: In this sentence, 'bank' means the side of a river (Meaning 2).
questions.misconception: A dictionary shows only one meaning for each word.

questions.stem: What is a glossary?
options: A list of words and their meanings at the back of a book
A dictionary of all English words
hints: A glossary is found in a textbook.
It explains difficult words from the book.
questions.explanation: A glossary is a list of words and their meanings, often found at the back of a book.
questions.misconception: A glossary is the same as a dictionary.

questions.stem: A science book has a glossary. It lists 'habitat: the place where an animal lives'. What does 'habitat' mean?
options: The place where an animal lives
hints: The glossary tells you directly.
It is about where an animal lives.
questions.explanation: According to the glossary, 'habitat' means the place where an animal lives.
questions.misconception: A glossary is the same as a dictionary.

questions.stem: A storybook has a glossary with the word 'enormous: very big'. What is the meaning of 'enormous'?
hints: The glossary gives the meaning.
'Enormous' means very big.
questions.explanation: The glossary says 'enormous' means very big.
questions.misconception: A glossary is the same as a dictionary.

questions.stem: The word 'light' can mean 'not heavy' or 'brightness'. Which meaning fits: 'The bag was light to carry.'?
hints: The sentence is about carrying a bag.
If a bag is easy to carry, it is not heavy.
questions.explanation: In this sentence, 'light' means not heavy.
questions.misconception: A dictionary shows only one meaning for each word.

questions.stem: The word 'bark' can mean 'the sound a dog makes' or 'the outer covering of a tree'. Which meaning fits: 'The bark of the tree was rough.'?
options: The outer covering of a tree
hints: The sentence is about a tree.
Trees have bark on the outside.
questions.explanation: In this sentence, 'bark' means the outer covering of a tree.
questions.misconception: A dictionary shows only one meaning for each word.

questions.stem: The word 'watch' can mean 'to look at' or 'a small clock worn on the wrist'. Which meaning fits: 'She looked at her watch to check the time.'?
options: A small clock worn on the wrist
hints: She is checking the time.
A watch tells time.
questions.explanation: In this sentence, 'watch' means a small clock worn on the wrist.
questions.misconception: A dictionary shows only one meaning for each word.

questions.stem: What should a personal glossary include?
hints: A glossary helps you remember words.
It lists words and what they mean.
questions.explanation: A personal glossary should include new words and their meanings.
questions.misconception: The internet always gives the correct meaning.

questions.stem: You are not sure how to spell the word that means 'a place where sick people are treated'. Which spelling is correct?
hints: Check the dictionary.
The correct spelling is 'hospital'.
questions.explanation: The correct spelling is 'hospital'. A dictionary can help you check spelling.
questions.misconception: The internet always gives the correct meaning.

questions.stem: Which word is spelled correctly?
hints: Check each spelling in a dictionary.
The correct spelling is 'beautiful'.
questions.explanation: The correct spelling is 'beautiful'.
questions.misconception: You can find any word by opening the dictionary at random.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B3.2.7.1: Understand and analyse texts read
indicator.objective: Use self-correction strategies to make meaning when reading texts

skills.description: Notice when a word or sentence does not make sense while reading.
Use strategies to fix reading errors (e.g. rereading, sounding out, looking at pictures, asking a peer).
Reread a sentence or paragraph to correct a misunderstanding.
Use surrounding words or pictures to figure out a tricky word.
Pause and correct a word immediately after saying it incorrectly during read-aloud.
Explain what they do when they get stuck on a word.

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 questions at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4.
misconceptions: Good readers never make mistakes.
If I don't understand a word, I should just skip it and keep reading fast.
Reading fast is more important than reading correctly.
Self-correction means stopping and asking the teacher every time.

questions.stem: If you read a sentence and it does not make sense, what should you do?
hints: If it does not make sense, you need to fix it.
Good readers stop to check.
questions.explanation: When a sentence does not make sense, you should stop and think about it to fix the meaning.
questions.misconception: If I don't understand a word, I should just skip it and keep reading fast.

questions.stem: A pupil reads: 'The cat barked at the moon.' What is wrong with this sentence?
options: The moon is not in the sky.
Cats do not like the moon.
hints: Think about what cats do.
Cats meow, they do not bark.
questions.explanation: The sentence does not make sense because cats meow, they do not bark. The pupil should notice this and self-correct.
questions.misconception: Good readers never make mistakes.

questions.stem: A pupil reads: 'The fish flew in the sky.' Why should the pupil stop and self-correct?
options: Because the sentence is too long.
hints: Think about what fish can do.
Fish swim, they do not fly.
questions.explanation: The sentence does not make sense because fish cannot fly. A good reader would notice this and self-correct.
questions.misconception: Good readers never make mistakes.

questions.stem: What is a good strategy when you do not understand a word?
options: Look at the pictures or words around it
Ask a friend to read it for you
hints: Pictures and surrounding words can help.
This is called using context clues.
questions.explanation: Looking at pictures or the words around a tricky word can help you figure out its meaning.
questions.misconception: If I don't understand a word, I should just skip it and keep reading fast.

questions.stem: You are reading and you say 'house' instead of 'horse'. What should you do?
hints: You made a mistake.
Good readers fix their mistakes.
questions.explanation: If you say the wrong word, you should go back and correct yourself to make sure the sentence makes sense.
questions.misconception: Self-correction means stopping and asking the teacher every time.

questions.stem: Which strategy helps you read a difficult word?
hints: Break the word into sounds.
Say each sound and blend them.
questions.explanation: Sounding out the word by saying each sound and blending them can help you read a difficult word.
questions.misconception: If I don't understand a word, I should just skip it and keep reading fast.

questions.stem: A pupil reads: 'The boy ate the ball.' Then he says, 'That doesn't make sense.' What should he do next?
hints: Rereading helps you check the words.
Maybe he read 'ball' instead of 'apple'.
questions.explanation: Rereading the sentence can help him see if he misread a word, like reading 'ball' instead of 'apple'.
questions.misconception: Good readers never make mistakes.

questions.stem: A pupil reads: 'The dog flew over the fence.' He stops and rereads the sentence. Why is rereading helpful here?
options: It helps him notice the mistake and fix it.
It helps him forget the mistake.
hints: Rereading helps you check if the words make sense.
Dogs cannot fly, so rereading helps him spot the error.
questions.explanation: Rereading helps the pupil notice that 'flew' is wrong and correct it to a word that makes sense.
questions.misconception: Reading fast is more important than reading correctly.

questions.stem: When is it a good idea to reread a sentence?
options: When it does not make sense
When it has a full stop
When it has a long word
hints: Rereading helps fix meaning.
Do it when something is confusing.
questions.explanation: You should reread a sentence when it does not make sense, to fix the meaning.
questions.misconception: If I don't understand a word, I should just skip it and keep reading fast.

questions.stem: Read: 'The farmer planted seeds in the soil. The seeds will grow into ___.' What word makes sense?
hints: What grows from seeds?
Use the clue 'farmer' and 'soil'.
questions.explanation: The context tells us the farmer planted seeds, so they will grow into plants.
questions.misconception: If I don't understand a word, I should just skip it and keep reading fast.

questions.stem: Read: 'The sky was dark and cloudy. Soon, ___ started to fall.' What word makes sense?
hints: Dark clouds often bring this.
It falls from the sky.
questions.explanation: Dark clouds and falling suggest rain, so 'rain' makes sense in the context.
questions.misconception: If I don't understand a word, I should just skip it and keep reading fast.

questions.stem: Read: 'The pupils were very hungry. They went to the ___ to buy food.' Which word fits best?
hints: Where do pupils buy food at school?
The clue is 'hungry' and 'buy food'.
questions.explanation: The context of being hungry and buying food points to the canteen.
questions.misconception: Good readers never make mistakes.

questions.stem: What should you do if you read a word incorrectly?
hints: Self-correction means fixing your mistake.
Go back and say the word correctly.
questions.explanation: When you read a word incorrectly, you should go back and correct it so the sentence makes sense.
questions.misconception: If I don't understand a word, I should just skip it and keep reading fast.

questions.stem: Why do good readers self-correct?
options: To make sure they understand what they read
hints: Self-correction helps understanding.
Good readers want to understand the text.
questions.explanation: Good readers self-correct to make sure they understand what they read.
questions.misconception: Reading fast is more important than reading correctly.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B3.2.7.1: Understand and analyse texts read
indicator.objective: Ask and answer factual, inferential and vocabulary questions about level-appropriate texts

skills.description: Answer questions whose answers are directly stated in the text.
Answer questions that require reading between the lines.
Use context to explain the meaning of a word from the text.
Form relevant factual, inferential or vocabulary questions about a text.
Point to the part of the text that supports an answer.
Tell whether a question is factual, inferential or vocabulary.

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 questions at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4.
misconceptions: The answer to an inferential question is always written directly in the text.
You can answer any question just by guessing.
A vocabulary question is just asking for a dictionary definition.
Factual questions are the only important type.

questions.stem: Where did Adwoa and her mother go?
hints: The first sentence tells you where they went.
They wanted to buy tomatoes and onions.
questions.explanation: The text says Adwoa and her mother went to the market in Techiman.
questions.misconception: Factual questions are the only important type.

questions.stem: What did Adwoa and her mother want to buy at the market?
hints: Read the second sentence.
They were going to buy vegetables.
questions.explanation: The text says they wanted to buy tomatoes and onions.
questions.misconception: You can answer any question just by guessing.

questions.stem: Why did Adwoa ask her mother for money?
hints: Adwoa was very thirsty.
She saw a woman selling something cold.
questions.explanation: Adwoa was thirsty, so she asked for money to buy cold water.
questions.misconception: The answer to an inferential question is always written directly in the text.

questions.stem: How did Adwoa feel after drinking the water?
hints: Look at the sentence after she drank the water.
The water helped her.
questions.explanation: The text says after drinking the water, Adwoa felt much better.
questions.misconception: Factual questions are the only important type.

questions.stem: Why was Adwoa thirsty?
hints: The first sentence tells you about the weather.
Think about how you feel on a hot day.
questions.explanation: The text says it was a hot afternoon, which is why Adwoa was thirsty.
questions.misconception: The answer to an inferential question is always written directly in the text.

questions.stem: How do we know that Adwoa's mother cared about her?
options: She gave Adwoa money to buy water.
She told Adwoa to stop complaining.
hints: Her mother did something kind for her.
She gave Adwoa something to buy water with.
questions.explanation: We know her mother cared because she gave Adwoa a coin to buy water when she was thirsty.
questions.misconception: The answer to an inferential question is always written directly in the text.

questions.stem: What might have happened if Adwoa had not drunk any water?
options: She would have felt even more thirsty and tired.
hints: She was already very thirsty.
Without water, her thirst would get worse.
questions.explanation: If Adwoa had not drunk water, she would have felt even more thirsty and tired because it was a hot day.
questions.misconception: You can answer any question just by guessing.

questions.stem: What does the word 'thirsty' mean in the story?
hints: Adwoa wanted to buy water.
Thirsty means your body needs water.
questions.explanation: 'Thirsty' means needing water. Adwoa wanted water because she was thirsty.
questions.misconception: A vocabulary question is just asking for a dictionary definition.

questions.stem: Read: 'They continued to the market.' What does 'continued' mean here?
hints: They kept going after buying water.
'Continued' means they did not stop.
questions.explanation: 'Continued' means they went on or kept going to the market after stopping for water.
questions.misconception: A vocabulary question is just asking for a dictionary definition.

questions.stem: Which word in the text is closest in meaning to 'coin'?
hints: A coin is used to buy things.
Her mother gave it to her.
questions.explanation: A coin is a type of money, so 'money' is closest in meaning.
questions.misconception: A vocabulary question is just asking for a dictionary definition.

questions.stem: Which sentence from the text tells you that Adwoa was thirsty?
options: They wanted to buy tomatoes and onions.
Adwoa and her mother went to the market.
hints: Look for the sentence that directly says she was thirsty.
It comes right after she sees the water seller.
questions.explanation: The sentence 'Adwoa was very thirsty' directly tells us she was thirsty.
questions.misconception: The answer to an inferential question is always written directly in the text.

questions.stem: Which part of the text shows that Adwoa's mother gave her money?
options: She asked her mother for some money to buy water.
Her mother gave her a small coin.
hints: Look for the sentence where her mother does something.
The mother gave something to Adwoa.
questions.explanation: The sentence 'Her mother gave her a small coin' shows that her mother gave her money.
questions.misconception: You can answer any question just by guessing.

questions.stem: Is the question 'Where did Adwoa and her mother go?' a factual or inferential question?
hints: The answer is directly stated in the text.
You can find it in the first sentence.
questions.explanation: 'Where did Adwoa and her mother go?' is factual because the answer is directly stated in the text.
questions.misconception: Factual questions are the only important type.

questions.stem: Is the question 'Why was Adwoa thirsty?' a factual or inferential question?
hints: The answer is not stated directly as 'because'.
You have to think about the hot afternoon.
questions.explanation: 'Why was Adwoa thirsty?' is inferential because you have to think about the clue (the hot afternoon) to answer it.
questions.misconception: The answer to an inferential question is always written directly in the text.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B3.2.7.1: Understand and analyse texts read
indicator.objective: Retell level-appropriate text in own, explain and illustrate

skills.description: Tell the main events of a story in the correct order using own words.
Explain the main idea or message of the text.
Draw a picture that shows an important part of the text.
Use a story map or herringbone graphic organizer to plan a retelling.
Pick out the most important idea or event in the text.

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 questions at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4.
misconceptions: Retelling means copying the exact words from the text.
Any picture is an illustration of the story.
The main idea is always the first sentence.
You don’t need to explain the meaning of the text if you can retell it.

questions.stem: What did Kwame find in his garden?
options: A small bird with a broken wing
hints: The story is about an animal.
It had a broken wing.
questions.explanation: Kwame found a small bird with a broken wing in his garden.
questions.misconception: Retelling means copying the exact words from the text.

questions.stem: What did Kwame do first with the bird?
hints: He found it in the garden.
Then he brought it somewhere.
questions.explanation: Kwame first took the bird home to care for it.
questions.misconception: Retelling means copying the exact words from the text.

questions.stem: What did Kwame make for the bird?
options: A soft nest in a basket
hints: He wanted the bird to be comfortable.
He made it in a basket.
questions.explanation: Kwame made a soft nest for the bird in a basket.
questions.misconception: Retelling means copying the exact words from the text.

questions.stem: Put these events in the correct order: (1) Kwame let the bird fly away, (2) Kwame found the bird, (3) Kwame fed the bird, (4) Kwame took the bird home.
hints: He found it first.
He took it home, then fed it, then let it go.
questions.explanation: The correct order is: found the bird (2), took it home (4), fed it (3), let it fly away (1).
questions.misconception: Retelling means copying the exact words from the text.

questions.stem: What is the main message of the story?
options: We should help animals in need.
hints: Kwame helped the bird.
He took care of it until it was strong.
questions.explanation: The main message is that we should help animals in need, just as Kwame helped the bird.
questions.misconception: You don’t need to explain the meaning of the text if you can retell it.

questions.stem: Why did Kwame let the bird fly away?
options: Because he was tired of it
hints: After two weeks, the wing was strong.
The bird could fly.
questions.explanation: Kwame let the bird fly away because its wing was strong again and it was ready to be free.
questions.misconception: You don’t need to explain the meaning of the text if you can retell it.

questions.stem: How do you think Kwame felt when the bird flew away?
hints: He smiled and waved goodbye.
He had helped the bird get better.
questions.explanation: Kwame felt happy and proud because he had helped the bird heal and now it was free.
questions.misconception: You don’t need to explain the meaning of the text if you can retell it.

questions.stem: A story map helps you...
options: organise the events of a story
hints: It helps you plan a retelling.
It shows beginning, middle, end.
questions.explanation: A story map helps organise the events of a story so you can retell it clearly.
questions.misconception: Retelling means copying the exact words from the text.

questions.stem: Which question would you answer in a story map for 'The farmer and the bird'?
hints: A story map includes characters.
The main character is Kwame.
questions.explanation: A story map includes questions like 'Who is the main character?', so that would be answered.
questions.misconception: A story map is just a list of words.

questions.stem: What is the story mostly about?
hints: The story is about a bird.
Kwame took care of it.
questions.explanation: The story is mostly about Kwame helping a hurt bird get better.
questions.misconception: The main idea is always the first sentence.

questions.stem: Which event is the most important in the story?
options: Kwame found the bird and helped it
hints: The whole story is about the bird.
Kwame's care for the bird is the main event.
questions.explanation: The most important event is Kwame finding the bird and helping it recover.
questions.misconception: The main idea is always the first sentence.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B3.2.7.2: Use knowledge, skills and techniques of reading to understand, interpret and appreciate a variety of literary texts
indicator.objective: Demonstrate understanding of the purpose and features of poems or rhymes and fables, etc

skills.description: Recognise whether a text is a poem, rhyme or fable.
Name features of each type (e.g. poems have stanzas and rhyming words; fables have animal characters and a moral).
Say why the text was written (e.g. to entertain, to teach a lesson).
Pick out the lesson or message in a fable or poem.
Say one way two text types are alike and one way they differ.
Use a specific feature to explain their understanding.

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 questions at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4.
misconceptions: All poems rhyme.
A fable is just any story about animals.
The purpose of every text is to entertain.
You don’t need to look at features to understand a text.

questions.stem: Which text is a fable?
hints: A fable has animal characters and a moral.
Text A has a tortoise and a lizard.
questions.explanation: Text A is a fable because it has animal characters and teaches a moral lesson at the end.
questions.misconception: A fable is just any story about animals.

questions.stem: Which text is a rhyme?
hints: A rhyme has lines that end with the same sound.
Text B has words like 'tree' and 'me'.
questions.explanation: Text B is a rhyme because it has lines that rhyme, like 'tree/me' and 'high/sky'.
questions.misconception: All poems rhyme.

questions.stem: How can you tell that Text A is a fable and not a rhyme?
options: It has animal characters and a moral, but it does not have rhyming lines.
hints: Fables have a moral and animal characters.
Rhymes have rhyming lines.
questions.explanation: Text A is a fable because it has animal characters and a moral. Text B has rhyming lines, which is a feature of a rhyme.
questions.misconception: A fable is just any story about animals.

questions.stem: Which of these is a feature of a fable?
options: Lines that end with the same sound
hints: Fables teach a lesson.
They often have animals as characters.
questions.explanation: Fables have animal characters and a moral lesson.
questions.misconception: A fable is just any story about animals.

questions.stem: Which of these is a feature of a rhyme?
options: Rhyming words at the end of lines
hints: Rhymes have a musical quality.
Words at the ends of lines sound the same.
questions.explanation: A rhyme has rhyming words at the end of lines, like 'tree/me' in Text B.
questions.misconception: All poems rhyme.

questions.stem: In Text B, which words rhyme?
hints: Say the words at the end of each line aloud.
The first two lines end with rhyming words.
questions.explanation: The words 'tree' and 'me' rhyme at the end of the first two lines of Text B.
questions.misconception: All poems rhyme.

questions.stem: Which feature is shared by both Text A and Text B?
hints: Text A has a tortoise and a lizard.
Text B has birds.
questions.explanation: Both texts have animal characters. Text A has a tortoise and a lizard, and Text B has birds.
questions.misconception: You don’t need to look at features to understand a text.

questions.stem: Why was Text A written?
hints: Text A has a moral at the end.
A fable is written to teach a lesson.
questions.explanation: Text A was written to teach a lesson, which is the moral: 'Cleverness is better than speed'.
questions.misconception: The purpose of every text is to entertain.

questions.stem: Why was Text B written?
hints: Text B is a rhyme about birds.
Rhymes are often written for enjoyment.
questions.explanation: Text B was written to entertain with a rhyming song about birds.
questions.misconception: The purpose of every text is to entertain.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of the last sentence in Text A: 'Moral: Cleverness is better than speed'?
options: To tell you what to eat
hints: A moral is a lesson.
The sentence tells you something to learn.
questions.explanation: The last sentence of Text A teaches the lesson that cleverness is better than speed.
questions.misconception: The purpose of every text is to entertain.

questions.stem: Which text is more likely to be found in a book of lessons for children?
hints: Which text teaches a lesson?
Fables are often used to teach lessons.
questions.explanation: Text A is more likely to be found in a book of lessons because it teaches a moral about cleverness.
questions.misconception: The purpose of every text is to entertain.

questions.stem: What is the moral of Text A?
hints: The moral is written at the end.
It is about being clever.
questions.explanation: The moral of the story is that cleverness is better than speed.
questions.misconception: A fable is just any story about animals.

questions.stem: What message does Text B give about the birds?
hints: The birds sing sweet songs.
They fly high into the blue sky.
questions.explanation: Text B shows birds that are happy and free, singing and flying high in the sky.
questions.misconception: The purpose of every text is to entertain.

questions.stem: How is Text A different from Text B?
options: Text A is a fable with a moral, while Text B is a rhyme with rhyming words.
Text A is a rhyme, while Text B is a fable.
hints: One text has a moral.
The other text has rhyming words.
questions.explanation: Text A is a fable with a moral, and Text B is a rhyme with rhyming words.
questions.misconception: You don’t need to look at features to understand a text.

questions.stem: How are Text A and Text B alike?
hints: Look at the characters in both texts.
Both texts have animals.
questions.explanation: Both texts have animal characters. Text A has a tortoise and a lizard, and Text B has birds.
questions.misconception: You don’t need to look at features to understand a text.

questions.stem: Pupil A says: 'Text A and Text B are the same because both are about animals.' Pupil B says: 'They are different because Text A teaches a lesson and Text B is a rhyme.' Who is correct and why?
options: Both are correct because the texts share some features but differ in others.
hints: Think about both the similarities and the differences.
One pupil talks about similarity, the other about difference.
questions.explanation: Both pupils are correct. The texts are alike because they both have animal characters, but they are different because one is a fable with a moral and the other is a rhyme.
questions.misconception: You don’t need to look at features to understand a text.

questions.stem: How does the rhyming in Text B make it sound when you read it aloud?
hints: Rhymes often have a musical feel.
Words that rhyme make the poem flow.
questions.explanation: The rhyming words make Text B sound musical and sing-song when read aloud.
questions.misconception: All poems rhyme.

questions.stem: How does the moral at the end of Text A help you understand the story better?
options: It tells you what lesson the story teaches.
hints: A moral is a lesson.
It helps you know what the story is teaching.
questions.explanation: The moral at the end of Text A tells you the lesson the story teaches: cleverness is better than speed.
questions.misconception: The purpose of every text is to entertain.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B3.2.7.2: Use knowledge, skills and techniques of reading to understand, interpret and appreciate a variety of literary texts
indicator.objective: Respond to stories with own opinion and value judgment

skills.description: Say whether they liked or disliked a story and why.
Judge whether a character's action was right or wrong and explain why.
Give a reason from the story for their opinion or judgment.
Connect the story's events or characters to their own values or experiences.
Share opinions and judgments clearly in a group discussion.
Listen to others' opinions and say whether they agree or disagree politely.

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 questions at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4.
misconceptions: Any opinion is fine as long as you say it loudly.
You need evidence to have an opinion.
A character is either completely good or completely bad.
Disagreeing with someone means you don't like them.

questions.stem: Did you like the story?
options: Yes, because Esi did the right thing.
No, because it was too long.
hints: Think about what Esi did.
It is a story about honesty.
questions.explanation: The best reason for liking the story is that Esi showed honesty by returning the purse.
questions.misconception: Any opinion is fine as long as you say it loudly.

questions.stem: Which part of the story did you find most interesting?
options: When Esi found the purse and decided to return it.
When they walked home from school.
When Yaa said they should keep the money.
When the old woman thanked them.
hints: The most interesting part is usually the main action.
It is when Esi makes her choice.
questions.explanation: The most interesting part is when Esi finds the purse and makes the choice to return it, because it shows her honesty.
questions.misconception: A character is either completely good or completely bad.

questions.stem: Was Yaa's suggestion to keep the money right or wrong?
options: Wrong, because the money did not belong to them.
Wrong, because the purse was old.
hints: The purse belonged to someone else.
Keeping something that is not yours is wrong.
questions.explanation: Yaa's suggestion was wrong because the money belonged to someone else, and it is not right to keep what is not yours.
questions.misconception: A character is either completely good or completely bad.

questions.stem: Was Esi's decision to return the purse right or wrong?
options: Right, because it was the honest thing to do.
Wrong, because they could have used the money.
Right, because Yaa told her to.
Wrong, because the old woman did not notice.
hints: Esi returned something that belonged to someone else.
Honesty means doing the right thing.
questions.explanation: Esi's decision was right because returning the purse was the honest thing to do.
questions.misconception: You need evidence to have an opinion.

questions.stem: How did Yaa feel at the end of the story, and was that feeling right?
options: She felt ashamed, and that was right because she knew her suggestion was wrong.
She felt happy, and that was right because she got the money.
She felt angry, and that was right because Esi did not listen to her.
She felt nothing, and that was right because she did not care.
hints: The story says Yaa felt ashamed.
She felt ashamed because she knew keeping the purse was wrong.
questions.explanation: Yaa felt ashamed, and that was right because she realised her suggestion to keep the money was wrong.
questions.misconception: A character is either completely good or completely bad.

questions.stem: Which sentence from the story shows that Esi was honest?
options: Esi said, 'No, someone has lost this. They will be sad. We should try to find the owner.'
Yaa said, 'Let us keep the money!'
The old woman was very happy.
hints: Look for what Esi said.
Honesty is shown in her words.
questions.explanation: Esi's words show her honesty because she wanted to return the purse to its owner.
questions.misconception: You need evidence to have an opinion.

questions.stem: Which part of the story shows that Yaa knew her suggestion was wrong?
options: Yaa felt ashamed at the end.
hints: Look at the last sentence.
Yaa felt something that showed she knew she was wrong.
questions.explanation: Yaa felt ashamed at the end, which shows she knew her suggestion to keep the money was wrong.
questions.misconception: A character is either completely good or completely bad.

questions.stem: Which sentence best supports the idea that Esi cared about other people's feelings?
options: Esi said, 'Someone has lost this. They will be sad.'
hints: Look for Esi's words about the owner.
She thought about how the owner would feel.
questions.explanation: Esi's words 'They will be sad' show she cared about the owner's feelings.
questions.misconception: You need evidence to have an opinion.

questions.stem: If you found a purse on the ground, what would you do?
hints: Think about what Esi did.
Honesty is important.
questions.explanation: The right thing to do is try to find the owner, just like Esi did.
questions.misconception: Any opinion is fine as long as you say it loudly.

questions.stem: Yaa changed her mind after seeing the old woman. Have you ever changed your mind about something after seeing someone else's actions?
options: Yes, I once copied a good behaviour I saw.
No, I never change my mind.
Yes, I once kept something that was not mine.
No, I don't care about others.
hints: Think about a time you learned from someone.
It could be at home or school.
questions.explanation: Many people have changed their minds after seeing someone do the right thing, just like Yaa did.
questions.misconception: A character is either completely good or completely bad.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B3.2.7.2: Use knowledge, skills and techniques of reading to understand, interpret and appreciate a variety of literary texts
indicator.objective: Use visualisation strategy (form mental images when reading text) to enhance understanding of level-appropriate texts

skills.description: Create a picture in their mind of what is happening in the text.
Describe in words the picture they see in their mind.
Draw a picture based on what they imagined while reading.
Say whether a given picture matches the mental image a text creates.
Include sights, sounds or feelings in their mental image.
Say how making a picture in the mind helps them understand the story better.

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 questions at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4.
misconceptions: Visualising means drawing exactly what is in the text.
You only visualise when there are pictures in the book.
Everyone sees the exact same picture in their mind.
Visualising is a waste of time; reading the words is enough.

questions.stem: When you read about the dark and cloudy afternoon, what do you see in your mind?
hints: Dark and cloudy means the sky is grey.
Think of a day when it looks like rain.
questions.explanation: The words 'dark and cloudy afternoon' make you picture grey clouds covering the sky.
questions.misconception: Everyone sees the exact same picture in their mind.

questions.stem: After reading 'The trees were bending', what picture forms in your mind?
options: Trees with their branches moving in the wind
hints: Bending means the trees are not straight.
The wind is blowing hard.
questions.explanation: The trees bending in the wind makes you picture their branches moving strongly.
questions.misconception: Visualising means drawing exactly what is in the text.

questions.stem: Read: 'The rain fell heavily on the roof.' What image comes to mind?
options: Water pouring down on the roof
hints: Heavily means a lot of rain.
Think of a strong downpour.
questions.explanation: The words 'fell heavily' make you picture a lot of rain pouring onto the roof.
questions.misconception: You only visualise when there are pictures in the book.

questions.stem: Which picture best matches the sentence: 'The rain fell heavily on the roof'?
options: A picture of the sun shining on a roof
A picture of heavy rain falling on a roof
A picture of a dry roof
A picture of snow on a roof
hints: Heavy rain means a lot of water.
Look for the picture with rain.
questions.explanation: The sentence describes heavy rain on the roof, so the picture with heavy rain is the best match.
questions.misconception: Visualising means drawing exactly what is in the text.

questions.stem: Which picture best matches 'The children looked out of the window and saw the water running down the street'?
options: Children playing outside in the sun
Children looking out a window at a wet street
hints: The sentence says they are looking out a window.
They see water running down the street.
questions.explanation: The best match is children looking out a window at a wet street.
questions.misconception: You only visualise when there are pictures in the book.

questions.stem: Which picture best matches 'The wind was blowing hard'?
options: A picture of a calm day
A picture of trees bending in the wind
A picture of a sunny beach
A picture of a dry, dusty road
hints: Hard wind makes things bend.
Trees bending show strong wind.
questions.explanation: The picture of trees bending in the wind best matches the strong wind.
questions.misconception: Everyone sees the exact same picture in their mind.

questions.stem: A pupil draws a picture of children playing outside in the sunshine. Does this picture match the story 'The Rainy Day'?
options: No, because the story is about rain and the children are inside looking out.
Yes, because the story mentions children.
No, because the story is about snow.
hints: The story says it is a rainy day.
The children are inside looking out the window.
questions.explanation: The picture does not match because the story is about a rainy day, and the children are inside looking out, not playing outside.
questions.misconception: You only visualise when there are pictures in the book.

questions.stem: Which of these is a sound you might include in your mental image of the rainy day?
options: Pit-a-pat of rain on the roof
hints: The story mentions a sound.
It is the sound of rain on the roof.
questions.explanation: The story says the sound was 'pit-a-pat, pit-a-pat', which is the sound of rain on the roof.
questions.misconception: Visualising is a waste of time; reading the words is enough.

questions.stem: Which of these is a feeling you might include in your mental image of the rainy day?
hints: The story says the air felt cool and wet.
Use that detail in your mental image.
questions.explanation: The story mentions that the air felt cool and wet, so you could include that feeling in your mental image.
questions.misconception: Everyone sees the exact same picture in their mind.

questions.stem: How does making a picture in your mind help you understand the story better?
options: It helps you remember the details.
hints: Visualising helps you remember what you read.
It makes the story more real.
questions.explanation: Making a mental picture helps you remember details and understand the story better.
questions.misconception: Visualising is a waste of time; reading the words is enough.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B3.2.7.2: Use knowledge, skills and techniques of reading to understand, interpret and appreciate a variety of literary texts
indicator.objective: Read level-appropriate texts independently

skills.description: Choose a level-appropriate text to read on their own.
Read a short text independently without asking for help on every word.
Answer simple questions about a text they read independently.
Use self-correction and context clues without teacher help.
Tell or write one or two sentences about what they read.
Read for a longer period without losing focus.

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 questions at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4.
misconceptions: Independent reading means reading without understanding.
I should only read books with pictures.
If I get stuck, I must stop reading.
Reading independently means reading as fast as possible.

questions.stem: Which book is best for you to read on your own?
options: A book with very small words and no pictures
A book with simple words and some pictures
A book with long, hard words
hints: A level-appropriate book has words you can read.
Pictures can help you understand.
questions.explanation: A book with simple words and some pictures is best for independent reading because it matches your reading level.
questions.misconception: I should only read books with pictures.

questions.stem: How do you know if a book is right for you to read alone?
options: You can read most of the words and understand the story
hints: The book should not be too hard or too easy.
You should be able to understand most of it.
questions.explanation: A right book for independent reading is one where you can read most words and understand the story.
questions.misconception: Reading independently means reading as fast as possible.

questions.stem: What should you do if you are reading on your own and you see a word you do not know?
options: Stop reading and close the book
Try to sound it out or use the words around it
Ask a friend to read it for you
hints: Good readers try to figure out the word.
You can use the letters or the sentence to help.
questions.explanation: You should try to sound out the word or use context clues instead of stopping.
questions.misconception: If I get stuck, I must stop reading.

questions.stem: If you read a sentence that does not make sense, what should you do?
hints: Rereading helps you understand.
Try again to make sense of it.
questions.explanation: Rereading the sentence slowly can help you understand what it means.
questions.misconception: Reading independently means reading as fast as possible.

questions.stem: Who is the main character in the story 'The Kind Farmer'?
hints: The story is about a farmer.
His name is Ato.
questions.explanation: The main character is Ato, the kind farmer.
questions.misconception: Independent reading means reading without understanding.

questions.stem: Where did Ato live?
options: In a small village near Kumasi
hints: The story tells you where Ato lived.
It is near Kumasi.
questions.explanation: Ato lived in a small village near Kumasi.
questions.misconception: Independent reading means reading without understanding.

questions.stem: What did Ato give the hungry dog?
hints: The dog was hungry and tired.
Ato gave it something to eat and drink.
questions.explanation: Ato gave the dog food and water.
questions.misconception: Independent reading means reading without understanding.

questions.stem: You are reading alone and you see the word 'village'. You are not sure what it means. What can you do?
options: Look at the words around it to guess its meaning
hints: Use the other words in the sentence to help you.
The story says 'small village near Kumasi'.
questions.explanation: You can use the surrounding words like 'small' and 'near Kumasi' to guess that a village is a small town.
questions.misconception: If I get stuck, I must stop reading.

questions.stem: If you read 'The dog wagged its tail', and you are not sure what 'wagged' means, what clue in the story can help you?
options: The dog was happy because Ato fed it.
The dog was thin and tired.
The dog came to the gate.
hints: The dog had just been fed.
Dogs wag their tails when they are happy.
questions.explanation: Since the dog was happy after eating, 'wagged' probably means moving its tail happily.
questions.misconception: Independent reading means reading without understanding.

questions.stem: You are reading alone and come across the word 'thin'. What does 'thin' likely mean in 'The dog looked thin and tired'?
hints: Thin is the opposite of fat.
The dog was hungry, so it was thin.
questions.explanation: 'Thin' means not fat, especially because the dog was hungry and tired.
questions.misconception: Independent reading means reading without understanding.

questions.stem: Which sentence best summarises the story 'The Kind Farmer'?
options: A farmer named Ato feeds a hungry dog, and the dog becomes his friend.
A farmer named Ato lives in a small village.
A dog runs away from home.
A farmer feeds his chickens and goats.
hints: A summary tells the main events.
What happened with the dog?
questions.explanation: The best summary includes the main events: Ato feeds the dog and the dog becomes his friend.
questions.misconception: Independent reading means reading without understanding.

questions.stem: What helps you read for a longer time without getting tired?
options: Reading a book that is very hard
Taking a short break and then continuing
hints: Stamina means you can keep going.
A short break can help you focus.
questions.explanation: Taking a short break and then continuing helps you build reading stamina.
questions.misconception: Reading independently means reading as fast as possible.

questions.stem: If you are reading alone and you lose focus, what should you do?
options: Take a deep breath and start reading again from where you stopped
Close the book and never open it again
hints: You can refocus your attention.
Try again from where you stopped.
questions.explanation: Taking a deep breath and starting again from where you stopped can help you regain focus.
questions.misconception: Reading independently means reading as fast as possible.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B3.2.9.1: Read texts fluently
indicator.objective: Read long texts with good pace, accuracy and expression

skills.description: Read a longer text at a steady, comfortable speed.
Read words correctly with few errors.
Use voice to show meaning and feeling.
Pause at full stops and commas, change voice for question marks and exclamation marks.
Notice when reading is too fast or too slow and adjust.
Say what good reading sounds like.

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 questions at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4.
misconceptions: Fluent reading means reading as fast as possible.
Expression means shouting or reading in a funny voice.
Punctuation marks are only for writing, not for reading aloud.
Accuracy means reading every word perfectly on the first try.

questions.stem: What does reading at a good pace mean?
options: Reading as fast as you can
Reading at a steady, comfortable speed
hints: Good pace is not too fast and not too slow.
You should be able to understand what you read.
questions.explanation: A good pace means reading at a steady, comfortable speed so you can understand and be understood.
questions.misconception: Fluent reading means reading as fast as possible.

questions.stem: What does reading with accuracy mean?
options: Reading words correctly with few mistakes
hints: Accuracy is about reading words correctly.
You do not need to be perfect every time.
questions.explanation: Reading with accuracy means reading words correctly with few mistakes.
questions.misconception: Accuracy means reading every word perfectly on the first try.

questions.stem: Which sentence should be read with a loud, excited voice?
options: The boy laughed and kept running.
hints: Look for words that show strong feeling.
The mother is shouting.
questions.explanation: 'Stop!' should be read with a loud, excited voice because the mother is shouting.
questions.misconception: Expression means shouting or reading in a funny voice.

questions.stem: How should you read the sentence: 'Finally, he tripped and fell.'?
options: With a sad or concerned voice
hints: Tripping and falling is not a happy thing.
Show that something bad happened.
questions.explanation: The sentence should be read with a sad or concerned voice because falling is not a happy event.
questions.misconception: Expression means shouting or reading in a funny voice.

questions.stem: What should you do when you see a full stop (.) while reading aloud?
hints: A full stop marks the end of a sentence.
Take a short pause.
