questions.explanation: At a full stop, you should pause briefly because it marks the end of a sentence.
questions.misconception: Punctuation marks are only for writing, not for reading aloud.

questions.stem: How should you read a sentence that ends with a question mark (?)?
options: With a rising voice at the end
With a falling voice at the end
hints: A question mark shows a question.
Your voice goes up at the end.
questions.explanation: When reading a question mark, your voice should rise at the end to show it is a question.
questions.misconception: Punctuation marks are only for writing, not for reading aloud.

questions.stem: How can you tell if you are reading too fast?
options: You are not understanding what you read
You are pausing at full stops
hints: If you read too fast, you might not understand.
Check if you can follow the story.
questions.explanation: If you are reading too fast, you may not understand what you read, which is a sign to slow down.
questions.misconception: Fluent reading means reading as fast as possible.

questions.stem: Which of these is a feature of good reading?
options: Reading with clear words and expression
hints: Good reading is clear and expressive.
It should be easy to listen to.
questions.explanation: Good reading is clear, expressive, and easy to understand.
questions.misconception: Fluent reading means reading as fast as possible.

questions.stem: What does good reading sound like?
hints: It should sound natural.
The reader uses expression.
questions.explanation: Good reading sounds smooth and expressive, with clear words and appropriate pauses.
questions.misconception: Fluent reading means reading as fast as possible.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B3.2.9.1: Read texts fluently
indicator.objective: Recognise more than two hundred high frequency words with automaticity

skills.description: Read common high-frequency words instantly.
Spot and read high-frequency words within sentences quickly.
Put high-frequency words together with other words to make meaningful sentences.
Notice high-frequency words that were misread and correct them.
Group high-frequency words by type (e.g. pronouns, prepositions, verbs).
Say why reading common words quickly helps reading.

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 questions at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4.
misconceptions: High-frequency words are the same as hard words.
You only need to know the meaning of a sight word, not recognise it quickly.
Sight words are only for Basic 1.
It is fine to skip a sight word when reading.

questions.stem: Which of these is a high-frequency word?
hints: High-frequency words are very common in reading.
You see them in almost every sentence.
questions.explanation: 'The' is a high-frequency word because it appears very often in reading.
questions.misconception: High-frequency words are the same as hard words.

questions.stem: Which word is a high-frequency word?
hints: High-frequency words are common and short.
'And' is used very often.
questions.explanation: 'And' is a high-frequency word because it is a very common word in English.
questions.misconception: Sight words are only for Basic 1.

questions.stem: Which word is a high-frequency word that means 'the opposite of no'?
hints: It is a common word used to agree.
It is very short.
questions.explanation: 'Yes' is a high-frequency word that means the opposite of 'no'.
questions.misconception: High-frequency words are the same as hard words.

questions.stem: Which set contains ONLY high-frequency words?
hints: High-frequency words are common words like pronouns, articles, and helping verbs.
'The', 'and', 'was', 'they' are all common.
questions.explanation: 'The', 'and', 'was', 'they' are all high-frequency words.
questions.misconception: High-frequency words are the same as hard words.

questions.stem: In the passage, which word appears most often?
hints: Scan the passage for the word 'the'.
It appears many times.
questions.explanation: 'The' is the high-frequency word that appears most often in the passage.
questions.misconception: You only need to know the meaning of a sight word, not recognise it quickly.

questions.stem: Find the high-frequency word in this sentence from the passage: 'They had a big red ball.'
hints: Which word is a common helping word?
'Had' is a high-frequency verb.
questions.explanation: 'Had' is a high-frequency word in the sentence.
questions.misconception: It is fine to skip a sight word when reading.

questions.stem: Which high-frequency word appears in the sentence: 'A man saw the ball and stopped his car'?
hints: Look for a common word.
'Saw' is a high-frequency word.
questions.explanation: 'Saw' is a high-frequency word in the sentence.
questions.misconception: It is fine to skip a sight word when reading.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses high-frequency words correctly?
hints: With 'they', use 'were' in the past.
Subject and verb must agree.
questions.explanation: 'They were happy' is correct because 'they' takes 'were' in the past tense.
questions.misconception: You only need to know the meaning of a sight word, not recognise it quickly.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence with the correct high-frequency word: 'I ___ going to the market.'
hints: With 'I', use 'am'.
I am, you are, he is.
questions.explanation: With 'I', the correct high-frequency word is 'am': 'I am going to the market.'
questions.misconception: You only need to know the meaning of a sight word, not recognise it quickly.

questions.stem: A pupil reads: 'The children was playing in the park.' What high-frequency word is wrong?
hints: 'Children' is plural.
Use 'were' with plural subjects.
questions.explanation: The high-frequency word 'was' is wrong. It should be 'were' because 'children' is plural.
questions.misconception: It is fine to skip a sight word when reading.

questions.stem: A pupil reads: 'He pick up the ball.' What high-frequency word is missing or wrong?
hints: The action happened in the past.
The past tense of 'pick' is 'picked'.
questions.explanation: The word 'pick' is wrong. It should be 'picked' because the action happened in the past.
questions.misconception: It is fine to skip a sight word when reading.

questions.stem: Which of these is a pronoun?
hints: A pronoun replaces a noun.
'They' replaces the names of people or things.
questions.explanation: 'They' is a pronoun because it replaces a noun.
questions.misconception: High-frequency words are the same as hard words.

questions.stem: Sort these high-frequency words: 'the', 'and', 'was', 'they', 'in', 'a'. Which group is correct?
options: Articles: the, a; Conjunctions: and; Verbs: was; Pronouns: they; Prepositions: in
Articles: and, a; Conjunctions: the; Verbs: they; Pronouns: was; Prepositions: in
Articles: the, in; Conjunctions: and; Verbs: was; Pronouns: they; Prepositions: a
Articles: the, a; Conjunctions: in; Verbs: was; Pronouns: they; Prepositions: and
hints: Articles are 'a', 'an', 'the'.
Conjunctions join ideas, like 'and'.
questions.explanation: The correct grouping is: Articles: the, a; Conjunctions: and; Verbs: was; Pronouns: they; Prepositions: in.
questions.misconception: High-frequency words are the same as hard words.

questions.stem: Why is it helpful to recognise high-frequency words quickly?
options: It helps you read faster and understand the story better.
hints: If you recognise common words quickly, you can focus on the meaning.
You do not have to stop and sound out every word.
questions.explanation: Recognising high-frequency words quickly helps you read faster and focus on understanding the story.
questions.misconception: You only need to know the meaning of a sight word, not recognise it quickly.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B3.2.9.1: Read texts fluently
indicator.objective: Use self-correction strategy to make meaning from texts (repeated)

skills.description: Hear or see when they have mispronounced or misread a word.
Reread a word or sentence to correct a mistake and keep the meaning.
Use surrounding words or the sentence meaning to correct a misread word.
Adjust intonation to make meaning clear when self-correcting.
Use self-correction while reading aloud in a group or pair.
Explain what they do when they realise they have read something wrong.

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 questions at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4.
misconceptions: Self-correction means starting the whole book again.
Only slow readers need to self-correct.
If I misread a word, the meaning does not matter.
Intonation has nothing to do with self-correction.

questions.stem: Which sentence does NOT make sense?
options: The cat is sleeping on the mat.
The fish is flying in the sky.
The girl is reading a book.
hints: Think about what animals can do.
Fish live in water, not in the sky.
questions.explanation: 'The fish is flying in the sky' does not make sense because fish cannot fly. A good reader would notice this mistake.
questions.misconception: If I misread a word, the meaning does not matter.

questions.stem: What should you do if you read a sentence and it does not make sense?
hints: Rereading helps you check the words.
Take your time to understand.
questions.explanation: You should reread the sentence slowly to check the words and make sense of it.
questions.misconception: Self-correction means starting the whole book again.

questions.stem: Read: 'The farmer planted seeds in the ___.' Which word makes sense?
hints: Where do farmers plant seeds?
Use the clue 'farmer' and 'seeds'.
questions.explanation: The context tells us seeds are planted in the soil, so 'soil' is the correct word.
questions.misconception: If I misread a word, the meaning does not matter.

questions.stem: What does 'self-correction' mean?
options: Fixing your own mistake when reading
Asking the teacher to read for you
Skipping words you do not know
hints: Self means you do it yourself.
Correction means fixing a mistake.
questions.explanation: Self-correction means noticing and fixing your own mistake when reading.
questions.misconception: Self-correction means starting the whole book again.

questions.stem: A pupil reads: 'The dog meowed at the moon.' What is wrong?
options: The moon is not in the sky.
Dogs do not like the moon.
hints: Think about the sound a dog makes.
Dogs bark, they do not meow.
questions.explanation: The sentence is wrong because dogs bark, they do not meow. A good reader would notice this and self-correct.
questions.misconception: If I misread a word, the meaning does not matter.

questions.stem: Read: 'The sky was dark and cloudy. Soon, ___ started to fall.' Which word fits?
hints: Dark clouds often bring this.
It falls from the sky.
questions.explanation: Dark clouds and falling suggest rain, so 'rain' makes sense in the context.
questions.misconception: If I misread a word, the meaning does not matter.

questions.stem: Why is rereading a sentence helpful when you are confused?
options: It helps you understand the words better.
hints: Rereading gives you another chance to understand.
You might notice a word you read wrong.
questions.explanation: Rereading helps you understand the words better and catch mistakes.
questions.misconception: If I misread a word, the meaning does not matter.

questions.stem: A pupil reads: 'The boy ran to the shop to buy a book, but the shop was closed. So he bought a book.' Which word makes the sentence silly?
hints: If the shop was closed, he could not buy anything.
The last word is the problem.
questions.explanation: If the shop was closed, he could not buy a book, so 'bought' makes the sentence silly. The pupil should notice this and self-correct.
questions.misconception: If I misread a word, the meaning does not matter.

questions.stem: After rereading a sentence, you still do not understand it. What should you do next?
options: Read the sentence before and after it for clues
Stop reading and close the book
hints: Context clues can help.
The sentences around it might explain it.
questions.explanation: If rereading does not help, you can read the sentences before and after for clues.
questions.misconception: Self-correction means starting the whole book again.

questions.stem: Read: 'The teacher asked the pupils to be quiet, but they continued to make noise. She had to raise her voice to be ___.' Which word fits best?
hints: The teacher wants the pupils to hear her.
She raised her voice so she could be heard.
questions.explanation: The context shows the teacher raised her voice so she could be heard over the noise.
questions.misconception: If I misread a word, the meaning does not matter.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B3.4.13.1: Support an opinion in writing
indicator.objective: Write a short paragraph to support an opinion or claims with clear reasons

skills.description: Clearly state a position on a simple topic.
Give clear, relevant reasons to support the opinion.
Put the opinion and reasons into a short, logical paragraph.
Use words like because, so, also, first to connect reasons to the opinion.
Write a short paragraph that clearly supports an opinion or claim with reasons.
Judge whether a given argument has a clear opinion and relevant reasons.

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 questions at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4.
misconceptions: An opinion is a fact.
Any reason is good enough, even if it is unrelated.
You can just state your opinion without giving a reason.
Linking words like because are not necessary in a short paragraph.
You have to agree with the teacher's opinion to write well.

questions.stem: Which of these is an opinion?
hints: An opinion tells what someone thinks or feels.
It cannot be proven true or false.
questions.explanation: 'Rice is the best food' is an opinion because it is what someone thinks, not a fact.
questions.misconception: An opinion is a fact.

questions.stem: Which sentence clearly states an opinion?
options: I think fufu is better than rice.
hints: Look for 'I think' or 'I believe'.
An opinion tells what someone thinks.
questions.explanation: 'I think fufu is better than rice' clearly states an opinion.
questions.misconception: You have to agree with the teacher's opinion to write well.

questions.stem: Opinion: 'Rice is better than fufu.' Which is the best reason to support this?
options: Because rice is easier to cook.
Because fufu is made from cassava.
hints: The reason should explain why rice is better.
It should be relevant to the opinion.
questions.explanation: 'Because rice is easier to cook' is a relevant reason to support the opinion that rice is better.
questions.misconception: Any reason is good enough, even if it is unrelated.

questions.stem: Opinion: 'We should not waste water.' Which is the best reason?
options: Because water is precious and many people need it.
hints: The reason should explain why we should not waste water.
Think about why water is important.
questions.explanation: 'Because water is precious and many people need it' is the best reason because it directly supports the opinion.
questions.misconception: Any reason is good enough, even if it is unrelated.

questions.stem: Which is the best order for a short argument?
options: State your opinion first, then give reasons.
Give reasons first, then state your opinion.
hints: An argument starts with the opinion.
Reasons come after.
questions.explanation: The best order is to state your opinion first, then give reasons to support it.
questions.misconception: Linking words like because are not necessary in a short paragraph.

questions.stem: Which paragraph is best organised?
options: I think rice is better than fufu. First, rice is easier to cook. Also, rice is cheaper.
First, rice is easier to cook. Also, rice is cheaper. I think rice is better than fufu.
I think rice is better than fufu. I have a dog. Also, it is raining.
Rice is a food. Fufu is a food.
hints: Start with the opinion.
Then give reasons that support it.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph is best organised because it starts with the opinion and then gives two relevant reasons.
questions.misconception: Linking words like because are not necessary in a short paragraph.

questions.stem: Which word can you use to link an opinion to a reason?
hints: It shows the reason for something.
It is used in sentences like 'I like rice ___ it is sweet'.
questions.explanation: 'Because' is a linking word used to connect an opinion to a reason.
questions.misconception: Linking words like because are not necessary in a short paragraph.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence: 'I like school ___ I learn new things.'
hints: The sentence gives a reason.
Use the linking word that means 'for the reason that'.
questions.explanation: 'Because' is the correct linking word to show the reason.
questions.misconception: Linking words like because are not necessary in a short paragraph.

questions.stem: Read this argument: 'I think football is the best game. It is fun.' Does it have a clear opinion and a relevant reason?
hints: The opinion is 'football is the best game'.
The reason is 'it is fun'.
questions.explanation: The argument has a clear opinion and a relevant reason ('it is fun').
questions.misconception: Any reason is good enough, even if it is unrelated.

questions.stem: Which argument is stronger?
options: I think we should plant trees because they give us shade and clean air.
I think we should plant trees because I like trees.
I think we should plant trees because it is Tuesday.
I think we should plant trees because my friend has a tree.
hints: A strong argument gives specific, relevant reasons.
Which reason is most related to why trees are useful?
questions.explanation: The first argument is stronger because it gives two clear, relevant reasons (shade and clean air).
questions.misconception: Any reason is good enough, even if it is unrelated.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B3.4.14.1: Write on the events of the day
indicator.objective: Write picture events using simple sentences

skills.description: Recognise and name common events of the day.
Arrange the events in the correct chronological order.
Create or select pictures that clearly represent specific daily events.
Write simple sentences that accurately describe what is happening in the pictures.
Ensure the written sentence accurately matches the drawn or given picture.
Present the completed picture-sentence work to a partner or the class.

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 questions at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4.
misconceptions: Any picture can go with any sentence.
Events of the day don’t need to be in a specific order.
A sentence doesn’t need to describe the picture exactly.
Writing about daily events means writing a long story.
You only need to write the sentence, not draw the picture.

questions.stem: Which of these is an event of the day?
hints: Think about things you do every day.
You do this in the morning.
questions.explanation: Waking up is a daily event because it happens every morning.
questions.misconception: Writing about daily events means writing a long story.

questions.stem: Which event happens in the morning?
hints: Morning is the start of the day.
What do you do before school?
questions.explanation: Eating breakfast happens in the morning.
questions.misconception: Events of the day don’t need to be in a specific order.

questions.stem: Which event happens last in the day?
hints: What do you do at night?
It is the last thing you do before sleeping.
questions.explanation: Going to bed happens last in the day.
questions.misconception: Events of the day don’t need to be in a specific order.

questions.stem: Put these events in the correct order: (1) Eat breakfast, (2) Wake up, (3) Go to school.
hints: What do you do first when you wake up?
You wake up before you eat.
questions.explanation: The correct order is: wake up (2), eat breakfast (1), go to school (3).
questions.misconception: Events of the day don’t need to be in a specific order.

questions.stem: Put these events in order: (1) Brush your teeth, (2) Wake up, (3) Take your bath.
hints: You wake up first.
Then brush your teeth, then take your bath.
questions.explanation: The correct order is: wake up (2), brush your teeth (1), take your bath (3).
questions.misconception: Events of the day don’t need to be in a specific order.

questions.stem: Put these events in order: (1) Go to bed, (2) Eat dinner, (3) Do homework.
hints: Do homework before dinner.
Go to bed last.
questions.explanation: The correct order is: do homework (3), eat dinner (2), go to bed (1).
questions.misconception: Events of the day don’t need to be in a specific order.

questions.stem: A picture shows a boy eating rice. Which sentence matches the picture?
hints: Look at what the boy is doing.
He has food in front of him.
questions.explanation: 'The boy is eating rice' matches the picture.
questions.misconception: A sentence doesn’t need to describe the picture exactly.

questions.stem: Picture: A girl is sleeping in bed. Sentence: 'The girl is reading a book.' Does the sentence match the picture?
hints: Look at what the girl is doing in the picture.
The sentence says she is reading, but the picture shows her sleeping.
questions.explanation: The sentence does not match because the picture shows the girl sleeping, not reading.
questions.misconception: Any picture can go with any sentence.

questions.stem: Picture: A boy is eating. Sentence: 'The boy is eating.' Does the sentence match the picture?
hints: The sentence says the boy is eating.
The picture shows the boy eating.
questions.explanation: The sentence matches the picture because both show the boy eating.
questions.misconception: A sentence doesn’t need to describe the picture exactly.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B3.4.2.1: Copy and write sentences correctly
indicator.objective: Copy short paragraphs clearly

skills.description: Identify features of clear handwriting in a model or sample.
Copy a short paragraph legibly and correctly, ensuring clear letter formation.
Use correct spacing between letters and words in the copied paragraph.
Keep letters aligned correctly on the writing line.
Copy the paragraph without missing or adding words.
Check their own copied paragraph against the original for clarity, spacing, and accuracy.

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 questions at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4.
misconceptions: Clarity means writing as fast as possible.
Spacing between words doesn't matter as long as you can read it.
Alignment means making all letters the same height.
Copying means writing your own version of the text.
Neat handwriting is only important for exams.

questions.stem: Which of these shows clear handwriting?
options: Letters that are easy to read
Letters that are joined together in a messy way
Letters that are all the same height
hints: Clear handwriting means you can read it easily.
Messy writing is not clear.
questions.explanation: Clear handwriting means the letters are easy to read.
questions.misconception: Clarity means writing as fast as possible.

questions.stem: What is wrong with this sentence? 'Thecatisonthemat.'
options: There are no spaces between words.
hints: Look at the spaces between the words.
Words should be separated by spaces.
questions.explanation: The words are not separated by spaces, so it is hard to read.
questions.misconception: Spacing between words doesn't matter as long as you can read it.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a feature of clear handwriting?
options: Letters are all different sizes and slanted randomly
hints: Clear handwriting is neat and readable.
Random sizes and slants make it messy.
questions.explanation: Letters that are all different sizes and slanted randomly are not a feature of clear handwriting.
questions.misconception: Alignment means making all letters the same height.

questions.stem: Why do we put spaces between words when writing?
options: To make the writing easy to read
hints: Spaces separate words.
Without spaces, it is hard to read.
questions.explanation: Spaces between words make writing easy to read.
questions.misconception: Spacing between words doesn't matter as long as you can read it.

questions.stem: Which sentence has correct spacing?
hints: Look for spaces between words.
Each word should be separated.
questions.explanation: 'The dog is big.' has correct spacing between words.
questions.misconception: Spacing between words doesn't matter as long as you can read it.

questions.stem: What does it mean to keep letters aligned on the writing line?
options: All letters sit on the line
All letters are the same height
hints: Alignment is about sitting on the line.
Letters should rest on the line.
questions.explanation: Keeping letters aligned means they sit on the writing line.
questions.misconception: Alignment means making all letters the same height.

questions.stem: Which is an example of poor alignment?
options: Letters that sit on the line
Letters that float above the line
Letters that are the same size
hints: Poor alignment means letters do not sit on the line.
They might float or sink.
questions.explanation: Letters that float above the line are not aligned correctly.
questions.misconception: Alignment means making all letters the same height.

questions.stem: What does copying accurately mean?
options: Writing the same words as the original
hints: Accurate means correct.
You should write exactly what is there.
questions.explanation: Copying accurately means writing the same words as the original without changing them.
questions.misconception: Copying means writing your own version of the text.

questions.stem: A pupil copies 'The dog is big' but writes 'The dog is bag.' What mistake did the pupil make?
hints: Compare the two sentences.
The word 'big' became 'bag'.
questions.explanation: The pupil changed the word 'big' to 'bag', so the copy is not accurate.
questions.misconception: Copying means writing your own version of the text.

questions.stem: After copying a paragraph, what should you check?
options: If you wrote the same words as the original
If you wrote faster than your friend
If you used a blue pen
hints: Check if your copy matches the original.
Look for missing or extra words.
questions.explanation: You should check that your copy matches the original words and is accurate.
questions.misconception: Neat handwriting is only important for exams.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.sub_strand: Sub-Strand 3: Writing /Copying Letters - Small and Capital
indicator.content_standard: B3.4.3.1: Use general skills, strategies and knowledge of letter-sounds to write legibly and boldly
indicator.objective: Use letter-sound relationships to represent most letters in words correctly

skills.description: Identify the letter or letter pattern that makes a specific sound in a word.
Write words correctly by sounding them out and choosing the right letters.
Form both capital and small letters clearly and correctly.
Identify a misspelled word and fix it using letter-sound knowledge.
Ensure that every sound in a spoken word is represented by a letter or letter group when writing.
Say why a particular letter or group of letters was used to spell a word.

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 questions at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4.
misconceptions: Every letter makes only one sound, always.
The name of a letter is the same as the sound it makes.
If a word sounds right, any spelling of those sounds is correct.
Capital and small letters have different sounds.
Legibility doesn't matter if the spelling is correct.
You can spell any word correctly just by guessing.

questions.stem: Which letter makes the first sound in the word 'sun'?
hints: Say the word 'sun' slowly.
Listen to the very first sound.
questions.explanation: The word 'sun' starts with the /s/ sound, which is made by the letter s.
questions.misconception: The name of a letter is the same as the sound it makes.

questions.stem: Which two letters make the /sh/ sound in 'ship'?
hints: Say 'ship' slowly.
The first sound is /sh/.
questions.explanation: The digraph 'sh' makes the /sh/ sound in 'ship'.
questions.misconception: Every letter makes only one sound, always.

questions.stem: Which letter pattern makes the /ai/ sound in 'rain'?
hints: Look for the two vowels together.
The sound is in the middle of the word.
questions.explanation: The vowel digraph 'ai' makes the /ai/ sound in 'rain'.
questions.misconception: Every letter makes only one sound, always.

questions.stem: Which letters spell the word you hear: /k/ /a/ /t/?
hints: The first sound /k/ can be spelled with c.
The middle sound is /a/.
questions.explanation: The sounds /k/ /a/ /t/ make the word 'cat'.
questions.misconception: You can spell any word correctly just by guessing.

questions.stem: Which letters spell the word you hear: /sh/ /o/ /p/?
hints: The first sound is /sh/, spelled 'sh'.
The middle sound is /o/.
questions.explanation: The sounds /sh/ /o/ /p/ spell the word 'shop'.
questions.misconception: If a word sounds right, any spelling of those sounds is correct.

questions.stem: A pupil writes 'kat' for the animal that says 'meow'. What is the correct spelling?
hints: The /k/ sound at the start of 'cat' is spelled with c.
The word is 'cat'.
questions.explanation: The correct spelling is 'cat' because the /k/ sound at the beginning is spelled with 'c'.
questions.misconception: If a word sounds right, any spelling of those sounds is correct.

questions.stem: A pupil writes 'becoz' for the word that means 'for the reason that'. What is the correct spelling?
hints: The word is 'because'.
It has 'au' and 'se' at the end.
questions.explanation: The correct spelling is 'because'. 'Becoz' is a phonetic spelling and is not correct.
questions.misconception: If a word sounds right, any spelling of those sounds is correct.

questions.stem: How many sounds are in the word 'frog'?
hints: Say 'frog' slowly.
/f/ /r/ /o/ /g/ – count each sound.
questions.explanation: The word 'frog' has four sounds: /f/ /r/ /o/ /g/.
questions.misconception: Every letter makes only one sound, always.

questions.stem: Which spelling represents all the sounds in the word you hear: /sh/ /ee/ /p/?
hints: The /sh/ sound is spelled 'sh'.
The /ee/ sound is spelled 'ee'.
questions.explanation: The sounds /sh/ /ee/ /p/ spell 'sheep'.
questions.misconception: If a word sounds right, any spelling of those sounds is correct.

questions.stem: Why do we use 'ck' at the end of 'duck' instead of just 'k'?
options: Because 'ck' is the correct spelling pattern after a short vowel
Because 'k' is not a real letter
hints: After a short vowel sound, we often use 'ck'.
Think of other words like 'back' and 'sock'.
questions.explanation: We use 'ck' at the end of 'duck' because after a short vowel sound, 'ck' is the correct spelling pattern.
questions.misconception: Every letter makes only one sound, always.

questions.stem: Why is the word 'phone' not spelled 'fone' even though it sounds like it starts with /f/?
options: Because 'ph' is a letter pattern that makes the /f/ sound
Because 'f' is not allowed at the start of words
hints: 'Ph' is a digraph that makes the /f/ sound.
Words like 'photo' and 'phone' use 'ph'.
questions.explanation: 'Phone' is spelled with 'ph' because 'ph' is a digraph that makes the /f/ sound in words borrowed from Greek.
questions.misconception: If a word sounds right, any spelling of those sounds is correct.

indicator.subject: English Language
indicator.content_standard: B3.4.4.1: Draw and label simple pictures
indicator.objective: Make a list of objects found in the environment

skills.description: Recognise and name objects found in a specific environment.
Write a list of objects found in a chosen or given environment, using invented or standard spelling.
Review and correct the spelling of listed objects using resources.
Draw a simple picture of an environment and label the objects in it correctly.
Group objects by where they are typically found.
Share the drawn and labelled picture with the class, explaining what was included.

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 questions at difficulty 1, 7 at difficulty 2, 5 at difficulty 3, 3 at difficulty 4.
misconceptions: Any object can be found in any environment.
Spelling does not matter at all when making a list.
A label does not need to point to the specific object.
You cannot draw an environment you have not visited.
Only the teacher can decide what objects are important.

questions.stem: Which of these objects would you find at a bus stop?
hints: Think about what people use while waiting for a bus.
People sit on it.
questions.explanation: A bench is found at a bus stop because people sit on it while waiting for a bus.
questions.misconception: Any object can be found in any environment.

questions.stem: Which of these objects would you find in a classroom?
hints: Think about what the teacher writes on.
It is usually at the front of the class.
questions.explanation: A blackboard is found in a classroom because the teacher writes on it.
questions.misconception: Any object can be found in any environment.

questions.stem: Which object does NOT belong at a market?
hints: A bed is for sleeping.
You would not find a bed at a market.
questions.explanation: A bed does not belong at a market because markets are for buying and selling, not sleeping.
questions.misconception: Any object can be found in any environment.

questions.stem: Which list has all words spelled correctly?
hints: Check each word carefully.
The correct spellings are 'desk', 'chair', 'board'.

questions.stem: Which word is the simple past form of 'walk'?

skills.description: Recognise adverbs in sentences.

questions.stem: Which word does 'beautifully' describe in this sentence? 'She sang beautifully at the party.'
